## RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "RuPaul’s Drag Race and Philosophy Sissy That Thought" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "RuPaul’s Drag Race and Philosophy Sissy That Thought" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Foreword" **·** Gender Performativity — Kate Bornstein's foreword argues that Drag Race is the first pop phenomenon to present drag life and performance as a continuum rather than a one-night bar show, letting viewers watch queens learn their gender 'at the level of values' rather than rules. She frames drag as 'the proudly flamboyant performance of a broken binary' at the heart of postmodern gender theory, pointing to the casual pronoun shifts among contestants as theory in action. Quoting Season 11 winner Yvie Oddly on how different aesthetics show the possibilities of human experience, she casts both RuPaul and the show's contestants as gender royalty who embody values no one grew up with rules for.
- ch. 8 "On Philosophers and Drag Queens" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Allegory of the Cave — The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.
- ch. 9 "Category Is … Speak, Think, Read, Werk" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "1. RuPaul Is a Better Warhol" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Volpert maps Baudrillard's four levels of simulacra onto Drag Race's 'realness': faithful copies (Trinity the Tuck's tucking tutorial, the Season 10 Cher challenge), distorted copies (Sasha Velour and Eureka's nerve, double wig reveals), simulations masking an absent reality (Vanjie's nonsense-word meme, Valentina replacing the judges' verdict with her own fantasy), and the pure hyperreal (Bob the Drag Queen as a queen made entirely by the show, BenDeLaCrème's self-elimination as uniqueness with no referent). She then argues RuPaul is a better Warhol because Warhol merely produced superstars like Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis, profiting while they died unmourned, whereas Ru could compete in her own challenges and returns love to her girls. Realness, she concludes with Ru's Billboard interview and the Season 3 'Pop Art Ball', is always a wink: the facade talking about facade.
- ch. 11 "2. Reading Is Fundamental" **·** John Searle, Plato — McDonald takes Dorian Corey's Paris Is Burning definitions as the foundation for a speech-act analysis of reading versus shade in The Library challenge: reads require uptake from the target and state the insult as at-issue content (Jujubee's 'your grill is fucked up', Latrice's 'illiterate fuck'), while shade smuggles the insult in through implicature and presupposition without needing uptake (Bianca's 'What's your name again?', Aja's Valentina rant), with direct unplayful attacks like Shangela's sugar-daddy rant at Mimi Imfurst as a third category. She tests Plato's superiority theory, Kantian-style incongruity theory and relief theory to argue that a good read works as catharsis, letting queens laugh at the slurs and insecurities that wound them outside the werkroom. Comparing drag lingo to Polari, the secret language of 1950s British gay men, she shows language building solidarity and safety, and leaves the appreciation-versus-appropriation question for fans open.
- ch. 12 "3. What Should a Queen Do" **·** David Hume, John Stuart Mill — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — Sznajder uses All Stars' winner-eliminates-you twist (Naomics Smalls cutting Manila, BenDeLaCrème quitting) to ask what a rational queen should do, grounding instrumental rationality in Hume's 'reason is the slave of the passions'. She runs the Ultimatum Game (Latrice rejecting a 99-to-1 split from Valentina), diminishing marginal utility (Trixie's twenty-dollar tip then and now), expected utility with the pink mystery box, and a Trixie–Shangela Prisoner's Dilemma in which rational utility-maximizers eliminate each other when cooperation would leave both better off. The clash between the normative theory and what queens and experimental subjects actually do leads her to the chapter's 'No Sure Thing Principle': Drag Race's plot twists always add an option game theory never modeled, as BenDeLaCrème saw.
- ch. 13 "4. Is It Immoral to Read Someone to Filth" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, Arthur Schopenhauer, Sigmund Freud, Henri Bergson, Herbert Spencer — The Golden Mean; Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Birnie stages Alexis Michelle's hurt at the Season 9 body-shaming reads against Bianca Del Rio's 'rolodex of hate' to ask whether reading is immoral. He surveys the philosophical ethics of humor — Plato's Philebus on laughter as malicious delight in others' self-ignorance, Hobbes's 'sudden glory', Schopenhauer on why ridicule hurts, the Stoics' ideal of never laughing, Aristotle's eutrapelia as the golden mean between vulgar buffoon and boor, the Spencer–Freud relief theory, and Bergson's laughter as society's corrective — before endorsing the play theory: reads are consensual mock-aggression, verbal sport honed by marginalized black and Latinx ball culture. From this he derives three guidelines (play signals and consent, timing and audience given the show's younger mainstream viewers, openness to challenge) and concludes Katya's bus-stop read of Roxxxy was acceptable while stereotype reads need care.
- ch. 14 "Category Is … The Reality of It All" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "5. RuPaul versus Zarathustra" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God; The Übermensch — The van der Wielen sisters read RuPaul against Nietzsche's Zarathustra: both are outcasts who descend from solitude bearing a spiritual teaching in a marketplace that mocks them, and both announce that inherited values are ungrounded — Zarathustra through the death of God and the call to become the over-man, Ru through 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' and the cosmic life force that makes every identity a costume. But where Zarathustra refuses followers and shuns the people's values, Ru's creed polices female stereotypes (long hair, breasts, heels) and pulls the cart of consumerist values — money, fame, individualism — so that she comes to resemble the priests and wise men Zarathustra condemns. Her openly admitted fakeness and opportunism (the Wigstock 'gender fuck' abandoned for the glamazon brand) leave the chapter asking who flies higher: the tragic free spirit or the pragmatic, honestly dishonest superstar.
- ch. 16 "6. Looking for Realness" **·** Martin Heidegger — Dasein (being-there); Authenticity — Gilpin and Nagy define Drag Race realness as an ongoing process of performative becoming read through Heidegger's Dasein: being-in-the-world and being-with others in the werkroom and Untucked, historicity in the childhood-photo rituals, Jinkx's 'Lunch with RuPaul' and the show's Stonewall and HERstory numbers, and freedom as authenticity, as when Monique Heart describes finding liberation only once she 'put on a wig and a dress'. They then filter this through Goffman's dramaturgy — self-expression versus self-presentation, impression management, and fronts of setting, appearance and manner — arguing that Drag Race collapses Goffman's front stage/backstage divide because backstage vulnerability is itself a required performance. Realness ultimately demands perceived emotional vulnerability plus commercially viable professionalism, and RuPaul alone validates which queens have achieved it.
- ch. 17 "7. The Sublime Sabotage of the Inner Saboteur" **·** Immanuel Kant — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Free Will vs Determinism — Ryan reads Drag Race ontologically through Kant's two forms of the sublime from the Critique of Judgment: the spinning-prop disaster challenge in 'RuPocalypse Now', where queens like Jiggly Caliente are overwhelmed and then rise ('I couldn't let my fall be the death of me'), embodies the mathematically sublime, while Violet Chachki's sixteen-inch corset cinch and oxygen tank on the 'Death Becomes Her' runway dramatizes the dynamically sublime, the recognition of a power in us greater than what threatens us. She argues the queens' testimonies — Chi Chi on growing up poor, black and queer in the Deep South, Kim Chi's fear of her mother, Katya's confessed terror of failure — show free will and authenticity overcoming the determinism of normative structures of gender, race and class. The 'inner saboteur' is overcome through sublime self-overcoming and the solidarity of werkroom heart-to-hearts, even within a capitalist reality-TV machine she checks against the Paris Is Burning appropriation critique.
- ch. 18 "8. Playing with Glitter" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilles Deleuze — Language Games; Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); The Rhizome — This chapter argues that play is Drag Race's deep structure, developed through three philosophers. Wittgenstein's language games explain the show's word-play: 'realness' subverts its own reference to mean the iconic fake, 'herstory' is history played with from a queer perspective, and lip syncs are rule-following whose rules only exist in application. Gadamer's account of play with 'a life of its own' — requiring willingness and openness to the Other — explains why half-hearted players lose, from Porkchop and Tammie's mouthed-nothing lip sync to Gia Gunn and Trixie breaking character in Snatch Game, and why the Evil Twins and makeover challenges are designed to force queens to open up. Deleuze's rhizome (with Bakhtin's carnivalesque) grounds the claim that drag decentering the human — Lil' Poundcake, dragged pancakes, Sharon Needles — and the finale's carnival dissolve the official binaries of male/female and good/bad.
- ch. 19 "Category Is … Drag Race Family Values" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "9. Another Wig Underneath" **·** Judith Butler, Jean-Paul Sartre, Edmund Husserl, Simone de Beauvoir — Gender Performativity; The Look (hell is other people); One Is Not Born a Woman — Cooper argues that the 'vulnerability' Drag Race demands is really a marketable persona, not truth. Working through Butler's Gender Trouble (built on Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes a woman'), she concedes drag reveals gender's imitative structure, but shows it also confirms identity: Latrice Royale's padded 'Natural Woman' lip sync reads as authentic, and trans queens like Peppermint and Gia Gunn use drag to articulate womanhood, with Husserl's intersubjectivity invoked to insist that constructed gender is no less real for not being empirical. Willam's edit-spliced 'I'm not acting' breakdown and Shannel's deliberate wig-doff show honesty becoming inconsequential next to spectacle, while Untucked's Interior Illusions Lounge is framed as Sartre's No Exit hell of unending observation. Against RuPaul's 'born naked' self-help nihilism ('identity is a joke'), she ends warning that the show no longer lets Katya take off the chicken suit.
- ch. 21 "10. And the Rest Is Drag" **·** Judith Butler — Gender Performativity; Heteronormativity — Oliver Norman takes RuPaul's lyric 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' from 'Born Naked' and asks whether its claim that everyone does drag all the time contradicts a show that crowns one drag superstar. Through Judith Butler's Gender Trouble and 'Gender is Burning' he reads drag as a play on gender that can either parody the male/female binary or reinforce it (the Mary Cheney misogyny charge, Michelle Visage's 'show woman not boy' critique, fishy queens like Courtney Act and trans queens like Gia Gunn). He then deploys Erving Goffman's Presentation of Self in Everyday Life: everyday social roles - the doctor's white coat, Alaska's Mae West on Snatch Game, the ideal pageant queen - are scripted performances with 'ideal types,' so the muscle-car seducer in the song is doing unwitting drag. The resolution: 'drag as ontology' is the low everyday form everyone performs, while Drag Race stages the high-art form that consciously fucks with the social script.
- ch. 22 "11. Lip Sync for Your Life" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Perspectivism — Guilel Treiber reads the Season Ten reunion blow-up - Asia O'Hara blaming the show for letting The Vixen walk out, RuPaul insisting people must 'want to meet halfway' - as an unresolvable conflict between two value systems. The show's official 'C.U.N.T.' virtues (charisma, uniqueness, nerve, talent) are individualistic, market-driven values that professionalize drag, while the implicit 'A.S.S.E.' values (acceptance, solidarity, support, empowerment) descend from LGBTQ+ history from Stonewall and Marsha P. Johnson to ACT-UP. Using Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals and its project of the 'revaluation of all values,' he argues values gain worth through conflict rather than progress, so there is no view from nowhere that settles the dispute. Miss Congeniality, the queens' revolt over Valentina's title, and Tammie Brown's clash with RuPaul show the show's magic lies in never deciding between the two - even though market pressure keeps devaluing solidarity.
- ch. 23 "12. The Importance of Being Fabulous" **·** Judith Jarvis Thomson, Peter van Inwagen — Holly Onclin asks whether female impersonation is essential to the art of being a drag queen, testing the folk definition against Drag Race cases like Sasha Velour's bald head, Milk's goatee, the 'Bearded and Beautiful' runway, and the Season Ten super-macho 'Trade' photoshoot. Borrowing the statue-and-clay argument from Judith Jarvis Thomson and L.A. Paul, she argues a drag queen is no more identical to her conventionally feminine attributes than a statue is identical to its clay, so a queen survives losing wigs, padding, and femininity. Using Dominic Lopes's buck-passing theory of art and Peter van Inwagen's point that folk concepts are strictly inaccurate (the sun doesn't literally 'rise'), she classifies drag queens as works in the art of being a drag queen, with female impersonation a contingent convention like paper in origami. Via Kendall Walton's make-believe analysis of representation, she concludes the constant in all drag - from Snatch Game to butch male realness - is the impersonation of celebrity itself, making every queen an Oscar Wilde-style celebrity figure.
- ch. 24 "Category Is … Learning from the Queens" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "13. The Origins of Self-Love" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Plato, bell hooks — The Ethics of Ambiguity; Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Existence Precedes Essence; Buddhism — Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.
- ch. 26 "14. You Want Some Privacy You Better Work" *(no index entry yet)* — Alice Fox argues that identity is self-generated, dynamic, and self-disclosing, so algorithmic 'blackbox personas' that infer traits users never disclosed - like her Boris scenario, where Grindr ads could out a closeted Drag Race fan to his conservative family - wrongly override self-identified identity and enable stereotyping, election manipulation, and persecution of LGBTQ+ people. Drawing on Giorgio Agamben's 'ethical spaces' from Nudities and Samuel von Pufendorf's duty to protect fellow humans ('benefits par excellence'), she claims a moral responsibility to defend everyone's personas against surveillance capitalism, since institutions will not. Drag Race supplies the training manual: queens' mastery of persona creation and transformation - Kim Chi vs Sang-Young Shin, Alaska vs Justin Honard, Snatch Game's celebrity personae that defeat even facial recognition - teaches obfuscation, consistency, and fluidity (Finstas, ad blockers, varied routines) so algorithms cannot tell the authentic from the gag.
- ch. 27 "15. Fire WERK with Me" *(no index entry yet)* — Carolina Are examines the Facebook group Fire WERK With Me, where fans mash up Drag Race and Twin Peaks, as a 'sub-subculture' whose memes, shade, and catchphrases ('Miss Vanjie,' 'Stop relying on that body' aimed at Laura Palmer's body) only double insiders can decode. She argues that the show's diffusion of drag language from Paris Is Burning, its meta-commentary on reality-TV formats like America's Next Top Model, and the Doppelganger motif shared with Lynch's show (drag queen in and out of drag vs good and evil Agent Cooper) exemplify meta-reality and convergence culture: fans become producers whose meme creation co-authors the shows' meaning. The group's 'meta-shade' - such as Alyssa Edwards's 'Girl, look how orange you fucking look' read redirected at Kyle MacLachlan's tanned evil Doppelganger - shows online fandom as performative, educational interpretation rather than trolling.
- ch. 28 "16. Death Becomes Her" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Epicurus, Martin Heidegger, Socrates, Plato — Death Is Nothing to Us; The Myth of Sisyphus; Existence Precedes Essence; Being-Toward-Death — Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.

## Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Rush and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction frames Rush as a 'thinking man's band': a cult favorite deliberately outside the mainstream whose fusion of virtuosic, structurally complex music with lyrics on social, scientific, and historical themes triggers both fierce devotion and passionate hatred in listeners. It sketches the band's history from its 1968 Toronto cover-band beginnings through Neil Peart's 1974 arrival and the album-oriented-rock success of Moving Pictures ('Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight'), arguing that Rush's lasting achievements come when thoughtful lyrics and progressive/hard music work together. It invites readers to treat each essay as one voice in an ongoing dialogue and to accept that being different, like Rush, is not a bad thing.
- ch. 6 "PART I - To the Margin of Error" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down" *(no index entry yet)* — Auxier interleaves a memoir of sneaking off to Rush's 1977 Memphis concert (the Halloween-weekend ruse with his friend Brice, beers at J-Wags Lounge, the first hangover, and the setlist from 'Bastille Day' through '2112') with a philosophical defense of the band. He rejects the charge that Rush is a vehicle for Ayn Rand's objectivism, arguing Rand was a novelist with 'philosophical moments' whose analogy-built system is not philosophy, and that Peart quickly outgrew her influence by Moving Pictures. Working from Susanne Langer, he claims Rush assimilates lyrics to music (so 'Tom Sawyer' and 'Limelight' need no poetic standard), that music is a 'virtualization' of time creating the illusion of felt life, and that Rush's live processed sounds are second-order virtualizations whose only real test is whether the music is good.
- ch. 8 "Coda" **·** Cultural Hegemony — Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.
- ch. 9 "The Heart and Mind United" **·** The Dialectic — Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.
- ch. 10 "No Heart to Lie" **·** Authenticity — Reuland uses YouTube drum covers of 'The Body Electric', 'Subdivisions', and 'YYZ' to analyze Rush's 'aesthetic of replicability': songs built as artifacts meant to be reproduced note-for-note, signaled by literal codes like the Morse-code intro to 'YYZ' and the binary '1001001' the android of 'The Body Electric' must crack to become human. He explains why critics deride this anti-expressive virtuosity by way of Amiri Baraka's racial coding of technique, Pierre Bourdieu's account of how 'natural' taste is legitimated while studied learning bears class stigma, and Mary Bucholtz's picture of nerds as hyper-white; the fans' literal meritocracy parodies the information economy's promise that skill converts directly into success. Finally he reads 'Limelight' as Rush's skepticism toward performance as a 'gilded cage' of inauthenticity, so that play-along videos recode performance as self-improvement that cannot be faked.
- ch. 11 "He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes" **·** Plato, Walter Benjamin, Aristotle — Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms — Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.
- ch. 12 "PART II - The Ebb and Flow of Tidal Fortune" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Enjoy These Moments" **·** Epictetus — The Dichotomy of Control; Living in the Present — Earleywine argues that Rush's lyrics trained a generation in the core moves of cognitive-behavioral therapy, an idea he traces back to Epictetus before Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck rediscovered it against Freudian orthodoxy. He maps specific distortions onto specific songs: 'Witch Hunt' on dichotomous labeling, 'Distant Early Warning' ('black and whites of youth') on all-or-nothing thinking, 'Emotion Detector' on emotional reasoning, 'Vital Signs' and 'Totem' on thoughts altering perception, and 'Subdivisions' ('Conform or be cast out') as realistic critique rather than maladaptive thought. The final step, acting on examined values and savoring the present ('Time Stand Still', 'The Camera Eye', 'Chain Lightning'), makes the songs the incarnation of their own advice: just listen.
- ch. 14 "Smashing Critics’ Pumpkins" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms — Reisch reconstructs the rock-critical case against Rush ('pretentious', 'ridiculous', Greg Kot's jibe that Peart drums 'like he's working out a calculus formula') as resting on an implicit Platonism: the Forms fix what a 'real' rock'n'roll band is, so a band mixing rock with philosophy, literature, and mathematical precision seems to violate the metaphysical grain of the universe rather than merely disappoint a taste. He explains the Forms through Plato's trees and the Form of the song ('La Villa Strangiato' and 'Happy Birthday'), reads Jack Black's 'one atom' praise of Peart as mathematics-as-highest-knowledge, and treats the 'Aristocrats' joke and UFO mocking Geddy Lee as incongruity humor at kinds illicitly combined. Dropping the Platonic metaphysics of kinds collapses the critics' syllogism into a bare insistence that different is bad, which is the revenge Gene Simmons ('What kind of band is Rush? It's Rush.') and Billy Corgan ('they just don't fit in a neat box') already delivered.
- ch. 15 "Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Henry David Thoreau — Existence Precedes Essence; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Walden (deliberate living) — Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.
- ch. 16 "Hope" **·** Lucretius, Epicurus — On the Nature of Things; Atomism; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia); Faith and Reason — Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.
- ch. 17 "Tallying the Total" **·** Jacques Derrida — Deconstruction — Kreuger applies Derrida's 'Differance' to how Rush gets valued: Hugh Syme's starman, pentagram, and bunnies are signs whose meaning defers down a chain, so no description of Geddy Lee ever touches the thing itself, and the band's twenty-four gold albums (economic value) never settle the contested question of cultural value that critics deny and fans affirm. Time defers value too: 'Time Stand Still' and the concert ticket sell a moment already gone, bootlegs and leaks chase the unrepeatable experience, and radio distance once hid songs like '2112' from value. 'The Spirit of Radio' carries the thesis in its own lyric, 'bearing a gift beyond price, almost free', where 'the words of the profits' on the studio walls measure sold value against integrity, and deferral finally emerges as Derrida's 'condition of possibility' that lets Rush's cultural value recover through Colbert, Rock Band, and I Love You, Man.
- ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" **·** Aristotle, Albert Camus, Socrates, Jean-Paul Sartre — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Absurd; Faith and Reason — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.
- ch. 19 "PART III - I Want to Look Around Me Now" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 20 "A Single, Perfect Sphere" **·** David Chalmers, René Descartes — The Hard Problem of Consciousness; Mind–Body Dualism; The Apollonian and the Dionysian — Reads Rush's 'Hemispheres' as a correction to Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: Apollo's gifts of reason leave the people joyless, Dionysus's release into passion leaves them starving in winter, and Cygnus is made god of Balance because human nature thinks and feels at once. Against Descartes's two substances and the 'Robots Plus' picture, the author argues feeling is not supernatural icing on a machine but how survival-minded organisms stay in phenomenal contact with the world, so physicalism needs deepening rather than a nonphysical mind.
- ch. 21 "“I Want to Look Around Me Now”" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Feminism — Charts Rush's gradual saturation with synthesizers, sequencers, and electronic percussion from 'Subdivisions' and 'Distant Early Warning' to 'Time Stand Still,' explaining the adoption through Wajcman's gradual-modification model and feminist analyses of technology as a male skill domain — including de Beauvoir's point that technical prowess underwrites virility, which the author applies to Rush fans' valorizing of the trio's chops. It closes by casting the band's handling of music technology as Bourdieu's habitus, granting Rush 'relative autonomy' from the hi-tech pressures of the 1980s.
- ch. 22 "Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do" *(no index entry yet)* — A music-theoretic account of how Rush's music signifies only for competent listeners: the vocal pauses of 'Entre Nous' paint separation while its related keys paint unity, the 'Oriental riff' and pentatonics of 'A Passage to Bangkok' and 'Tai Shan' evoke nonspecific otherness, space-music textures open '2112' and 'Cygnus X-1,' and tritones brand evil in 'Witch Hunt,' 'The Necromancer,' and 'YYZ.' It ends by noting the irony that Rush uses its own electric voice to portray the bad guys, concluding with 'Entre Nous' that otherness and difference can be synthesized into a greater whole.
- ch. 23 "Does Rush Offer a Way Out" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, René Descartes — The Private Language Argument; Language Games; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Brain in a Vat — Uses Rush's 1980s lyrics about facades and trust — 'Limelight''s strangers, 'Show Don't Tell''s refusal to take things on faith, 'War Paint''s lying mirror, and the synthesizer as an instrument that can fake any other sound — to stage skepticism about other minds, running from Descartes's cogito through solipsism and behaviorism. Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box and private-language argument dissolve the inner/outer confusion as a grammatical one, and 'Turn the Page' supplies the way out of the fly-bottle: nothing survives a vacuum, and with other people all we can do is be reminded.
- ch. 24 "Counterparts Lee’s Voice and Peart’s Drums" **·** Walter Benjamin — Takes the rock critics' vilification of Geddy Lee's 'shrill' voice versus fans' devotion to Neil Peart's drumming and explains the fan's pleasure through Roland Barthes's 'cruising': the listener repeatedly works through 'Tom Sawyer,' 'Between the Wheels,' and 'Animate' for the fresh catch of Peart's fills, which act as the Benjamin-style distraction by which the distracted mass absorbs the work of art. Lee's voice thus becomes an integral counterpart — the mundane the listener cruises past to reach the hooks that reward the quest.
- ch. 25 "PART IV - The Blacksmith and the Artist" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Straining the Limits of Machine and Man" **·** Martin Heidegger, Karl Marx, Aristotle — The Question Concerning Technology; Alienation — Reads Peart's ambivalence about technology through Heidegger's techne as revealing and Marx's account of the worker: 'Working Man''s no-time-for-living day, '2112''s priests whose 'great computers' smash the protagonist's guitar, 'Manhattan Project''s Oppenheimer problem, and 'Test for Echo''s 'video vertigo.' Against Ellul-style autonomous technology the chapter insists Peart believes we still control our machines, and it ends with Rush mastering its own studio gear — and the motorcycle of Ghost Rider as the machine that carries Peart through grief.
- ch. 27 "Humanism Needs Its Evangelists, Too" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Faith and Reason; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Treats Snakes & Arrows ('Far Cry,' 'Armor and Sword,' 'Faithless') as secular humanism stung by resurgent fundamentalism, and reads Peart's revolutionary trilogy — 'Beneath, Between and Behind,' 'Bastille Day,' 'A Farewell to Kings' — as Enlightenment humanism already anxious about its own decline. The core argument is rhetorical: Rush deliberately clothes humanist content in sacred and mystical language ('Something for Nothing''s Lord's Prayer motif, 'Jacob's Ladder''s storm read through Spinoza's God-as-nature and the experience of the sublime) because humanism needs evangelists who inspire wonder rather than mere argument.
- ch. 28 "There’s Something Here that’s as Strong as Life" **·** Robert Nozick, John Stuart Mill, Adam Smith — Ethical Egoism; The Minimal State; On Liberty — Argues Rush's lyrics cohere as libertarianism: Rand's rational self-interest in 'Anthem' and 'Something for Nothing,' Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument and Hayek's knowledge problem behind '2112' and 'The Trees,' Mill's 'experiments in living' in 'Witch Hunt' and 'Nobody's Hero,' and market-enabled tolerance and cosmopolitanism in 'Heresy,' 'Territories,' and 'Tai Shan.' Like Cygnus resolving Apollo and Dionysus, libertarianism takes the best of left and right, with individualism the constant running through Peart's career.
- ch. 29 "Hardly Rand-y Peart" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel — Utopia and Dystopia — Sets '2112' against Rand's Anthem to vindicate Peart's claim to be 'no one's disciple': both are egalitarian dystopias, but where Rand's Equality 7-2521 is a born transgressor who escapes to rebuild civilization, Rush's nameless protagonist is an indoctrinated conformist whose smashed guitar leaves him in Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and despair. Read as a romance of social disillusionment tinged with Nietzsche's joyful wisdom and gift-giving virtue, the song treats egalitarian leveling as nihilism and overturns Anthem's optimistic egoism — so it is hardly Rand-y at all.
- ch. 30 "Outro" **·** Cultural Hegemony — Asks how Rush is Canadian: CanCon radio quotas, the band's hybrid of British prog and Anglo-American hard rock, and McLuhan's 'flexible' national character, before a detailed musical reading of 'The Trees' — its 6/8-to-4/4 shifts, countertenor outburst, and woodpecker solos — as an aural 'Royal Commission' that may satirize legislated equality like Canadian content regulations defending against US media dominance. Bakhtin's monologic worldview frames the Oaks, and the chapter closes with later Canadian signs from the inukshuk cover of Test for Echo to Trailer Park Boys.

## Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail

- ch. 1 "Globalization and Contemporary Art" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** William James — The Meaning of Life; The Will to Believe — In this Foreword, John Rousmaniere argues that sailing's 'numinous' moments — like his own experience of stillness on a becalmed ketch mid-Atlantic, when the skipper cut the engine and the crew felt suspended between sky and sea — are paths to genuine philosophical truths, not embarrassing flights of fancy. He enlists William James's 'Varieties of Religious Experience' and James's nautical metaphor for free will (the passenger who volunteers to take the helm) to argue that such mystical feelings can 'team up' with reason rather than opposing it. He insists mystery and craft must work together: piety is no substitute for seamanship (Shelley drowned in an unseaworthy boat), yet competence and numinous experience nurture each other.
- ch. 7 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — The Unexamined Life; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Patrick Goold's introduction frames the whole volume by applying Socrates' 'ti esti?' question to sailing — asking what sailing essentially is — and concludes there is no timeless essence (counterexamples like iceboating and windsurfing defeat every definition), so the reflective sailor, like the philosopher, must proceed without certainty. He then invokes Aristotle's notion of telos/final cause to ask what draws people to sailing's danger and discomfort, previewing the essays: Part I finds self-knowledge and virtue in facing peril (Stillwaggon, Jobson, Lebens on eudaimonia, Hutch), while later parts treat sailing as a path to flourishing through Zen, Stoicism, Spinoza, aesthetics, and physics.
- ch. 8 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** The Meaning of Life — Jack Stillwaggon recounts his 1965 voyage as a seventeen-year-old crewing the replica HMS Bounty from New York to Florida — fires aboard, thirty-five-foot seas, seasickness, a crewman nearly left to die — and asks why modern people abandon comfort to court danger and discomfort. His answer is that we face the sea to prove something to ourselves about our worth and abilities: like the paratrooper who stays under fire or the soldier earning his 'red badge of courage,' the survived ordeal becomes a cherished high point that adds meaning to an otherwise 'silly' comfortable existence, leaving him more at peace and expecting more of himself thereafter.
- ch. 11 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Gary Jobson, writing from a long racing career with no philosophical vocabulary, offers practical wisdom on generating the inner strength and courage to win: focus on the task at hand rather than the outcome, visualize the race, stay calm under adversity, and 'have fun.' Through stories of Buddy Melges, Ted Turner's Fastnet, and Dennis Conner's America's Cup comeback, plus his own collegiate turnaround under coach Graham Hall, he argues resolve (not luck) drives comebacks, and he treats leadership, mentorship, patience, and consistency as cultivated traits of character — an implicit account of the virtues a competitive sailor must build.
- ch. 12 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Aristotle, Søren Kierkegaard — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Golden Mean — Crista Lebens narrates a C-Scow sail on an inland lake — preparing the boat, casting off, coming about, capsizing, returning to the pier — as a journey toward Aristotelian eudaimonia (human flourishing). She argues sailing demands phronesis (practical wisdom) as body-knowledge, that coming about requires the Greek 'middle path' between being 'in irons' and capsizing, and that competence 'cannot be faked' so sailing forces one to live 'in truth' (via Werth's and Kierkegaard's account of the crowd 'in untruth'). Using Borgmann's device/thing distinction, she casts the sailboat as a 'thing' that calls forth skilled engagement, unlike the powerboat as a 'device' of consumption, and links truth to the beauty of a well-trimmed sail.
- ch. 13 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Laozi — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Meaning of Life — Richard Hutch develops a phenomenology of 'moral presence' — an assertion of human integrity in the face of despair when nothing else can be done — from the autobiographies of solo ocean sailors. He identifies three pathways: technical finesse (Robin Knox-Johnston, whose 'God helps those who help themselves' pragmatism Hutch reads as the Taoist wu-wei, action through non-action), cosmic quest (Bernard Moitessier's mystical communion, slingshot instead of radio), and personal test (Kay Cottee's epiphany near Cape Horn, transforming terror into fascination via Otto's mysterium tremendum et fascinans). He frames sailing as tragic-comic drama with technology as a deus ex machina, arguing that doing nothing is often the zenith of value.
- ch. 14 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Dogen, The Buddha — Zen Buddhism; Buddhism — James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.
- ch. 16 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; Premeditatio Malorum — Gregory and Tod Bassham argue Stoicism is the seaman's philosophy of agency, teaching a clear-eyed grasp of what we can control, influence, or not control at all. Using Epictetus's play metaphor and 'you will fetter my leg but not my will,' Seneca and Marcus Aurelius on fear, they map three techniques onto sailing: cheerful resignation (Gerry Spiess righting Yankee Girl, Shackleton's James Caird crew laughing amid the Southern Ocean), self-sufficiency (splicing lines, emotional independence on a cramped boat), and negative visualization / premeditatio malorum (practicing docking under sail, imagining lost rudders). Skip Allen scuttling Wildflower and Dinelli's endurance illustrate the trichotomy of control and freedom of mind.
- ch. 17 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Heraclitus, Baruch Spinoza, Parmenides, Derek Parfit — Everything Flows / Logos; Ship of Theseus; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Steven Horrobin sorts sailors into three kinds — the cultural-iconography poser, the racer chasing a land-based prize, and the 'sailor of the third kind' for whom the open-ended voyage is an end in itself — and argues the third lives 'in the shadow of Heraclitus.' Against the substantialist ontology of Parmenides and Democritus (persons and boats as fixed things), he defends a process view in which everything, like a wave, is a passing fluctuation of one universal substance; citing Spinoza, self-becoming is the super-process reflecting itself. He dissolves the Ship of Theseus paradox (and Parfit's parallel-ship version) by making identity the continuity of a process's function rather than fixed parts, arguing the violent, corroding life of a boat reveals the flux beneath apparently stable things.
- ch. 18 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** The Meaning of Life — Nicholas Hayes describes the Chicago-to-Mackinac race, cataloguing its boats (passenger trains, Model Ts, booster rockets, retreads), its nights (darkest, stormy, breathless, velvet, brightest), and its sailor-types (tweener, superhero, teammate, yogi, minister, salt) to build toward a claim about an 'awareness shift.' He argues that far from land and its electric lights, sailors slip into a place where the emotional self meets 'the most real and primitive world' and confronts a new relationship with time, culminating on the 'day of hope' in the realization that one controls nothing but oneself and owns nothing but one's time — 'Everything is now' — a transcendence he loosely likens to skepticism and enlightenment themes.
- ch. 20 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Andy Clark, David Chalmers, René Descartes — The Extended Mind; Mind–Body Dualism — Steve Matthews uses windsurfing to analyze Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' — the loss of self-awareness in skilled action between boredom and anxiety — and argues its intensity comes from 'integration,' where footstraps and harness bind sailor to kit so the equipment becomes 'an extension of oneself.' Invoking Descartes' own admission that mind and body form a unity (not merely pilot in a vessel), he applies Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis: the windsurfer's kit and body form a coupled cognitive system, so 'I' extends to include the gear. He distinguishes true flow from mere goal-satisfaction (rejecting the ocean-cruiser's landfall as flow) and, via Velleman, locates flow's value in intrinsically motivated action that is its own end.
- ch. 21 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Dewey — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Experience and Education; Free Will vs Determinism — Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.
- ch. 22 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Golden Mean — Jesse Steinberg and Michael Stuckart distinguish instrumental from intrinsic value (using Frankena's list) across sailing's gear, knowledge, and aesthetics, then argue via Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that sailing is a route to eudaimonia through the cultivation of virtue. They show sailing exemplifies courage as the golden mean between cowardice and foolhardiness (deciding whether to go out in twenty-knot winds, judging teen solo circumnavigators), being hard-working (the mean between laziness and workaholism), and cleverness (jury-rigging, navigation). They contend sailing demands a broader, deeper range of virtues than golf, bowling, or power-boating, making it an especially rich — though not the only — path to a flourishing, happy life.
- ch. 23 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(no index entry yet)* — Sebastian Kuhn asks whether Einstein's relativity bears on sailing and answers that its philosophical underpinnings do. He shows sailors constantly juggle multiple reference frames (water, ground, boat, stars) and that Galilean relativity — the laws of nature holding in every inertial frame — suffices to understand tacking, apparent wind, and current, using the example of a boat drifting with a river feeling becalmed. He then explains special relativity's constant speed of light forcing revised notions of simultaneity, length, and time (illustrated with GPS light-pulse timing), and general relativity's curved spacetime (parallel ships meeting at the pole, time running slower low on the mast), noting GPS must correct for both effects to fix a sailor's position.
- ch. 25 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Zeno of Elea, Plato — Zeno's Paradoxes; Theory of Forms — John D. Norton poses three sailing paradoxes — how a wind-powered boat sails into the wind, faster than the wind, and whether 'making its own wind' makes it a perpetual-motion machine — echoing Zeno's paradoxes of motion and measure as engines of philosophical clarity. He resolves the first two by rejecting the causal truism that an effect cannot exceed or oppose its cause (the wind's force, resolved into drive and beam components against a resistant hull, is the real cause), using this to argue causal principles are elastic labels grafted onto science, never laws it must obey. For the third he builds an idealized wind-turbine boat thought experiment showing created-wind energy is exactly consumed by counter-force, and debates James Brown's Platonist view (that thought experiments 'see' laws in a Platonic realm, like grasping the ideal triangle) against his own deflationary view that they are merely picturesque argument.
- ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** Aristotle, Maimonides, Friedrich Nietzsche — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Death of God; Free Will vs Determinism — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- ch. 27 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" **·** The Meaning of Life — Hilaire Belloc's essay 'The Channel,' serving as the volume's literary epilogue, argues that the 'glamour in the mind' and 'freshness of beginnings' our ancestors knew can be recovered by using the body simply and hardly — best of all by sailing a small boat under twenty-five feet across the Channel. Narrating his own first crossing from the Goodwins to Calais, drifting on the ebb and waiting for the flood, he presents sailing as the 'old drama by which the soul of a healthy man is kept alive,' teaching terror, salvation, exultation, and repose as lived realities rather than mere words. He closes by withholding the tale of the stormy return, imploring readers not to hear of it but to sail it themselves.
- ch. 28 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" *(notes)*

## Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
