## Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Table of Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Series Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Bad Batch" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "IntroductionnoteSet" *(no index entry yet)* — Editors Eberl and Decker explain why this follow-up to their 2005 Star Wars and Philosophy volume is organized chronologically across the films, The Clone Wars, Rebels, The Bad Batch, Rogue One, Solo, and The Mandalorian. They situate the book against Disney's 2012 canon reset, the TV revival, and the 'Fandom Menace' backlash against diverse casting, arguing Star Wars holds a mirror up to the culture wars. The introduction previews the volume's questions, from natural law and the ethics of the Force to droid love, hope in dark times, and whether you should eat Baby Yoda.
- ch. 8 "Part I EPISODES I–III" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "“Now This Is Podracing!”" **·** Laozi, Zhuangzi — Taoism (Daoism); Wu Wei (effortless action); Yin and Yang — Johnson reads The Phantom Menace as having distinctly Daoist flavors: Shmi's 'you cannot stop the change any more than you can stop the suns from setting,' the Naboo-Gungan 'symbiont circle,' and midi-chlorian symbiosis all express the Daoist unity of opposites and the constant flow of change. He argues Qui-Gon Jinn acts as a Daoist sage practicing wu wei — 'concentrate on the moment,' 'another solution will present itself' — while nearly everyone else in the film makes wrong predictions and grasps at outcomes. Even Anakin's accidental 'Oops!' victory over the Droid Control Ship is presented as success without trying, the practical meaning of 'Do or do not. There is no try.'
- ch. 10 "Bringing Balance to the Force" **·** David Hume — The Naturalistic Fallacy; Is–Ought Problem; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Harter argues that Revenge of the Sith manipulates audiences into fearing the medical technology that saves Anakin on Mustafar, portraying his prosthetic transformation into Vader as horrifying when in real bioethical terms saving a burn victim with ventilators, feeding tubes, and prosthetics is something we applaud. He diagnoses Lucas's framing as the naturalistic fallacy (what is natural is good), grounded in Hume's is-ought gap, and flags the mirror-image 'technological fallacy' of assuming enhancement like General Grievous's cyborg body must be good. The chapter concludes that technology is value-neutral and its worth depends on the context of use — which is what it means for Anakin and Luke, both maimed and prosthetized, to 'bring balance to the Force.'
- ch. 11 "Jedi and Sith Ethics “Similar in Almost Every Way”" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Natural Law; Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Shea, Archer, and Banning argue that Star Wars' moral framework is natural law ethics in the tradition of Aristotle and Aquinas: the light side humanizes (Force healing, Qui-Gon's spirit surviving death, Grogu curing Greef Karga) while the dark side dehumanizes (Maul's bisection, Palpatine's deformation, Anakin's disfigurement), and apparent counterexamples like Luke's lost hand always trace back to prior vice. Aquinas's claim that the most general principles of natural law can never be blotted out explains why 'there is still good in' Vader and why redemption is always possible. The Jedi and Sith codes embody opposed views of human nature — relational, altruistic, and accepting of mortality versus atomistic, egoistic, and obsessed with cheating death through midi-chlorian manipulation.
- ch. 12 "A New Hope Inclusive Representation in the Galaxy" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler — Woman as the Other; Feminism; Objectification — Lakka uses Beauvoir's The Second Sex (the Mother/Mistress dichotomy, woman tied to nature and denied transcendence) and Butler on the mother-daughter separation to argue that Revenge of the Sith reduces Padme from the active senator and warrior of the first two prequels to a pregnant figure confined to her apartment, whose death gets read as martyrdom or even 'mom-shaming.' She reads Anakin's jealousy, interrogations ('Obi-Wan's been here, has he not?'), and Force-choke on Mustafar — explicitly paralleled with Othello and Desdemona — as an abusive relationship, suggesting Padme's death may be a feminicide. The deleted Petition of the 2000 scenes, and successors like Rey, Ahsoka, Rose Tico, and Jyn Erso, point toward the inclusive representation the galaxy still needs.
- ch. 13 "Part II CLONE WARS, REBELS, AND THE BAD BATCH" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Moral Autonomy" **·** Michel Foucault — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Free Will vs Determinism — Challans reads the clone army as a Foucauldian project of discipline: Kaminoan reconditioning, punishment of 'aberrance,' and the inhibitor chips produce the 'docile bodies' that made Order 66 executable, with Palpatine's propaganda framing the Jedi as traitors to supply its legitimacy. Milgram's obedience experiments explain why most clones became 'agentic' executioners, while the rare independence of Rex, Fives, and Tup in the Umbara arc — 'we are not a bunch of unthinking droids!' — shows how fragile moral autonomy is. He concludes that military competence itself requires independent judgment, as his Delta Force versus Rangers comparison after Mogadishu illustrates, making Rex the exemplar of the moral autonomy the chips were designed to destroy.
- ch. 15 "“We Were Trained to Be Keepers of the Peace, not Soldiers”" **·** Cornel West — Democracy; Class Struggle — Shakibnia reads The Clone Wars through Cornel West's three dogmas threatening democracy — free-market fundamentalism, aggressive militarism, escalating authoritarianism — and Chomsky's critique of inequality: Senator Halle Burtoni is a deliberate Halliburton/Cheney nod, and the banking-deregulation vote in 'Heroes on Both Sides' mirrors the US military-industrial complex. He argues the Separatist people's movement ('Corporations do not rule us!') was justified in seeking self-determination, while 'Sabotage' shows the Jedi losing legitimacy by becoming 'military weapons' — underpaid Temple worker Jackar Bowmani's squalid housing indicts the Republic's class divide. Ahsoka's departure and her maxim that 'it's every citizen's duty to challenge their leaders' model the accountability movement (like Black Lives Matter) that the Jedi failed to be.
- ch. 16 "You're Our Only Hope" **·** Charles W. Mills, Immanuel Kant, Peter Singer — The Racial Contract; Humanity as an End in Itself; Speciesism — Bein asks whether the galaxy's treatment of droids — Chopper's second-class status on the Ghost, Wuher's 'we don't serve their kind here,' the slur 'clanker' — amounts to racism. He argues Chopper and even the treacherous Hondo pass Kant's moral-agency litmus test and satisfy Singer's preference utilitarianism, making them persons whose abuse is wrong. Borrowing Charles W. Mills's argument that race is a social construct located in institutions rather than biology, he applies critical race theory to Star Wars: droid detectors, droids' legal status as property, and AP-5's 'no one rescues droids' internalized racism show anti-droid prejudice is structural 'situation normal,' so dismantling it takes political work, not just better arguments.
- ch. 17 "“Good Soldiers Follow Orders”" **·** Harry Frankfurt, John Locke, Aristotle — Second-Order Desires (personhood); Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — Brace uses Aristotle on numerical versus specific sameness, Locke's memory theory, and above all Frankfurt's second-order desires to argue the Jango Fett clones are distinct persons despite shared DNA: Fives's and Echo's accumulated memories and choices individuate them, and the Bad Batch's personalized quarters display what Yoda means by 'very different, each one of you are.' Frankfurt's 'wanton' frames Wrecker's impulsive Hulking, while Order 66 distinguishes freedom of action from freedom of will — Rex resists the chip's compulsion but cannot act on his second-order volition, so he never loses personhood. Crosshair's reveal that his chip was long removed recasts his loyalty to the Empire as a freely chosen (if immoral) second-order volition, his right as a person.
- ch. 18 "Do Not Ask Him to Be Rational" **·** Immanuel Kant, Iris Marion Young — Autonomy of the Will; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — The Rochas argue the Jedi Council's conduct across the Temple-bombing arc — letting Tarkin take jurisdiction, then expelling Ahsoka and handing her over for trial on flimsy evidence in 'The Wrong Jedi' — exposes a Jedi ethics corrupted by deference to hierarchy. Ahsoka's decision to walk away enacts Kantian moral autonomy (self-legislation) against the Council's heteronomy, while Anakin, despite sharing her doubts, seeks another master in Palpatine and falls into heteronomy instead. Using Baier's account of trust and Iris Marion Young on social roles, they contend the Jedi's repudiation of feeling was the real failure: emotions like Ahsoka's fear rightly guided her to distrust the Council and even to trust Ventress.
- ch. 19 "Something's Missing" *(no index entry yet)* — Malloy tests three theories of art against Sabine Wren's graffiti and the Syndulla Kalikori: representation fails (her work is stylized beyond recognition and the collaborative Kalikori depicts nothing), expression fails (generations of makers make the Kalikori's expressive unity mysterious), and the institutional 'artworld' theory fails because Thrawn's curatorial authority destroys what it preserves — ripping a phoenix tag off its wall or displaying a still-growing Kalikori strips them of meaning. He concludes that defining art by any single feature (content, creation, or institutional context) is doomed, since Sabine's and Hera's works both are and are not art on every theory, and philosophy must keep searching for why they count as art.
- ch. 20 "The End" **·** David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; The A-Series and B-Series of Time; Free Will vs Determinism — Berghofer uses the Rebels episode 'A World Between Worlds' to ask whether Ezra changed the past when he pulled Ahsoka out of her duel with Vader, arguing that past-changing time travel breeds contradiction: the grandfather paradox looms over his attempt to save Kanan ('if he is taken out of this moment, you all die'), and on the Lewis-style consistent model Ezra caused but never changed the past. He surveys presentism, eternalism, and the growing block to locate Star Wars' metaphysics of time — Ezra's travel rules out presentism, and the Mortis god's 'the future, by its nature, can be changed' fits a growing block with an open future. Anakin's tragedy of acting to prevent prophesied events and thereby causing them frames the whole analysis.
- ch. 21 "Part III ROGUE ONE AND SOLO" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "“Rebellions Are Built on Hope!”" **·** Bernard Williams, Immanuel Kant — Utilitarianism; Integrity Against Utilitarianism; Moral Luck; Deontology — Eberl asks whether Galen Erso, who knowingly resumed work on the Death Star while planting its exhaust-port flaw, is culpable for the deaths on Jedha, Scarif, and Alderaan. A utilitarian defense (his flaw net-saved the galaxy, per the negative-responsibility principle applied to the Death Star II 'Clerks' debate) founders on moral luck — everything depended on Luke's impossible shot — while Bernard Williams's integrity objection, via the chemist 'George' case, condemns his betrayal of conscience. The chapter finally deploys Thomistic tools for cooperation with evil: because Galen's contribution was mediate and remote (Tarkin ordered the firing, the gunners pulled the triggers, Leia's defiance provoked Alderaan's destruction) and the weapon would have been built without him, his collusion is justified by the reasonable hope — the 'new hope' — of the Death Star's destruction.
- ch. 23 "Trust in the Force of Others" **·** John Dewey, Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo — Democracy as a Way of Life; Humanity as an End in Itself; Just War Theory — MacMullan reads Rogue One through Dewey's 'Creative Democracy': democracy is not Senates or constitutions but a lived faith in one's neighbors, and the Empire's deepest violence is the distrust it breeds — Cassian executing Tivik, Saw torturing Bodhi with Bor Gullet, Draven ordering Galen's assassination. Cassian violates Kant's Formula of Humanity by reducing Tivik to a container of secrets, and the Rebels' dirty-war methods strain Augustine's just-war conditions, yet Chirrut and Baze's friendship ('I'm not alone. I have you!') becomes the seed of recovered trust that stays Cassian's finger on the trigger at Eadu. The Yavin council's free debate and the Tantive IV corridor relay — Rebels dying to pass the Death Star plans hand to hand past Vader — enact Dewey's claim that democracy lives in personal attitudes and neighborly trust: rebellions are built on hope in each other.
- ch. 24 "“You Like Me because I'm a Scoundrel”" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Richard Rorty, Michel de Montaigne, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Pragmatism; Que sais-je? (Montaigne's skepticism) — Decker asks whether Han Solo can truly evade philosophy, opening with Aristotle's Protrepticus proof that one must do philosophy either way. Han's demystifying skepticism ('no mystical energy field controls my destiny,' 'That's not how the Force works!') is paired with Wittgenstein's Tractatus, which dismisses traditional philosophical questions as senseless and offers therapy for the philosophical itch, and with Montaigne's skepticism about book learning — though Han's orphan scrumrat education exposes the class privilege behind Montaigne's 'sweet pillow' of ignorance. His anti-authoritarianism is read through Emerson (via Cornel West) and Rorty's pragmatism as anti-authoritarianism: build philosophical reflections around political hopes rather than foundations, which is why the 'everyday people' of the Disney+ era, epitomized by the scoundrel, break the spell of the Skywalker grand narrative.
- ch. 25 "Humanoids and Droids Having Sex" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love — Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.
- ch. 26 "Beyond the Whimsy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Jowitt argues that L3-37's activism in Solo ('Droid rights! We are sentient!') exposes a real problem in philosophy of law: the Coronet Spaceport's 'all droids must be registered' treats sentients as property, and Austin's legal positivism (law as command backed by sanction, which he says also describes Enfys Nest's threats) cannot condemn this. Building a Kantian natural-law argument, he claims that if droids like L3, C-3PO, BB-8, and D-O are rational beings covered by the categorical imperative, then any rule classifying them as property cannot give us a reason to obey it and so is not valid law at all. Lando's grief over dying L3 and our sadness at C-3PO's memory wipe in The Rise of Skywalker show we already treat droids as moral persons, so Beyleveld's precautionary principle says they deserve legal personhood - paralleling real-world AI-inventorship (DABUS) and animal-personhood litigation.
- ch. 27 "Part IV EPISODES IV–VI" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "“An Energy Field Created by All Living Things”" **·** Baruch Spinoza — Conatus (striving to persist); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); The Unconscious — Baur argues that the Jedi metaphysics is non-dualistic rather than a simple good-versus-evil opposition, reading the Force through Spinoza: ideas become more or less true as they cohere with other ideas (so 'Luke loves Leia', 'Han is a mercenary', and 'Vader is evil' all need qualification), and everything seeks power by the conatus that Yoda and Obi-Wan attribute to the Force. The light side seeks power in balance with other things while the dark side, per the Sith Rule of Two, plays a zero-sum game. Luke's arc mirrors Oedipus: denying his inherited psychological likeness to Vader only enacts it, and only by acknowledging and owning the anger he inherited from his father can he gain power over it and enable Vader's redemption and his own.
- ch. 29 "“Master Skywalker. There Are Too Many of Them. What Are We Going to Do ”" **·** Gottfried Leibniz — Cook and Kellen ask what makes the Luke of A New Hope the same fictional character as the Luke of The Last Jedi, the Thrawn Trilogy, or fan fiction like Old Man Luke. They reject sameness of name, Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles (Luke_ANH lacks Luke_TLJ's internal properties such as being a jaded Jedi Master), and the authorial say-so account of Routley and Thomasson, which by transitivity forces the contradiction that Zahn's married, child-having Luke is identical to the Last Jedi recluse who never met Mara Jade. They defend a 'Perspectival Account' on which identity claims are true or false only relative to the story from which we interpret them, so each viewing of A New Hope shows innumerably many distinct yet connected Lukes - 'ontological excess' spanning canon, Legends, Infinities, and the Muppet Show.
- ch. 30 "Yoda's Theme" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Geist (World Spirit) — Eldem uses Hegel's 'Force and the Understanding' from the Phenomenology of Spirit to explain Yoda's X-wing lesson: force is essential to matter rather than external to it, so 'size matters not' - lifting a rock and a ship are the same task within a relational ontology where things are constituted by bifurcated forces (gravity, magnetism) whose opposites form unities, like the light and dark sides or the Rey-Ben dyad. Geist plays the role the pre-Socratics gave the arche, and via Houlgate's reading it grounds the Force's social dimension: love as the force that binds people, explaining Vader's final sacrifice and the connections between the saga's heroes. The hero is the one who grasps this interconnection and sacrifices for community, as Yoda does when he finally raises the ship.
- ch. 31 "“Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”" **·** Confucius — Xiao (filial piety); Li (ritual propriety); Ren (benevolence/humaneness) — Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.
- ch. 32 "Part V THE MANDALORIAN" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "“This Is the Way”" **·** Adam Smith, Peter Singer — The Impartial Spectator; Speciesism; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions — Holdier uses the imagined scene of stormtroopers roasting Grogu over a cookfire to test moral sentimentalism: our disgust at eating Baby Yoda either perceives moral truth, informs our motivations, or simply is our judgment, but popular sentiment cannot settle its aptness, since our culture happily eats sentient chickens - the same inconsistency fans felt when Grogu ate the Frog Lady's eggs in 'The Passenger'. Adam Smith's impartial spectator supplies the corrective standard: if a bias-free spectator would recoil at a Grogu barbecue, that feeling is appropriate, and by parity the same spectator should recoil at factory-farmed meat (via Singer's speciesism and Kasperbauer's infrahumanization). So Din Djarin's sentimental attachment to the Child, which overrides Guild code in 'The Sin', is vindicated as genuinely moral rather than merely subjective.
- ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Michel Foucault, John Locke — The State of Nature; Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Social Contract; Philosophy of Love — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- ch. 35 "“So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.
- ch. 36 "Purpose or Futility" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Teleological Suspension of the Ethical; The Stages on Life's Way; The Leap of Faith; Authenticity — Tiernan reads Din Djarin as an Abraham figure from Fear and Trembling: like Kierkegaard's knight of faith, he teleologically suspends the ethical when he surrenders Grogu to the Jedi despite paternal attachment, just as Abraham consented to sacrifice Isaac. The chapter maps his journey onto Kierkegaard's three stages - the aesthetic temptation of settling down with Omera on Sorgan, the ethical duty of the Resol'nare and the Way, and the religious leap of faith in which purpose is regained by being given up. To become a true Mandalorian he must paradoxically abandon the creed that defines him, twice removing the helmet he swore never to remove - for the Morak facial scan and to bid Grogu farewell.
- ch. 37 "A New Sound for Star Wars" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean — Belluomini applies Aristotle's Politics Book 8 - music imitates emotion and thereby forms character - to Ludwig Goransson's Mandalorian score, showing how the bass-recorder motif and the 'broken children's tune' of Grogu's Theme render the compassion and conflict Din hides beneath his helmet, from the hovercrib encounter to the mudhorn rescue. Because well-ordered, balanced emotional movements dispose listeners toward virtue, the swelling orchestral versions that score Din taming the blurrg or his rock-styled confidence in 'Mando is Back' cultivate the viewer's own courage, care, and honor alongside the show's moral argument. Aristotle's intellectual enjoyment - delight in the fit between music and imitated feeling - explains why Gorransson's thematic recall makes the season feel like one film, culminating in the farewell cue that ties Grogu's goodbye to their first meeting.
- ch. 38 "Part VI EPISODES VII–IX" *(front)*
- ch. 39 "“I'm in Charge Now, Phasma, I’m in Charge!”" **·** W.E.B. Du Bois — Double Consciousness — Perez reads Finn through Stuart Hall's account of 'black' as a politically constructed category and Du Bois's 'social heritage of slavery': as the first helmetless Black stormtrooper, Finn simultaneously evokes the Nazi Sturmtruppen and a child enslaved by the First Order, and his self-naming with Poe enacts Hartman's claim that the enslaved must fashion new identities to be free. The chapter then uses colorism, Feagin's white racial frame, and Bloomquist's minstrel studies to argue that Boyega's Finn was sidelined - minimized in marketing, reduced to comic relief and Rose's rebukes, denied his native accent like a linguistic stereotype - wasting the trilogy's most timely story, while Jannah's Company 77 and The Bad Batch hint at the fuller reckoning with stormtrooper slavery Star Wars never attempted.
- ch. 40 "The Last Jedi A New Hope" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — Consequentialism; Faith and Reason — Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.
- ch. 41 "Abilities Some Considered to Be Non‐organic" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power — Shores stages the fandom debate over 'Jake Skywalker' - Star Wars Theory's charge that Rian Johnson betrayed the character versus the Auralnauts' defense - and resolves it with Deleuze's forces of becoming, drawn from Nietzsche's will to power: bodies are whirlwinds of competing forces defined by affecting and being affected, and Luke's defining trait is extreme self-variance, from whiny farm boy and X-wing quitter to Trench Run hero. On this reading The Last Jedi's broken Luke is not a betrayal but a supreme becoming-other: his powers of transformation overpower even the Force's pull on Ahch-To, and his lethal Force projection exemplifies Deleuze's noble combat-between-oneself (the ascending, light-side will to become) rather than the Emperor's self-destructive will-to-dominate, the scorpion that cannot change its character.
- ch. 42 "Overcoming Death through the Force of Love" **·** Plato, Socrates — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Philosophy of Love — Lawler reads the nine-film saga as a love story in three acts structured by Plato: Anakin and Padme's passionate love - which Diotima's ladder in the Symposium treats as the necessary first rung the Jedi wrongly condemn - drives his fall, in a Phaedrus-style conflict between the upward rational horse and the downward sensuous one. The original trilogy centers the detached Platonic love of Luke and Leia, while the Rey-Kylo 'dyad in the Force' fulfills Aristophanes' halfling myth of reunited other halves and brings balance, just as Alcibiades' failure to climb beyond the first rung parallels Anakin's fixation on one person. When Ren revives the dead Rey in a Romeo-and-Juliet inversion, the chapter concludes Yoda was wrong: the Force transforms into the dead rather than them into it.
- ch. 43 "“And I, I'm All the Jedi!”" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Okapal uses Aristotle's three friendships to frame the saga as a story of desert children seeking community: utility friendships like Hondo Ohnaka's and the Sith Rule of Two, where Darth Bane's apprentice is a mere instrument and Sidious calls Maul, Tyranus, and Vader 'easy to replace', stand against the other-regarding virtuous friendships of Obi-Wan, Kanan, and the Rey-Finn-Poe triad, where friends sacrifice for each other's sake as Ezra learns about Kanan in 'A World Between Worlds'. Luke's premature departure for Cloud City fails the 'for the other's sake' test Yoda poses. Rey can only choose the Jedi community knowingly once she learns she is Palpatine's granddaughter, and her closing claim 'I'm Rey Skywalker' is a choice between two value systems - the plural, other-regarding Jedi Code versus the self-regarding 'I' of the Sith Code - making friendship and community, not blood, the root of identity.
- ch. 44 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 45 "End User License Agreement" *(front)*

## Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Stephen Colbert and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Philosophy for Heroes" *(no index entry yet)* — Aaron Allen Schiller's introduction presents Colbert as a cultural institution (Time's 100 Most Influential, Emmy and Peabody awards, a 2008 presidential run) and a faux-pundit who does not report the news but 'feels the news at us' through the WØRD, Better Know a District, the ThreatDown, and the calls to action his fan army, the Colbert Nation, obeys. It argues philosophers love him because he 'tortures logic like Mozart writes symphonies,' playing with Truth and Reality through his coinages truthiness and wikiality so thoroughly that no future philosophical tract on the nature of Truth will be complete without considering truthiness. The book, it says, is for anyone who finds those concepts 'under their skin' without quite knowing why.
- ch. 8 "FIRST SEGMENT - The WØRD First Principles of Colbertian Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Where Do We Go from Here" **·** Socrates, John Locke — Moral Relativism; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.
- ch. 10 "Explaining Moral Doubt" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, John Locke, Nel Noddings, John Stuart Mill, Thomas Hobbes — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.
- ch. 11 "Under-Confidence in Reason Once It’s Easier Said, then It’s Done" **·** Socrates, Jacques Derrida — The Unexamined Life; Deconstruction — Roben Torosyan turns Colbert into a negative textbook for critical thinking: the character embodies the exact opposite of the American Philosophical Association's seven critical-thinking dispositions (inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, confident in reason), from refusing to imagine Lisa Randall's extra dimensions, to 'the market doesn't lie' about the Bible, to placing himself above Maimonides, Socrates, and Aquinas in the stem-cell Formidable Opponent. Each section names the fallacies his shtick commits - appeal to popularity, appeal to ignorance, composition, circular reasoning, wishful thinking, appeal to consequences - using real WØRD bits like the Iraq 'no casualties' monologue and the cake-metaphor exchange about the war. The WØRD's self-undermining bullet points are read as Derridean deconstruction (différance): every assertion shot through with what differs from and defers it. Watching Colbert fail at the examined life Socrates recommended, the viewer learns to catch such abuses in pundits and in themselves.
- ch. 12 "Sin, Play, and the “Synagogues of Satan”" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Heraclitus, Thomas Aquinas, Protagoras — Virtue Ethics (arete); Cardinal and Theological Virtues; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Rachael Sotos argues the Report performs Platonic play: like the divine puppet of Plato's Laws with its competing cords, Colbert reveals what moves us (fear, hope, the ThreatDown bears, the 'golden cord' of the good) and so teaches freedom through play. Colbert's pompous self-authority - claiming to be 'the canon and measure' of virtue in I Am America - parodies Aristotle's serious man (spoudaios, megalopsychos) and the sophists Protagoras and Prodicus with their Orpheus voices, proving Heraclitus right that 'time is a child at play' and Aristotle wrong that play is mere medicinal rest. Tracking the war on fun from Chrysostom through Aquinas's eutrapelia (there is sin in a lack of play) to Erasmus's Praise of Folly and the Puritans' ban on theaters as 'Synagogues of Satan,' she reads Colbert's playing-at-sin - the man-seed eugenics bit, the 'black friend' boasts, the Ellen DeGeneres Paradox on Wikiality - as Erasmian folly that heals America's Puritan hangover in the culture wars.
- ch. 13 "Conclestions" **·** Bertrand Russell — Sense and Reference — Jason Southworth asks how viewers understand Colbert's deliberately confusing coinages ('wordanista,' 'superstantial,' 'Lincolnish,' 'freem,' and the title 'I Am America (And So Can You!)'). Borrowing Russell's view that names abbreviate definite descriptions (the 'spot check test'), he argues these utterances are paraphrasable and therefore meaningful rather than nonsense, distinguishing meaning from reference and literal from non-literal meaning. He then applies Grice's cooperative principle and conversational maxims to derive implicatures: the gut speech violates 'do not say what you believe to be false' and so implies truthiness-as-visceral-feeling, 'wordinista' imports Sandinista-style radicalism, and 'John, tear me a new one' generates the kitten-woodchipper joke. Since context fixes meaning, even dictionary-less words like 'freem' can be decoded, and the Wordinistas at Webster's are unnecessary.
- ch. 14 "SECOND SEGMENT - The ThreatDown Truthiness" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Wishing and Dogmatism" **·** Harry Frankfurt — On Bullshit; The Will to Believe — Matthew Pierlott argues Colbert the satirist conflates two things his character, Stephen, merges: truthiness (trusting gut and heart over external authorities like dictionaries) and bullshit in Frankfurt's exact sense - speech indifferent to truth, which Pierlott finds in Hillary Clinton's dismissal of economists on the gas-tax holiday and likens to Steve Careill's habitual pleasantries versus Jon Stewart's honesty and Stephen's lies. He defends gut and heart as evidence-bearing tools - knowing a candidate's 'heart' from character evidence (the Westmoreland Ten Commandments interview), gut intuitions as unconsciously processed experience, and choosing which of the two Cheneys (1994 quagmire prophet or 2003 liberators booster) to trust - so in an information-saturated democracy truthiness is a necessary part of any orientation toward truth. The real enemy is dogmatism, the 'Dark Side of Truthiness' that cuts off future evidence, while wishful thinking kept modest (optimism that people are honest) can even be beneficial, a Jamesian willing-to-believe.
- ch. 16 "It-Getting The Truth about Truthiness" **·** Sextus Empiricus, David Hume, Michel de Montaigne, Nagarjuna, Pyrrho — Pyrrhonian Skepticism (suspension of judgment); Philosophical Skepticism; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Ethan Mills runs a 'Better Know a Skeptic' four-parter applied to the show: Pyrrhonian skepticism (Sextus Empiricus's suspension of judgment and living by appearances, played out in the Jon-says-worst-versus-Stephen-says-greatest Bush debate), Modern skepticism (Montaigne's fideist custom-worship and Hume's dream argument for why knowledge of couches, Doritos, and presidents is impossible), and Indian skepticism (Nagarjuna's circle that means of knowledge cannot be established without things known, illustrated with Stephen Sr. and Stephen Jr. as both father and son, plus Jayarasi's destruction of epistemology). He adds 'political skepticism' - the American sense that political knowledge is impossible - which breeds wikiality, an internet relativism ('reality we just agreed on') that the WØRD's own bullet points ('Wikipedia can tell a lie') undermine. Truthiness, he concludes, is Stephen's false cure for political skepticism: commitment without facts, a 'truthiness of the appearances'; but Sextus shows skeptics can still act on appearances without dogmatism, so we can vote and argue on the best evidence, as in Sagan's science-as-democracy, without certainty.
- ch. 17 "But Does Political Satire Promote Democratic Values" **·** Michel Foucault, Herbert Marcuse — One-Dimensional Man — Michael Tiboris and Kory Schaff answer their title question affirmatively: Colbert's satire promotes democratic values by practicing Foucault's parrhesia - fearless speech that speaks the truth freely, functions as criticism of interlocutor and self, and flows from moral duty - unlike bumper-sticker assertion, since it enters risky dialogue and invites being refuted. Against this stands a corporate-consolidated media ('monopoly of meaning' from GE, Viacom, News Corp, Time-Warner) whose framing, slanting, and spinning - McCain's 'transcendental' war, the Obama-dresses-like-Ahmadinejad story, WMD as Word of the Year - exemplify Marcuse's one-dimensional thought absorbing oppositional language ('clean bomb,' 'harmless fall-out'). The WØRD models parrhesiastic critique by speaking media's own language while the bullet points undercut it ('Definitions will greet us as liberators'), exposing how politicians and pundits merely appear truthful and teaching viewers their own duty of critical assessment.
- ch. 18 "Philosophy in the Age of Truthiness" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — David Detmer explains how the twentieth century's scientific persuasion techniques plus electronic media, American anti-elitism ('science is elitist... Gravity Without Representation'), the conflation of a legal right to an opinion with its being right, and journalism's bankrupt objectivity doctrine produced the age of truthiness that Colbert satirizes (Britannica and the Panama Canal, Limbaugh, O'Reilly, and Coulter as the 'gasbags'). He then rebuts the book's implicit challenge that philosophers' appeals to intuition are themselves truthiness: self-evident truths like 'cruelty is wrong' or Euclid's axioms are needed to stop the infinite regress of justification, and they differ in kind from gut-feelings about historical or political claims whose denial is easily conceived. The Report's nightly ridicule of truthiness therefore serves Socrates' dictum that the unexamined life is not worth living, showing philosophy's value to a public that lets pundits decide by gut.
- ch. 19 "THIRD SEGMENT - Better Know a Philosopher" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 20 "Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Allegory of the Cave; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); The Myth of Sisyphus — Ralkowski asks whether Colbert is America's Socrates, comparing Colbert's ironic interviews (Caitlin Flanagan on feminism, Harvey Mansfield on manliness, Howard Dean's superdelegates, the ABC Stephanopoulos-Gibson debate) to Socrates' definitional refutations of Euthyphro and the Athenian elite. Like Socrates in Plato's cave allegory, Colbert is a shadow on the wall undermining truthiness from within, yet both fail: audiences laugh, guests collect the campaign-donation 'Colbert Bump,' and nothing changes, making America the self-satisfied one who is ignorant of its ignorance. Through Nehamas's contrast of Socratic and Platonic irony and the Symposium's demand that the greatest work read as both tragedy and comedy, the chapter concludes Colbert may be America's Plato — condemning and laughing at us like a Sisyphean liberator who knows we will not leave the cave.
- ch. 21 "Avowal, not an Owl" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Stone builds a theory of humor from Wittgenstein's philosophy of language: Colbert's Starbucks-withdrawal 'ThreatDown' skit, the peg-leg-pirate quip at the Constitution Center, and the flip from '68% disapprove of the job he's doing' to '68% approve of the job he's not doing' all work as aspect-change (seeing-as), making us see an ordinary scene under a new aspect. Getting the joke requires a shared form of life (recognizing the Starbucks logo, knowing the Danish-cartoon controversy that made Colbert's suspiciously flattering entry on Islam the punchline) plus a personal Humorous Attitude and an avowal — laughter, or the Washington press corps' respectful silence at the 2006 Correspondents' Dinner, which Colbert converted into a second aspect-change for the larger TV and blog audience.
- ch. 22 "Moving On" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Alasdair MacIntyre — Authenticity — Frazier reads the show through Freud: Stephen play-acts both the repressed religious-right superego (Dobson, Hagee, his terror of bug sex) and the aggressive American id, so his improvised irony — shielding his crotch from Michael Stipe, mangling Teddy Roosevelt's big-stick maxim for Joe Sestak, sneering at the women's-softball sportsmanship story — works as therapeutic catharsis that lets viewers laugh at and tame their own aggression and hang-ups. Against MacIntyre's charge that irony corrodes culture, he enlists Kierkegaard's picture of the ironist who outdoes a view's 'ludicrous enthusiasm' (the U.S.A.! chant at Naomi Wolf, the gun-control interview that collapses into a case against itself), concluding that the man who merely played the true patriot was the more authentic American.
- ch. 23 "What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Will to Power; Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment — In full truthiness voice, Michaud explains Colbert's failed 2008 presidential run — the South Carolina Democratic Executive Council's 13-3 vote keeping him off the ballot — as exactly what Nietzsche predicted: the resentful weak, the 'sheep,' hold the super-man down by redefining meekness as strength. He walks through will-to-power as self-overcoming, the lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable from the Genealogy, and Christianity as slave morality, then 'corrects' Nietzsche by relocating slave morality in the liberal media rather than God, ending with Colbert as the man of the future who 'affirms life without resentment.'
- ch. 24 "FINAL SEGMENT - What Stephen Colbert Tells Us about Being America" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Truthiness and the Denial of Responsibility" *(no index entry yet)* — Schiller finds a calculated tension in Stephen: he claims impossible literal colorblindness ('People tell me I'm white and I believe them') while staging a nationwide search for a new black friend whose only function is to license racially insensitive talk, as in the Rosa Parks 'Overrated' WØRD where he misreads Alan's cursing as agreement. Working through the N-word debate (Kennedy's Intentionalism, Asim's Eradicationism, Chris Rock's double standard) and Michael Eric Dyson on Hurricane Katrina, he argues Stephen claims the rights of linguistic license while shirking its responsibilities, and that truthiness is the same posture writ large — the 'rhetoric of complexity' by which politicians deny responsibility for the problems they refuse to understand.
- ch. 26 "I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion" **·** Socrates, Plato, Adam Smith, Thomas Hobbes — The Invisible Hand; Justice in the Republic — Smith dissects Stephen's free-market worship — the market as a God requiring faith, 'the market has spoken' on global warming, supply-side economics, and the plan to run universities as businesses with credit-card-swiper desks and tuition priced by marketability. Against this he deploys Socrates in the Republic: a practice is defined by its aim, so a physician aiming at his own wealth is not practicing medicine badly but moneymaking, and by the same argument a corporatized university whose primary aim is shareholder profit is no longer higher education — privatization alters its nature and so destroys it, while Smith's invisible hand is exposed as the South Park gnomes' missing Step Two and wikiality as supply-side epistemology where facts are supplied by majority vote instead of known.
- ch. 27 "Who Watches the Watchers" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Peter Singer — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Climate Ethics — Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O. Wilson's four-Earths arithmetic on unsustainable consumption and greenwashed market 'solutions' to global warming, and Baudrillard's Consumer Society account of news packaged for consumption beside the ads, they ask whether the Colbert Nation's ironic participation resists corporate media or completes it, concluding freem converts even critique into one more purchase.
- ch. 28 "TAKE THE ISHIHARA RACE TEST" *(no index entry yet)* — A mock color-blindness test: readers check figures to see whether they, like Stephen, suffer 'Colbertian Race Blindness,' an affliction of whites that confuses racial equality with racial indifference. The race-blind view history through that impairment — Civil Rights supposedly proved blacks and whites have 'perfectly identical cultures,' and Dr. King's colorblind society becomes a nation where everyone is one color, white — a gag that dramatizes the book's chapter on race by taking Stephen's 'I don't see race' literally.
- ch. 29 "Citizens of the Colbert Nation" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Factinista’s Choice" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Stephen Colbert and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Stephen King and Philosophy

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; The Meaning of Life; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.
- ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" **·** David Hume, Augustine of Hippo, Søren Kierkegaard, Anselm of Canterbury, Thomas Aquinas — The Problem of Evil; Despair (sickness unto death); Faith and Reason — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- ch. 5 "Female Subjectivity in Carrie" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Woman as the Other; One Is Not Born a Woman; Feminism — Kellye Byal reads Carrie White through Beauvoir's The Second Sex, treating Carrie's first menstruation, her mother Margaret's ascetic 'Mystic' piety, and Miss Collins/Sue Snell's push toward makeup and the prom as two imposed versions of 'feminine destiny.' Carrie is caught between rejecting femininity (becoming an outcast/monster) and assuming it (surrendering her subjectivity to immanence and the male gaze), so her telekinesis becomes an externalized act of authentic, radically free agency against both scripts. Byal argues her tragic death indicts a failed community of women who never posit themselves as Subjects, illustrating Beauvoir's claim that female subjectivity needs a solidarity of others in which to thrive.
- ch. 6 "“Sometimes Dead Is Better”" **·** Nick Bostrom, Bernard Williams — Immortality and the Soul; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); The Meaning of Life — Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.
- ch. 7 "“Gan Is Dead”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Death of God — Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.
- ch. 8 "Rāma of Gilead" **·** Dharma; Karma and Rebirth — Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.
- ch. 9 "What’s Wrong with Roland" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Consequentialism; The Greatest Happiness Principle — Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.
- ch. 10 "Stephen King and Aristotelian Friendship" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Bertha Alvarez Manninen reads The Body (Stand by Me) and Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption through Aristotle's Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics on the three friendships. Andy and Norton/the guards exemplify friendships of utility (the tax help, the Rita Hayworth poster), the boys' tree-house camaraderie and Vern/Teddy exemplify pleasure friendships that dissolve as characters change, while Gordie-and-Chris and Andy-and-Red model enduring friendships of virtue rooted in mutual good will, shared confidences, and cultivating each other's excellence. Manninen then presses Aristotle: his strict 'only good men' criterion and his debt-bound, property-like view of the parent-child bond fail the flawed-but-loyal Andy/Red and the abusive fathers in The Body, showing human friendship is more complex than his taxonomy allows.
- ch. 11 "Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils" **·** Michel Foucault, Friedrich Nietzsche — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Potter and Cobb read Apt Pupil—the blackmail-driven 'teaching' relationship between the boy Todd Bowden and the fugitive Nazi Kurt Dussander—to argue that all effective teaching is propaganda: persuasion by nonrational means (ethos and pathos beyond logos). They analyze the shifting teacher-student dynamic through Foucault's Power/Knowledge, showing power as a fluid relational 'order' rather than a possession, with Russell's definition of power and Nietzsche's Genealogy on the pleasures of subordination explaining Dussander's relief in obeying. Citing Bernays and Chomsky, they contend Todd and Dussander's oppressive, sadism-soaked curriculum merely strips the artifice from ordinary schooling, which has always been a system of control—culminating in Todd's transformation into a killer.
- ch. 12 "The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia" **·** Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — The Panopticon (surveillance); Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge — Elizabeth Hornbeck analyzes King's Overlook Hotel through Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' arguing the hotel is a heterotopia—a socially produced space of crisis and deviance that juxtaposes and inverts normal relations, accumulating time as a 'chronic heterotopia' stuffed with its own ghosts and murders (Mrs. Massey, the Gradys, the 1921 photo). Cut off in winter, it strips away the norms of 'home' so Jack Torrance's inherited monsters (alcoholism, his father's abuse) can turn him from protector into a family-killer. She contrasts the maze-like Overlook with the panopticon of Grand Hotel and Bentham's surveillance-prison from Discipline and Punish, noting that King, unlike Foucault, treats transgression as horrific: the conservative horror genre restores the status quo only when Jack dies and the hotel burns.
- ch. 13 "Broadcast Dystopia" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil; Utopia and Dystopia; The Ethics of Political Violence — Foy and Dale read the Bachman dystopias The Running Man and The Long Walk through Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (collective coordination) and violence (coercion by implements), arguing King's states substitute broadcast spectacle for genuine power and so hemorrhage legitimacy the more violence they apply. The gladiatorial Games Network and the Walk pacify the masses while chants of 'KILL HIM' sever the affective bonds of humanity. The chapter invokes Arendt's Eichmann-in-Jerusalem 'banality of evil' to explain the soldiers, Hunters, and cheering citizens as ordinary people uncritically 'doing their jobs,' and reads Ben Richards's suicide flight into the Games Building and Garraty's exhausted walk as futile personal revolts that change nothing.
- ch. 14 "Stephen King and the Art of Horror" **·** Plato, Aristotle, David Hume — Allegory of the Cave; Virtue Ethics — Littmann stages a mock trial of King's horror using classical aesthetics: Plato prosecutes, condemning fiction as lies that misrepresent gods, afterlife, and paternal authority (Carrie's mother, Jack Torrance, the Loser's Club disobeying elders) and corrupt morals through spectacle. Aristotle counters that Poetics-style poetry is 'more philosophical than history' and that tragedy's catharsis purges pity and fear, which King echoes in Danse Macabre's claim that horror lances real terrors via Danny Torrance, Paul Sheldon, and Louis Creed. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' explains why we enjoy fictional suffering (Pennywise, Annie Wilkes) we would hate in life; Littmann finally revises Hume, arguing horror's pleasure is the spur to imagination rather than mere appreciation of artistic skill.
- ch. 15 "“You Weren’t Hired to Philosophize, Torrance”" *(no index entry yet)* — Bane uses The Shining and its rival adaptations to explain Roland Barthes's 'death of the author,' rooting it in Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy' that an author's intention is neither available nor desirable for judging a text. He shows the novel opening with Poe and Eliot epigraphs plus pop-culture jingles as Barthes's 'tissue of quotations,' then contrasts King's insistence that Jack Torrance is a good man driven by malevolent ghosts (the 'Author-God') with Kubrick's reading of Jack as already insane. Bane argues King's own 1997 miniseries ending betrays the film to defend his authority, concluding with Barthes that a text's unity lies in the reader's 'destination,' so King holds no more authority over The Shining than any reader.
- ch. 16 "What Happens to the Present When It Becomes the Past" **·** David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; The A-Series and B-Series of Time — Daniels asks whether the airline passengers in The Langoliers are truly time travelers and what theory of time their dead, tasteless past implies. Using David Lewis's distinction between 'personal time' and 'external time,' he shows the discrepancy between the characters' day-long journey and the few hours that elapse in the present qualifies them as genuine time travelers despite the deserted world. He then rules out presentism (incompatible with time travel via the 'nowhere problem') and eternalism (which denies any privileged present), arguing the vibrant, 'oomph'-laden moving now the characters race to rejoin fits the moving spotlight theory, while the langoliers merely consume the world's contents, not spacetime itself.
- ch. 17 "Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone" **·** Aristotle, Edmund Gettier — Fate and Foreknowledge; Free Will vs Determinism — Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.
- ch. 18 "Time Belongs to the Tower" **·** Immanuel Kant, William James — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; The Will to Believe — Auxier frames King as 'Tolkien meets Poe' and reads the Dark Tower's temporalization through the literary and psychological experience of time. Drawing on Susanne Langer's 'virtual present' and Sartre's psychology of imagination, he argues readers surrender their real present to a novel's suspended time, which he links to William James's 'will to believe' rather than mere suspension of disbelief. He uses Kant's distinction between amazement (seeing the seemingly impossible) and admiration (accepting it) to explain the psychological cost time travelers like Jake Epping and Wesley Smith should pay, faulting King for keeping ordinary heroes sane while displacing the strain onto insane 'gatekeepers,' and concludes the Tower is 'real' as the way each person binds possibility to their own lived past, present, and future.
- ch. 19 "Ur 88,416" **·** Immanuel Kant, David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — Auxier reconstructs the metaphysics of King's Tower across Ur and 11/22/63, treating imagination as a power that defies present time to reach the 'nowhen.' He maps King's multiverse onto Everett's many-worlds and Brian Greene's quantum/quilted multiverses, then extracts three 'laws of Dark Tower dynamics': the obduracy of the past (resistance proportional to how much the future would change), the conservation of harmony (time-strings converging like sympathetic guitar strings on an ideal order), and the danse macabre. He shows the 'reset' Jake believes in is really the creation of new Ur strings, dismantles Al Templeton's meat-buying and epistemic-radiation theories via thermodynamics, and closes with Kant's three functions of imagination to argue time travel is a 'plausible impossible' symbol we can imagine but never actually enact.
- ch. 20 "From Desperation to Haven" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Alasdair MacIntyre, Friedrich Nietzsche — Philosophical Pessimism; Ethics of Compassion; Virtue Ethics — Held reads The Tommyknockers, Desperation, and The Regulators through Arthur Schopenhauer's pessimism, arguing King's worlds are 'always already sunk in evil' and that the will to live swings life between pain and boredom even before the supernatural arrives. He identifies egoism as the root of King's cruelty (Hilly banishing David Brown to Altair-4, Bobbi turning her dog into a battery) and offers Schopenhauer's compassion-based virtue ethic, 'injure no one; help everyone,' as the answer, supported by MacIntyre on the degradation of happiness and set against Nietzsche's 'last man' and nihilism. Gard's rescue of David Brown ('the kid matters or nothing matters') and Johnny Marinville's self-sacrifice in Desperation exemplify the heroic, compassionate life that defies the dark.
- ch. 21 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 22 "Ka-tet Author Biographies" *(notes)*

## Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different

- ch. 1 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
