## Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

- ch. 1 "Globalization and Contemporary Art" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Written in the voice of the GhostFacers mourning their slain intern Alan Corbett, the introduction presents the volume as their covert infiltration of 'the industry of philosophy.' It reports that philosophy derives from the Greek philosophia, 'loving wisdom,' and jokes that the philosophers it recruited all 'readily admitted that they knew nothing' yet kept pursuing it, with a running gag about whether knowledge itself might be a tulpa. It frames the following essays as the GhostFacers' manifesto of truth about what exists in the Supernatural universe, ghosts and demons included and the Winchester 'Wine-chesters' excluded.
- ch. 7 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.
- ch. 9 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Potentiality and Actuality; Speciesism — Foresman and Tobienne deploy Aristotle's apparatus of essence and accident, the ten categories, and actuality versus potentiality to define the monster and explain the show's appeal. They test candidates against canon: whether hunting is essential or accidental to Sam after Azazel's kills, what John Winchester in 'Dead Man's Blood' treats as essential to vampire substance, and Madison's transformation in 'Heart' from actual human and potential werewolf into actual monster, concluding that monstrosity lies in thought and action rather than appearance, as the human-hunting but human Benders confirm. Tracing 'monster' to the Latin monstrum, a sign or omen, they argue monsters are monsters only through their relation to human self-importance, so our 'speciesist' prejudice is exactly why we love watching them hunted, and why we love Supernatural.
- ch. 10 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Just War Theory; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.
- ch. 11 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, David Hume — Free Will vs Determinism; Bad Faith; Compatibilism — Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.
- ch. 12 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham, Immanuel Kant — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism — Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.
- ch. 14 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; The Social Contract — Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.
- ch. 15 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx — Alienation; Class Struggle; Ideology and False Consciousness — Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.
- ch. 16 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Objectification; Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism — Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.
- ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Utilitarianism; Deontology; Just War Theory — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- ch. 18 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil — Haas uses Dean's stubborn refusal to believe in God, even after meeting Castiel, escaping Hell, and visiting Heaven, to run through the problem of evil. Casey's challenge in 'Sin City' states the logical problem; the free-will theodicy answers it but falters before Supernatural's designed horrors like the rugaru, a creature God built to suffer an irresistible hunger that ends with it eating its spouse. Dean's real objection is the evidential problem, that the amount and severity of apparently pointless evil makes the omni-God unlikely, and neither a 'natural order' defense (Dick Roman humanely farming humans for food) nor John Hick's soul-making theodicy explains suffering far beyond what character formation requires.
- ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Aquinas, William Paley — The Problem of Evil; The Watchmaker Argument (design); The Five Ways; Ockham's Razor — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- ch. 21 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Baruch Spinoza, George Berkeley, René Descartes, Immanuel Kant, John Locke — Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Forgiveness; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Chaib takes Ruby's line that Hell is 'forgetting what you are' and reads God's character through early modern philosophy: Descartes' supremely real being and deceiving demon frame Castiel's delusion of godhood and Ruby's manipulation of Sam, Spinoza's denial that evil exists (it is 'inadequate knowledge') explains the comprehensible motives of Crowley and Lucifer, Berkeley's claim that things persist only because God perceives them makes a dead God an existential threat, and Kant's 'moral theism' rebuts dogmatic atheism. With Hegel and Fromm, Hell becomes self-forgetting and communion with God becomes self-knowledge achieved through knowing others, the opposite of Ruby's Hell. The chapter concludes via Locke that closing Hell's gates would deny once-human demons the redemption tied to our very idea of God, so the brothers' forgiving love, unlike Michael and Lucifer's rigidity, reflects God's nature.
- ch. 22 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, W.V.O. Quine — Mind–Body Dualism; The Cogito; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.
- ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** Isaiah Berlin, Aristotle, Plato, Simone de Beauvoir, Friedrich Nietzsche — Two Concepts of Liberty; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- ch. 25 "Supernatural and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil — Evolutionary biologist Graves applies naturalist method to the Supernatural universe: assume natural explanations first, as the Catholic Church does before granting an exorcism, and only posit the supernatural where naturalism fails. He builds a naturalistic phylogeny in which souls behave like genetic codes (50,000 new souls when Balthazar unsinks the Titanic), and demons, ghosts, and most monsters derive from human souls, which explains why mundane salt, iron, fire, and burned bones work on them, while pagan gods killable by wooden stakes and dog's blood are 'more akin to monsters' than gods. The framework yields rules and predictions about the Colt, holy water, and the Croatoan virus, and even suggests God and Death may be natural beings obeying laws lesser beings do not share.
- ch. 26 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "Supernatural and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Supervillains and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "The Devils Get Their Due" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Ben Dyer's introduction argues that supervillains have effectively 'won' as comics matured: since the 1970s-80s turn (O'Neil/Adams Green Lantern, Miller's Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen), heroes like Batman, Superman, and Spider-Man acquired broken psychologies while villains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Lex Luthor were humanized until hero and villain barely contrast. Citing Stan Lee's claim that the supervillain is the most important character, Dyer announces the volume's project: to restore that contrast by analyzing the villain's relation to morality and society, asking whether tyranny can serve a good cause, whether an all-powerful being is limitless, whether anyone can truly desire evil, and why good henchmen are so hard to find.
- ch. 7 "4" **·** Plato, Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls, Niccolò Machiavelli, Cicero — Allegory of the Cave; The Banality of Evil; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The State of Nature — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- ch. 8 "8" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, J.L. Mackie, Thomas Aquinas, William of Ockham, Jeremy Bentham — Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Moral Relativism — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- ch. 9 "12" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Philippa Foot, John Stuart Mill, Augustine of Hippo, Jeremy Bentham, Arthur Schopenhauer — The State of Nature; Virtue Ethics (arete); Utilitarianism; Just War Theory — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- ch. 10 "15" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre, Elizabeth Anscombe — The Absurd; Amor Fati (love of fate); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Existence Precedes Essence — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- ch. 11 "19" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Plutarch, Daniel Dennett, René Descartes, Andy Clark — Compatibilism; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity; Embodiment (the lived body) — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- ch. 12 "The Rogue’s Gallery" *(notes)*
- ch. 13 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 14 "Supervillains and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 15 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am

- ch. 1 "Globalization and Contemporary Art" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(no index entry yet)* — This foreword by Rocky Rakovic, editor of Inked magazine, argues that tattoos were a 'harbinger of Twitter' – both are technologies of everyman self-expression born of a 'me generation' told it could be anything. It traces how reality-TV shows like Miami Ink and LA Ink, and figures such as Kat Von D, moved tattooing from the sailor-and-scofflaw margins into mainstream fashion, citing the Pew figure that forty percent of Americans aged 26–40 are tattooed. The connection to philosophy is thematic rather than argued: ink as individualist fashion that lets people 'scream their identity on their skin.'
- ch. 8 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; The Cogito; Personal Identity — Robert Arp's introduction takes Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' and its mind–body dualism (the conceivability argument that mind is distinct from body) and inverts it into the book's motto 'I am, therefore I ink': the tattooed person insists identity is bodily-based self-expression, challenging the Cartesian idea that the essential self is a non-bodily thinking thing. Arp flags Descartes' possible question-begging, then previews each chapter, framing tattoos as fertile ground for the philosophy of the person, personal identity over time, and self-expression.
- ch. 9 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** plutarch — Charles Taliaferro and Mark Odden survey the history and nature of tattooing – from the 3200 BCE Iceman's fifty-seven tattoos and Aetius' Constantinople recipe, through Leviticus' prohibition, Polynesian and Japanese irezumi, to Nazi concentration-camp numbering – to argue tattoos carry competing cultural (public) and individual (private) meanings. They advance a 'double skin' theory: a tattoo is both visible image and buried marking, juxtaposing interiority and exteriority. Their closing Lincoln puzzle ('calling a tail a leg doesn't make it a leg') stresses the body's stubborn reality and the 'inescapable seriousness' of permanently relabeling one's skin.
- ch. 12 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Jacques Lacan, Emmanuel Levinas, Immanuel Kant — The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real; The Face of the Other — Juniper Ellis shows tattoos resist any single interpretive scheme by running through cases: Loos and Lacassagne's criminological 'I tattoo, therefore I will commit murder'; the biblical Mark of Cain and St. Paul's stigmata as signs of protection and salvation; Lacan's claim that the tattoo is the first signifier that marks off the human subject; and Pacific tatau (Te Pehi Kupe's moko-as-signature, Queequeg's unreadable Moby-Dick tattoo) that incorporates a person into a collective. She reads Kant's Critique of Judgment dismissal of Maori tattooing and invokes Levinas' 'the face speaks' to argue a tattooed face is eloquent speech, crossing lines between individual and collective, saint and criminal.
- ch. 13 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(no index entry yet)* — Nicolas Michaud asks whether tattoos are art by testing three theories against them: art world (institutional) theory, under which tattoos are not yet art because the artworld has not admitted them; formalism (Clive Bell's 'significant form'), under which a well-composed tattoo qualifies but its human canvas is irrelevant; and Tolstoyan expressionism, under which an emotionally infectious tattoo (his example of a broken-chain tattoo over an abuse survivor's bruise) counts. He concludes tattoos are best understood as performance art – like Duchamp mustaching the Mona Lisa, the living, mortal, changing human canvas adds context and meaning, making tattoos reflect on art and our own death.
- ch. 15 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer, Simone de Beauvoir — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); Feminism; Objectification; The Male Gaze — Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.
- ch. 16 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Henri Bergson — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Feminism; The Male Gaze — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues contemporary female tattoos have lost their one-dimensional identifying function and instead create a new 'tattoo space.' He dismantles the paradoxical 'savage/civilized' and 'nature/purity' schemes (drawing on Baudrillard on the smooth, made-up female body-screen that reflects male desire) and Loos' 'ornament and crime' verdict on women's tattoos. He proposes that female tattoos have 'become graffiti' – a Bergsonian spatial 'center of action' and 'skinscape' that disperses meaning horizontally rather than branding an identity, recuperating the female body as a political body against commercialized post-political bodies.
- ch. 18 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** John Stuart Mill, Aristotle, Antonio Gramsci — Feminism; The Subjection of Women; Cultural Hegemony; Objectification — Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.
- ch. 19 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** John Locke, Judith Jarvis Thomson, W.V.O. Quine — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — Kyle Fruh and Emily Thomas use tattoos to attack two questions of personal identity. Against Locke's dominant psychological (memory) account and for the unpopular somatic (bodily) account defended by Judith Thomson and Eric Olson, they argue the depth of people's attachment to their tattoos – individuating them or marking group membership – shows we identify with our bodies. On the 'Who am I?' question they argue tattoos have an 'anchoring effect' in narrative identity: permanent, irremovable ink (contrasted with new laser-removable ink, and with dehumanizing forced Auschwitz numbers) fixes a commitment 'come what may,' echoing Quine's phrase, so that 'when you get a tattoo, you tattoo you.'
- ch. 21 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, G.W.F. Hegel, Immanuel Kant, Michel Foucault — Embodiment (the lived body); Personal Identity; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Rachel Falkenstern argues that although tattoos seem permanent, the embodied self is changing and finite, so tattoos are 'illusions of permanence.' Using Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology she dissolves the mind/body and self/tattoo boundary (we are our bodies, the world shapes us and we shape it); using the German aesthetic tradition from Kant to Hegel she reads a tattoo as a sensuous 'appearance of freedom' and links the Romantic notion of Bildung (self-formation) to choosing ink. She adds Foucault's aesthetic self-transformation and Shusterman's somaesthetics/Deweyan pragmatism to cast tattooing as reciprocal self-expression and self-creation that offers a glimpse of infinity within finitude.
- ch. 22 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, William James, John Dewey — Augustine on Time; Phenomenology; Everything Flows / Logos — Clancy Smith argues that a tattoo's ink is permanent but the memory it evokes is not, because the past no longer exists and recollection is always present and in flux (citing Heraclitus' river and William James on never-identical brain states). Using Augustine's 'present of things past' and Proust's Swann's Way, plus Dewey's immediate empiricism and Merleau-Ponty's critique of memory-as-projection, he contends that gazing at a tattoo (his 'Not Fade Away' epitaph tattoo, his friend Kalju's crossed-rifles, American History X's swastika) constructs a present meaning that tells us who we are now rather than recovering the past intact.
- ch. 23 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** John Stuart Mill — Free Will vs Determinism; On Liberty; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.
- ch. 25 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Immanuel Kant, Socrates — Free Will vs Determinism; Autonomy of the Will; The Unexamined Life — Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.
- ch. 26 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Judith Butler, Jean Baudrillard, Walter Benjamin — Gender Performativity; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Embodiment (the lived body) — Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.
- ch. 28 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Michel Foucault, Alvin Goldman — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Free Will vs Determinism; Personal Identity — Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.
- ch. 29 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Seneca, Socrates, Aristotle — Virtue Ethics; The Golden Mean; The Unexamined Life — Baker dismisses common objections to tattoos (shallow individuality, permanence, ugliness) as aesthetic rather than moral, then uses Greco-Roman virtue ethics—quoting Seneca's Moral Epistles on the soul, the balanced psyche, and matching one's norms to one's motivations—to isolate her real target: the 'tough tattoo.' She argues that a badass or tough-guy tattoo appropriates an outlaw subculture's imagery and, per Seneca's warning that approving a little violence approves it all, cultivates a vicious rather than virtuous psyche. Recalling friends who bragged about beatings, she invokes Socratic self-examination ('know thyself') to test whether looking tough is an accurate or worthy self-representation.
- ch. 31 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** John Stuart Mill — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); The Harm Principle — Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.
- ch. 32 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** John Stuart Mill — On Liberty; The Harm Principle; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.
- ch. 33 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Confucius, Mencius — Xiao (filial piety); Faith and Reason — Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.
- ch. 35 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** The Buddha, David Hume — Impermanence (anicca); Non-Self (anatman); The Four Noble Truths — Lynch, a tattooed Buddhist philosophy professor, tests his largely Buddhist body art (an Om-mani-padme-hum armband, Bodhidharma, the Buddha's face, the eight-spoked Wheel and lotus, a double-vajra) against the Buddha's Three Marks of Existence. He argues a 'permanent' tattoo need not contradict impermanence any more than Gruzalski's washed-away sandcastle if approached mindfully, that custom ink need not reify a self given the chariot analogy of no-self (which he links to Hume's bundle view), and that the pain of tattooing directly instantiates dukkha and can become an object of meditation and compassion. Mindful tattooing, he concludes, can itself be authentic Buddhist practice.
- ch. 36 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" **·** Thomas Aquinas, William Paley — The Five Ways; The Watchmaker Argument (design); The Meaning of Life — Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.
- ch. 37 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" *(notes)*

- ch. 7 "A Taste of Athens" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that the show's sugary surface hides systematic appearance/reality gaps: Nate the bumbling kit man is a tactical genius, Rebecca hires Ted to destroy the club, Jamie's arrogance masks a yearning for connection, and Ted's cheerfulness conceals trauma. Taking Trent Crimm's line that sport is a metaphor for life and Ted's dartboard speech about judgmentalism crowding out curiosity, it frames philosophy's questioning as the right tool for the show, then previews the volume's five parts (Augustine and Taoism, fear and friendship, masculinity and bullshit, Candide/Camus and music, Stoicism and redemption) via Nate's dumpy favorite restaurant A Taste of Athens.
- ch. 8 "Part I DO THE RIGHT‐EST THING" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Notes" **·** Augustine of Hippo — Strehlow argues Ted's question 'What do you love?' points to Augustine's ordo amoris: character is defined by how our competing loves are ordered. Jamie's self-gratifying cupiditas is contrasted with Dani Rojas's caritas ('football is life'), Rebecca's revenge on Rupert is a disordered love she abandons by trashing his headline, and the ghost-exorcism ceremony in 'Two Aces' becomes a collective reordering of loves. Using James K. A. Smith's cultural liturgies, he reads Roy's kebab shop and Richmond fandom as liturgies that make winning an idol, and shows how fathers and father figures (James Tartt's abuse, Sam's dad, Ted as father to Roy and Jamie, Augustine's Ambrose) reorder sons' loves toward the good.
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi, Confucius — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way) — Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.
- ch. 11 "Notes" **·** William James, Blaise Pascal — The Will to Believe; Faith and Reason — Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes — Ethical Egoism; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Begley and Biondi argue Ted is an ethical egoist in the Aristotelian-Randian sense: like Howard Roark of The Fountainhead (Ted's favorite book), he is a self-loving creator who loves his work, has a 'self-sufficient ego' immune to others' approval, and pursues long-range values, so his kindness and biscuits are rational self-interest, not selflessness. Against Hobbesian psychological egoism they distinguish genuine egoists from narcissists like Rupert and hedonists like Season 1 Jamie, defend Ted's divorce and the curse-reverse ceremony as only apparent sacrifices, and read his panic-attack therapy arc as the egoist's project of achieving inner wholeness.
- ch. 13 "Part II THE BEST VERSIONS OF OURSELVES" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Notes" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Authenticity — Latta uses James Hollis's Jungian 'Middle Passage' - the midlife collapse of our tacit contract with the universe and of the provisional personality built in life's first half - to read Ted's arc with Dr. Sharon Fieldstone: her bike accident and self-disclosure, his panic attacks, and his confession about his father's suicide force him to drop the coach persona and choose an authentic second half. The chapter interprets Ted's move to London as both flight from and working-through of paternal trauma, his distance from son Henry as the wound it exposes, and closes with Kierkegaard's journal demand to find 'a truth which is truth for me,' which Ted finds in the return home to Kansas.
- ch. 15 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Forte maps the Richmond cast onto Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: Rebecca, Nate, Roy, and Jamie begin incontinent or near-vicious; courage is the mean between Nate's cowardice and Roy's rashness; and their friendless misery illustrates why friendship (utility, pleasure, complete) is necessary for eudaimonia. Ted's coaching works as a modern strengths-based complement to Aristotelian habituation - Phoebe's Princess-and-Dragon play tempers Roy, Jamie's competitiveness is redirected into team play, Nate misses the mean and becomes mean - and the finale's 'progress over perfection' framing shows all of them as works in progress toward teloi.
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Philippa Foot, Cicero — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics — Loftin argues the Diamond Dogs enact Aristotle's complete friendship: Jamie and Rebecca fail at friendship because they misconceive the good as self-gratification, and following Philippa Foot's natural-kind account of human good (plus Cicero on goodwill and C. S. Lewis's Four Loves) he shows friendship is an intrinsic good of human beings as such. Ted's vulnerability before Beard, Nate, and Higgins invites them into virtuous activity, Higgins's defection from Rebecca's sabotage scheme displays friendship against a relationship fueled by hurt, and Nate's status-hunger explains why he mistakes Ted's laughter and Rupert's patronage for friendship.
- ch. 17 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, David Hume — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Humanity as an End in Itself; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Wible asks whether Ted's friendliness with players and staff constitutes moral friendship, testing it against Aristotle's three friendship types, Hume on solitude, and Bennett Helm's conditions (shared activity, intimacy, mutual care) plus a power-imbalance requirement Kant's respect for persons underwrites. This condemns Rebecca and Sam's relationship as a conflict of interest too risky to permit, questions Led Tasso and benching decisions, yet concludes that Aristotle's virtue friendship between coach and player is possible and preferable to Drewe's limited utility-friendship, since Ted's virtuous friendships make players better people while still knowing when to prioritize team over individual.
- ch. 18 "Part III MAN CITY" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Notes" **·** Harry Frankfurt — On Bullshit — Husmann and Kusko apply Frankfurt's On Bullshit distinction - the liar cares about truth while the bullshitter is indifferent to it - to argue Ted Lasso combats BS through correctness (accurately representing a shared world) before sincerity. Ted never fakes tactical knowledge and accepts hard truths like his divorce; the good guys (Sam's protest, Roy refusing a fake-injury ruse, Trent's fair profile) reject BS; Rupert is the show's virtuoso BS artist from the charity gala interruption to crashing the funeral; and Rebecca, Jamie, and Nate's arcs are measured as their movements up and down the BS spectrum.
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Arvan argues the show is really about positive masculinity - what it is to be a good man - read through Aristotle's virtue ethics: toxic masculinity (Rupert's domination, Jamie Sr.'s abuse, Nate's cruelty, Ted's suffer-in-silence self-reliance) is vice at an extreme, while the show's good men hit the golden mean by 'womaning up.' Led Tasso works as context-appropriate toughness, Roy's hug of Jamie and the darts speech's 'be curious, not judgmental' blend masculine and feminine virtues, phronesis is learned from experience as Beard teaches Nate forgiveness, and even Rupert's downfall shows vice backfiring as Aristotle predicts.
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** bell hooks, Friedrich Nietzsche — Feminism; The Ethics of Care — Young uses bell hooks's patriarchal masculinity (with Kate Manne on misogyny as enforcement) to read the show: Jamie is patriarchal terror's product, Rupert's promiscuity and Rebecca's subjection are two sides of male control, and Roy Kent's 'hard man' persona inherits the hardness Nietzsche praised and philosophy's traditional suspicion of emotion. Against this, hooks's definition of love as the will to nurture spiritual growth explains Ted's coaching, the training-room exorcism's shared vulnerability, Sam's openness, and Nate's status-hunger as the struggle to invert the gender pyramid, ending with Nate refusing Rupert's poisoned patriarchal gifts.
- ch. 22 "Notes" **·** Virtue Ethics — Austin weighs Lombardi's 'winning is the only thing' (embodied in Beard's protest when Ted refuses to bench Roy against Man City) against the sportsmanship tradition and Robert Simon's view of sport as a mutual quest for excellence through challenge. He argues the 'New Lasso Way' vindicates both: Ted's locker-room speech after relegation, his note to Jamie ('Way to make the extra pass') after Jamie's assist beats Richmond, Pep's cameo, and the retitling of Trent's book to The Richmond Way show that people matter more than winning while winning still matters, with Ted's humility ('It's not about me') as the ground of the balance.
- ch. 23 "Part IV MOSTLY FOOTBALL IS LIFE" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer — Virtue Ethics (arete) — Belluomini argues the show's score and soundtrack do genuine aesthetic and moral work, applying Aristotle's Politics Book VIII claim that music imitates emotion and disposes us toward virtue. He analyzes Celeste's 'Strange' narrating the divorce-signing and intercut romances, 'Wise Up' underscoring Rebecca's brave break with John Wingsnight, 'Piano Joint' carrying Rebecca's confession to Ted, 'She's a Rainbow' scoring Roy's run back to Nelson Road, 'Roy Walk Off' as a Jaws-style sentimental motif, and 'Spiegel im Spiegel' under Rebecca's anti-Super-League speech, closing with Schopenhauer's point that fitting music is a scene's most accurate commentary.
- ch. 25 "Notes" **·** Nick Bostrom, David Lewis — The Simulation Hypothesis; Possible Worlds — Jones takes Beard's 'tip our caps to the rascal pulling the strings' seriously and reconstructs Bostrom's simulation trilemma without the math: humanity goes extinct before simulating ancestors, advanced civilizations decline to run them, or we are almost certainly simulated. He then brings in David Lewis's modal realism to argue the different Teds - happily married in Kansas, the coach we watch, the rage-monster Led Tasso - are real possible people, and concludes that even if we are simulations our consciousness is real and meaningful: ancestor-simulations are the future tipping its caps to us.
- ch. 26 "Notes" **·** Albert Camus, Gottfried Leibniz — The Absurd; The Best of All Possible Worlds; Principle of Sufficient Reason — Blessing diagnoses Ted's 'rom-communism' as the naive optimism Voltaire satirized in Candide: Pangloss's 'best of all possible worlds' is Leibniz's greater-goods theodicy and Principle of Sufficient Reason, and its fatalism ('it will all work out exactly as it's supposed to') collapses under Ted's panic attacks and 'belief can't score goals.' Against it she sets Camus's The Plague: Dr. Rieux's absurd heroism, refusal of hope as 'philosophical suicide,' and 'strange hope' grounded in collective decency, arguing Ted's real, sustainable creed is Camus-like faith in teamwork and human goodness rather than belief that everything works out.
- ch. 27 "Notes" **·** The Best of All Possible Worlds — Freeman reads Ted as Chesterton's holy fool, in the lineage of Don Quixote and The Idiot and modeled on Innocent Smith in Manalive: his apparently foolish decisions (benching Jamie, the crooked BELIEVE sign meaning the room is 'outta whack') disclose a higher optimism that faces real evil, delights in Being as a gift, and loves the world patriotically like a relegation-threatened home team. The chapter then argues Ted's optimism diverges from Chesterton's by lacking its Christian foundation - Ted believes in belief itself, 'to which god and in what language?' - so the show can intuit but not justify the optimism it depicts.
- ch. 28 "Part V SMELLS LIKE POTENTIAL" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Civil Disobedience; Utilitarianism — The Baggetts use Trent Crimm's 'Richmond Coach Cover-Up Revealed' - where he names Nate as his anonymous source for Ted's panic attack and loses his job - as a case study in journalistic ethics. They test the duty to protect sources through Kantian universalizability (which maxim?) and rule utilitarianism (keep the rule even when breaking it would help here), consider whether Trent's willingness to pay the price resembles Thoreau-style civil disobedience, and trace how Ted's authenticity converted a cynical gotcha journalist into someone looking for deeper, more meaningful work, ending with The Richmond Way's renunciation of self-promotion.
- ch. 30 "Notes" **·** Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, Simone de Beauvoir — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; Woman as the Other — Quinn argues Rebecca is the show's Stoic: Marcus Aurelius's maxims about judgments, obstacles, and morning meetings with the ungrateful map onto her recovery from Rupert - accepting reality, forgiving as a choice within her control, the lion power pose, 'every disadvantage has its advantage' - with the dichotomy of control as her operating principle. Framed by Gen X self-reliance and second-wave feminism (Friedan's problem with no name, Beauvoir's woman as Other under Rupert), the chapter follows her from vengeful boss to mentor of Keeley and Nora, Bantr-era 'bossgirl' dater of Sam, and finally the Richmond family's matriarch.
- ch. 31 "Notes" **·** Martha Nussbaum — Forgiveness; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Mills asks why Nate is more hurt than relieved when Roy declines to headbutt him over kissing Keeley, while Jamie had to fight for forgiveness. Using Strawson's reactive attitudes - anger is how we take someone seriously as a member of the moral community - plus Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness and Radzik's transactional account of amends, she argues Roy's instant absolution dismisses Nate as a pitiable non-agent rather than a culpable moral equal. The chapter contrasts this with earned, transactional forgiveness across Season 3 (Nate apologizing to Will and Ted, Beard's own story of betrayal and forgiveness), showing the headbutt as the recognition Nate needed.
- ch. 32 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Forgiveness; Philosophy of Love; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.

## Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 4 "Title" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
