- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Confucius, Laozi, Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche — Authenticity; Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Taoism (Daoism); Wu Wei (effortless action) — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Laozi, Confucius, Zhuangzi — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way); The Junzi (exemplary person); Yin and Yang — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Confucius, Laozi, Immanuel Kant — Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Tao (the Way) — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Xunzi, Confucius, Mencius — Li (ritual propriety); Xiao (filial piety); Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual) — Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Mencius, Confucius — Human Nature Is Good; Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety) — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Immanuel Kant — Yin and Yang; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Jameson and Brace read Sense and Sensibility and Brokeback Mountain through Burke's and Gilpin's aesthetics of the sublime, the beautiful and the picturesque, mapped onto the Chinese yin/yang and qi of landscape. In Sense and Sensibility, manicured French/Brownian gardens (beautiful, sanctioned) versus wild picturesque nature (sublime, passionate) mirror Elinor's controlled sense and Marianne's storm-caught sensibility, with Willoughby's rescue and Brandon's steadiness keyed to landscape. In Brokeback Mountain the masculine sublime wilderness (yang) versus feminine confining civilization (yin) is built through tightly framed interiors, sweeping exteriors and an 'aesthetics of isolation' that exposes American freedom as a costly illusion for Ennis and Jack.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Xunzi, Mencius, Confucius, Zhuangzi, Laozi — Li (ritual propriety); Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual); Human Nature Is Good — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics; The Categorical Imperative; The Harm Principle — Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Wu Wei (effortless action) — Kroustallis reads Lust, Caution through perception rather than hidden emotion, arguing Wong Chia Chi abandons the disengaged, sight-only aesthetic of Mrs. Mak and comes to perceive Mr. Yee's world with her whole engaged body. He uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to justify the three graphic sex scenes as bodily, essentially ambiguous cognition (the lipstick-marked cup, the flat key as motor intentionality) that links perception directly to action without unconscious representations. He frames Wong's development toward harmony via Fang Dongmei's neo-Confucian 'creative creativity' and a yin-yang polarity of meek and strong, with rain and jasmine flowers as an engaged natural environment.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on the Soul; Personal Identity; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Michel Foucault — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Dale and Foy argue that across Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hulk and Brokeback Mountain, Lee presents a pessimistic, Sartrean philosophy of identity in which authentic selves are irreconcilable with a hostile social world. They read Jen's caged gender rebellion and Jade Fox's rejection, Bruce's suppressed origins and rage-fueled transformation, and Ennis and Jack's concealed love as hidden identities that produce dislocation, deception and disorder. Invoking Kierkegaard and Heidegger's dasein on authenticity and Foucault's Discipline and Punish, they show society disciplining deviance so each hero is displaced or destroyed—Jack beaten to death like Matthew Shepard, the Hulk exiled to the Amazon.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jacques Lacan — Ahimsa (nonviolence); The Mirror Stage; One-Dimensional Man — Zietsma reads Hulk and Taking Woodstock as antiwar films that subvert the hegemonic culture of heroic violence, fitting Lackey's category of universal (Gandhian/early-Christian) pacifism. He argues both films disturb their genre's expected narrative and demasculinize the hero: Elliot the gay nonviolent hero and the transgender vet Vilma, and a weeping Hulk who is rescued by Betty and finally gives up his power rather than kill David Banner. He reads the bathroom-mirror 'Puny human' scene as an inverted Lacanian mirror stage unmasking America's violent militarism, framing the Vietnam War and war on terror as violence that only begets more violence.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** The Buddha, Judith Butler, Michel Foucault — Heteronormativity; Compassion (karuna); Impermanence (anicca) — Kang argues Lee's Taking Woodstock desexualizes and 'recloset[s]' Elliot Tiber's gay coming-out memoir, substituting a fluid 'queer' openness for Tiber's political gay identity and framing his homosexuality as an incidental, situationally-straight product of the festival (the woman-centered threesome, the chaste kiss with Paul). Drawing on Sedgwick, Butler and Foucault's history of sexuality, she critiques how the film neutralizes homophobia and omits the gay Buddhist mentor Georgette, whose teaching on karma, samsara and dukkha grounds Tiber's self-acceptance and unconditional love—reducing a gay everyman's struggle to one 'not-normal freak' among a hundred thousand.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Jean-Paul Sartre, Harry Frankfurt, Aristotle — Philosophy of Love; Struggle for Recognition; The Look (hell is other people) — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; The Absurd — Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Carl Jung, The Buddha — Being-Toward-Death; Zen Buddhism; The Tao (the Way) — Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli, Sun Tzu — The Ends Justify the Means; Virtù and Fortuna; Just War Theory — Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.

## The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Personal Identity; Mind–Body Dualism; Eternal Recurrence — LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.
- ch. 9 "Part 1. On Being and Not Being One’s Self" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Charlie Kaufman, Screenwriter" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Baruch Spinoza, Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions — Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).
- ch. 11 "On Being John Malkovich and Not Being Yourself" **·** René Descartes, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Michel Foucault, John Dewey, Plato — Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body); Discipline and Docile Bodies — Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.
- ch. 12 "The Divided Self Kaufman, Kafka, Wittgenstein, and Human Nature" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; Language Games — Von der Ruhr reads Human Nature through Kafka's 'A Report to an Academy,' whose humanized ape frames the film's inverted arc (Puff raised as ape, civilized by Nathan, then reverted by Lila). Using Nietzsche's herd passage and Norman Malcolm on animal thought, he argues the human–animal difference is one of kind, so Lila's Rousseauian idealization of Puff as 'uncontaminated by civilization' and Puff's claim that 'words are evil' are confused. Invoking Wittgenstein's view that art should teach and that lying presupposes truth-telling, he faults the film's bleak, self-referential loves while crediting it as a mirror of the viewer's own thinking.
- ch. 13 "Unauthorized Autobiography Truth and Fact in Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Sigmund Freud, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plutarch — LaRocca uses Chuck Barris's claim to be a CIA assassin to argue that autobiography makes truth rather than reports fact: unlike the earnest Confessions of Augustine and Rousseau, Barris flaunts the narrator's unreliability, and (following Stanley Fish) the autobiographer 'cannot lie' because whatever he writes is the truth about himself. Kaufman amplifies Barris's love of Carlyle's Sartor Resartus — 'the tailor, retailored' — to cast writing as patchwork quotation, contrasting Nietzsche's 'drive to truth' against literary truth. The essay closes on Clooney's literalizing adaptation, which deauthorized Kaufman, to reopen the auteur-vs-screenwriter question of who authored the film.
- ch. 14 "Part 2. Being, or Trying to Be, with Others" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" **·** Aristotle, Michel de Montaigne — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Philosophy of Love — Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
- ch. 16 "I Don’t Know, Just Wait Remembering Remarriage in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson, William James — Philosophy of Love; Eternal Recurrence; The Private Language Argument — Day reads Eternal Sunshine as Cavell's Hollywood comedy of remarriage: the kaleidoscopic middle in 'Joel's head' is the couple's remarriage conversation, a 'green world' where they invent a shared childhood and learn what it means to have memories together. Against a tape-recorder model of memory, he invokes the later Wittgenstein's private-language argument to argue there is no private memory — what Joel remembers he can return to Clementine in conversation. He rereads Mary's Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence, not as the end of regret but as affirming it (Joel's 'I wish I'd stayed. I do.'), and claims viewers themselves remember the erased past for the pair across the hallway's ten seconds of waiting.
- ch. 17 "Charlie Kaufman, Philosophy, and the Small Screen" **·** Judith Butler — Heteronormativity; Gender Performativity; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Chambers reads Kaufman's TV sitcom Ned and Stacey through queer theory, arguing its marriage-of-convenience premise stages a critique of 'the normal.' Because Ned and Stacey only play at being husband and wife and never desire the romantic telos, the show troubles heteronormativity more than the openly gay Will & Grace, whose characters chase marriage and family. Chambers uses Butler's Lacanian notion of masquerade to claim there is no 'real' husband or wife beneath the role, only role-playing, and ties this to the philia (not eros) bond of the leads and to the masquerade running through Kaufman's films.
- ch. 18 "The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, William James, Thomas Nagel — The Private Language Argument; What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Personal Identity; Stream of Consciousness — Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).
- ch. 19 "Part 3. Being in the World, Partially" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Living a Part Synecdoche, New York, Metaphor, and the Problem of Skepticism" **·** Martin Heidegger, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Philosophical Skepticism; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Deming argues that Caden Cotard's attempt to build a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse enacts a skepticism toward the givenness of life—the belief that reality can be denied and remade as art. Drawing on Cavell's claim that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' and Heidegger on world, earth, and dwelling, he shows the play traps Caden rather than freeing him: to represent the world is to be flung outside it. He invokes Wittgenstein's image of language as an ancient city one can never step outside of, and Baudrillard's simulacra (Caden even considers titling the play 'Simulacrum'), to explain why the literal doubling fails to yield the 'true self' Caden seeks.
- ch. 21 "“There’s No More Watching” Artifice and Meaning in Synecdoche, New York and Adaptation" **·** Martin Heidegger — Authenticity; Existentialism — Hill argues that Adaptation and Synecdoche, New York both dramatize artists (the character Charlie Kaufman and Caden Cotard) struggling to portray 'real life' through artifice, and that Kaufman achieves authenticity not through neorealist naturalism but through surrealism and fantasy. He distinguishes the existentialist sense of authenticity—living self-awarely and choosing outside a community's rules (via Macquarrie)—from cinematic realism, tracing Kaufman's fusion of inner and outer life to Fellini's 8½. The chapter reads Synecdoche as an unflinching, near-horror examination of what it costs to make honest art, concluding its buried message is that creation is meaningless unless shared.
- ch. 22 "Human Nature and Freedom in Adaptation" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; Theory of Forms — Ganssle uses Adaptation's four main characters to test Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence against Walker Percy's account of immanence and transcendence. Laroche, endlessly adaptable ('Done with fish'), embodies Sartrean radical freedom and pure immanence; Donald owns his love ('You are what you love, not what loves you') and lives without bad faith; Orlean and Charlie are paralyzed in bad faith, unable to choose. Ganssle contrasts Sartre's rejection of a fixed human nature (grounded in atheism, against Plato's and Augustine's Forms) with Percy's view that persons are unlike infinitely mutable orchids, arguing the film sides with Percy: the antiessentialist self is 'lost in the cosmos.'
- ch. 23 "Synecdoche, in Part" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Michel de Montaigne — Amor Fati (love of fate); Transcendentalism; Philosophical Skepticism — Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.
- ch. 24 "Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power; Eternal Recurrence; Perspectivism; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.
- ch. 25 "Inconclusive Unscientific Postscript Late Remarks on Kierkegaard and Kaufman" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom); The Leap of Faith; Subjectivity Is Truth — LaRocca pairs Kaufman with Kierkegaard on anxiety as the constitutive human condition—not worry but 'the dizziness of freedom,' the awareness of radical possibility. He argues both use pseudonymity and 'indirect communication' to distance author from work so the audience confronts its own individuality: Kierkegaard's Haufniensis/Climacus, Kaufman's Caden Cotard and the character 'Charlie Kaufman' in Adaptation. The chapter analyzes acting as inhabitation vs. impersonation (Being John Malkovich vs. The Talented Mr. Ripley), the diegesis/mimesis layering (Plato and Aristotle) of Kaufman's doubles and replicas, and repetition/recursion as the Kierkegaardian leap that love, like faith, demands—so 'the end is built into the beginning.'
- ch. 26 "Filmography" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "List of Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Introduction" **·** Martin Buber, G.W.F. Hegel, René Descartes, Sigmund Freud, Thomas Hobbes — I–Thou Relation; Master–Slave Dialectic; Personal Identity; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film. It reads Following's needy Young Man through Buber's I/Thou (existing fully only when a Thou acknowledges you) and Hegel's master/slave dependence between Cobb and his mark, casts Inception's spinning top as a version of Descartes's dream argument about telling the real from the constructed, and invokes Hobbes when the Joker introduces 'a little anarchy' into Gotham. It frames Doodlebug as Nolan's most Freudian film and Interstellar as uniting personal identity, moral choice, and epistemology in Cooper's self-sacrifice.
- ch. 4 "Love, Value, and the Human Destiny in Interstellar" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — Humanity as an End in Itself; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Belluomini and Dunn use Interstellar's clash between Cooper's partial parental love and Professor Brand's species-level 'Plan B' to ask why the survival of humanity matters and what 'saving humanity' means. Drawing on Aristotle, they treat Cooper's daughter Murph as 'another self' loved as an end in itself and tie the good to individual happiness (eudaimonia), so 5,000 faceless embryos could never be the intrinsic good a real family is. They then turn to Kant to argue humans have unconditional value (dignity) as rational beings, which both grounds a reason to preserve the species AND condemns Brand's 'monstrous lie' as treating people merely as means to an end they do not share.
- ch. 5 "“Are You Watching Closely ”" **·** David Hume, John Locke, John Rawls, Thomas Hobbes — The Social Contract; Natural Rights; Justice as Fairness — Foy and Dale argue that Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy stages a conservative critique of liberal political theory. They set Locke's pre-political natural rights and Rawls's priority-of-rights ('each person possesses an inviolability... that even the welfare of society cannot override') against a Batman who wiretaps all of Gotham, tortures, and kidnaps Lau, treating social order as the thing that overrides individual rights. Batman is cast as a Humean conservative who grounds authority in habit and custom rather than an imaginary social contract, invoking Carl Schmitt's 'state of exception' (the Roman dictator Dent describes) and Burke's non-elected natural aristocracy to justify the billionaire elite Wayne saving a liberal order from the Joker's nihilism and Bane's Marxist-Leninist revolution.
- ch. 6 "Spinning Tops and Brains in Vats" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Robert Nozick, René Descartes, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato, Sextus Empiricus, William James — Subjectivity Is Truth; The Experience Machine; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — This bundle of essays reads Memento and Inception as epistemology. Knepp uses Peirce's icon/index/symbol triad and Plato's Phaedrus critique of writing to show Leonard Shelby's tattoos and Polaroids give a false illusion of permanent truth (he tattoos Teddy as 'John G.' on purpose). Hoffman uses Kierkegaard's subjective truth to contrast Leonard, who lies to himself while pretending to gather objective 'facts', with Cobb, who takes a Kierkegaardian leap of faith and walks away from the spinning totem to embrace his children. Watson runs the Cartesian/Pyrrhonist dream argument against Inception's totems, arguing beliefs can be valuable via intellectual virtue even if unverifiable, and Lindenmuth pits Nozick's experience machine against Cobb's choice of real children over the dream-shade of Mal to argue reality matters more than pleasure.
- ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Andy Clark, David Chalmers, Jacques Lacan, John Locke, Jean-Paul Sartre, Augustine of Hippo, Friedrich Nietzsche, Hans-Georg Gadamer — The Extended Mind; Personal Identity; The Dialectic; Personal Identity (memory theory) — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films. Fosl argues Nolan's selves (Leonard, Bill in Following, the Borden twins, Bruce Wayne) are unstable narratives signified through manipulable objects, invoking Locke on memory-based identity, Augustine on memoria, Nietzsche on forgetting and Sartre/Gadamer on the manipulable past. LaRocca applies Clark and Chalmers's Extended Mind Thesis to Memento, arguing Leonard's tattoos and Polaroids are literal external memories whose deliberate falsification ('Don't believe his lies') makes him morally culpable for murder. Willis uses Lacan's gaze and objet a to read Following's voyeur-becomes-viewed structure and 'the box' as a lure. McGowan reads Interstellar through Hegel: the mysterious 'they' who opened the wormhole are revealed as future humanity, dissolving substance into subject and licensing Cooper's retroactive causality as the 'ghost' who saves Murph.

- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Aristotle, Alasdair MacIntyre, Socrates — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — The editors' introduction argues that Eastwood, though no academic, does 'practical philosophy' through his films as a craftsman who inherits and then revises genres (revising the Western in Unforgiven, rethinking rugged individualism in Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino). Invoking MacIntyre's claim that we are only co-authors of interlocking narratives, it reads Eastwood's focus on decisive moral choices (Francesca's refusal to leave in Bridges of Madison County, Butch Haynes in A Perfect World) as a 'laboratory of moral psychology' echoing Aristotle's 'choice discriminates character.' It ties his concern with loss, justice, and Aristotelian friendship and flourishing (Grinnell on Million Dollar Baby) to a Socratic 'know thyself,' arguing his philosophizing is implicit and nonverbal rather than argued in words.
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Friedrich Nietzsche, Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus — Stoicism; The Death of God; Existentialism; The Dichotomy of Control — Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Alvin Plantinga, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine of Hippo — The Problem of Evil; The Five Ways; Faith and Reason — Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — Self-Reliance; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Couch reads two Eastwood gestures — Josey Wales's spitting and the Man with No Name's smiling — as expressions of self-reliance that generate a 'motivational polarity,' simultaneously repelling and attracting others. Drawing on Miller and Mason on contempt and disgust as moral attitudes, and on evolutionary coalitional psychology, he argues Wales's 'contemptuous disgust' (spitting on dead bounty hunters, at the Comancheros) marks moral boundaries and forms surrogate-family coalitions, while the Man with No Name's deceptive non-Duchenne smile in the Dollars trilogy conceals lethal intent yet occasionally shows genuine compassion (freeing Tuco). The self-reliant individual, adhering to his own moral compass, inevitably divides others into allies and foes.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes, Jürgen Habermas — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Natural Law; The Social Contract — Flynn contends certain Westerns depict a 'law that stands behind the law' — a moral/natural law transcending and grounding the weak civil order — using High Noon, where Hadleyville proves unworthy of Kane's rectitude. High Plains Drifter evolves this into divine, supernatural retribution: the nameless Stranger, a pale-horse agent of apocalyptic justice, precisely punishes Lago for abetting the marshal Duncan's murder (whipping the whippers, renaming the town Hell). Flynn argues this vision is dangerous: by insulating justice from deliberation and depicting it as revelatory and divine, it derides the discursive, civil processes (Habermas-style communicative action) actually needed to make justice 'ours,' risking mere private vengeance — 'deserve's got nothin' to do with it.'
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Sigmund Freud, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, Henry David Thoreau — The Unconscious; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Master and Slave Morality — Gilmore reads Unforgiven as Socratic wisdom done in images — the recognition that we do not know what we really want. He analyzes the opening montage (shadowed windows, the cut prostitute) as Freud's Primal Scene, the audience forced to interpret sex and violence without adequate concepts, which he calls the primal scene of philosophy itself. Drawing on Huizinga's Homo Ludens and Leone's Once Upon a Time in the West, he frames the gunslinger as a 'Bad Man at play' for mortal stakes, free of the repressions civilization demands. William Munny's banal Christianized 'goodness' versus the terrifying Bad Man that drink releases dramatizes Thoreau's 'quiet desperation' and a godless world where deserving is irrelevant.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Grinnell applies Aristotle's classification of friendship (utility, pleasure, and complete character-friendship between equals in excellence) to Million Dollar Baby and Gran Torino. Frankie/Maggie and Walt/Thao begin as incomplete, utility relationships across barriers of age, sex, and culture, then ripen into character-friendships of 'other selves' who pursue each other's good. He resolves the apparent paradox that friendship demands bringing about a death: Frankie euthanizes Maggie against his own wishes to honor her autonomy and whole-life excellence, while Walt engineers his own death and deceives Thao to spare him a vengeance that would destroy his character — each an Aristotelian sacrifice of self-interest for the friend that preserves the friendship's excellence.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Karen Hoffman traces the gun across Eastwood's career as an evolving argument about violence: Dirty Harry's .44 Magnum ends violence without cost to the shooter, High Plains Drifter and Pale Rider treat the gun as righteous retribution and a proof of masculine honor, but Unforgiven shows William Munny killing men who may not deserve it and dwelling on how killing brutalizes the shooter. In Gran Torino Walt Kowalski finally gives up the gun entirely, walking unarmed into Spider's gang and being gunned down in a Christlike pose so that Thao is spared both victimhood and the guilt of killing. The chapter argues Eastwood shifts from celebrating the gun as physical protection to warning of the psychological damage violence inflicts on its user.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Aristotle — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Knight and McKnight use Northrop Frye's master genres to chart Eastwood's move from romance (the superior hero who defends a community, as Jed Cooper in Hang 'Em High, the Stranger in High Plains Drifter, Harry Callahan in Dirty Harry) toward tragedy with Mystic River, where Jimmy Markum kills the innocent Dave as his daughter's murderer and, like Oedipus, recognizes his error too late. They read the law-versus-justice tension through Aristotle's point in the Nichomachean Ethics that the lawful and the just are not coterminous, and cite McClelland glossing Walt Kowalski's self-sacrifice in Gran Torino as a supreme instance of Aristotelian practical wisdom (phronesis) that solves multiple problems at once.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Phenomenology; The Hard Problem of Consciousness — Richard McClelland analyzes Eastwood's deployment of silence in Hereafter, cataloguing four types (from long soundless episodes during Marie's near-death experience to musical rests) and grounding them in neuroscience showing the auditory cortex represents silence as an object and spontaneously fills silence with self-generated signals. He argues Eastwood intuits how silence modulates attention and memory, limiting salient characters (Marie, George, the twins) so viewers attend to and remember key emotional beats. The chapter proposes 'neurocinematics' and a 'practical realism' whereby Eastwood's laconic, minimalist style and silences latch onto real, cross-cultural features of human cognition rather than merely subjective response.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** The Buddha, Aristotle — The Four Noble Truths; Immortality and the Soul — McClelland opens with the Buddha's claim that all life is suffering and reads Eastwood's aging-hero films (The Eiger Sanction, Firefox, Unforgiven, In the Line of Fire, Blood Work, Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, Gran Torino) as grounding two opposed inductions on the meaning of loss. The 'pessimistic induction' holds that many losses—Maggie's paralysis, Dave Boyle's abuse, Munny's dead—are irremediable, supporting an Aristotelian view that death dissolves the person with the body. The 'optimistic induction' draws on the science of ecological resilience to argue losses can be navigated with others' help; Walt's autonomous, meaning-making death exemplifies resilience. Hereafter's agnosticism about survival leaves Eastwood's own verdict on surviving death as 'I don't know.'
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Michel de Montaigne, Jean-Paul Sartre, Socrates — Authenticity; The Meaning of Life — Douglas McFarland argues that Hereafter is philosophical in Nehamas's sense of an 'art of living': its three characters (Marie, George, the boy Marcus) must fashion meaning in the face of absence and abandonment rather than settle the existence of an afterlife. He aligns their struggles with Augustine's grief over his mother's death in the Confessions, Montaigne's 'I portray not being but becoming' and his revision of Socrates' Phaedo claim that philosophy is practice for death, and Sartre's view that God's absence grounds the freedom to make meaning through work. George's turn from listening to the dead to genuinely seeing the living Marcus, and his letter to Marie, mark authentic self-fashioning in the here and now.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Absurd; Rebellion and Revolt; Existentialism — Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.

## The Philosophy of David Cronenberg

- ch. 1 "Cover Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Introduction" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity — Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'
- ch. 6 "Part 1. Body Horror and Bodily Transformation" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Fly and the Human Ironies of Disgust" **·** René Descartes, Martha Nussbaum — Mind–Body Dualism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Colin McGinn reads Cronenberg's The Fly as a meditation on human disgust and self-disgust: Seth Brundle's metamorphosis into Brundlefly does not cross an ontological boundary but dramatizes that the human being was already a loathsome organic monster, a 'god who shits.' McGinn ties this to a Cartesian mind-body duality (a fine mind trapped in a decaying insect shell mirrors our own embodiment) and, via Nussbaum, to how projected self-disgust stigmatizes despised groups; the cinematic image itself is an 'antidisgust medium' that lets us feel only quasi-disgust.
- ch. 8 "Tragedy and Terrible Beauty in A History of Violence and Eastern Promises" **·** Aristotle — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Personal Identity — Cynthia Freeland argues A History of Violence and Eastern Promises qualify as Aristotelian tragedies, using the Poetics' 'recognition and reversal' as Tom Stall is exposed as Joey Cusack and Nikolai's undercover identity is revealed. Analyzing the stairway sex scene, the Philadelphia gunfight, and Nikolai's naked bathhouse fight, she deploys Korsmeyer's notion of 'terrible beauty' (beauty in the horrific, like the bloody newborn) and Carroll/Gaut on empathy and identification, concluding both heroes commit an Aristotelian hamartia through their acceptance of violence.
- ch. 9 "Cronenberg as Scientist Antiessentialism, Sex as Remixing, and the View from Nowhere" **·** W.V.O. Quine, Thomas Nagel, Saul Kripke — Scientific Realism vs Anti-Realism; Personal Identity — Peter Ludlow argues Cronenberg's true horror is scientific antiessentialism: The Fly, Shivers, Videodrome, and eXistenZ collapse the supposedly essential boundaries between human and fly, organic and mechanical, real and virtual, sane and mad, good and evil. Drawing on Quine's rejection of essence, Kripke's empirical essentialism, and Darwinian biology, he reads Brundle's fusion and Renn's VCR-stomach as showing we have no essence; sex is 'remixing' of information to lock out parasites, and Cronenberg narrates from Nagel's impersonal 'view from nowhere' where humans are not special.
- ch. 10 "What Happens to Brundle Problems of Teleportation and Personal Identity in the Fly" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit — Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Paul Snowdon uses The Fly to press the metaphysics of teleportation and personal identity, asking whether the object leaving the first pod is identical to the one arriving or merely a replica (the reduplication problem). Adopting animalism, he argues Brundle likely ceases to exist at first teleportation, and that the fly-Brundle fusion is a new creature rather than Brundle, so Quaife's belief she is euthanizing Brundle is unsupported; a Lockean memory-based view (via Parfit) could vindicate her, but the audience's 'blind acceptance' of it gives that theory no evidential support.
- ch. 11 "Part 2. Psychology, Skepticism, and the Self" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "eXistenZial Angst" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Andy Clark, David Chalmers — Philosophical Skepticism; Brain in a Vat; The Extended Mind — Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.
- ch. 13 "“Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg" **·** Thomas Nagel, David Hume, Edmund Gettier — What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism — Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.
- ch. 14 "Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds" **·** Michel Foucault, Daniel Dennett, Sigmund Freud — Free Will vs Determinism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Personal Identity — Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.
- ch. 15 "Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg" **·** Sigmund Freud — Free Will vs Determinism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.
- ch. 16 "Self-Creation, Identity, and Authenticity A Study of A History of Violence and Eastern Promises" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Christine Korsgaard — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Personal Identity — Daniel Moseley distinguishes metaphysical from practical problems of personal identity, arguing A History of Violence and Eastern Promises explore the practical: who Tom/Joey and Nikolai really are, as a matter of self-creation and self-discovery of a 'practical identity' (Korsgaard). Using Sartre's bad faith and Cavell on movie-star 'individualities,' plus Charles Taylor's critique of individualist authenticity, he argues even the wicked Semyon exemplifies authenticity, so authenticity is not a moral ideal, and Nikolai's decent double life may be worth being less authentic.
- ch. 17 "Part 3. Words and Worldviews" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Fiction of Truth in Fiction Some Reflections on Semantics and eXistenZ" **·** David Lewis, Saul Kripke — Possible Worlds; Scientific Realism vs Anti-Realism — Graham Stevens uses eXistenZ to attack David Lewis's possible-world semantics for truth in fiction. Lewis analyzes 'according to the fiction f, p' as truth in the world(s) where the story is told as known fact; but eXistenZ's nested game-within-a-game ending, where even the characters cannot tell whether 'we are still in the game,' deliberately has no determinate world in which its events are fact. Stevens concludes fictions need not correspond to complete determinate worlds and proposes a stringent view: nothing is true in a fiction unless the fiction explicitly asserts it.
- ch. 19 "Re(ct)ifying Empty Speech Cronenberg and the Problem of the First Person" **·** Jacques Lacan, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilles Deleuze — The Mirror Stage; The Private Language Argument; The Unconscious — Brook W. R. Pearson examines the problem of the first person 'I' in Cronenberg through Lacan, Wittgenstein, and Deleuze/Guattari. He reads Spider's 'schizo-phonetic partition' and Tom/Joey's shifting use of 'I' in A History of Violence as Lacanian 'empty speech' and the narcissistic 'monument' of a censored unconscious chapter that resurfaces; Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Moore's paradox recast Joey's split as an illegitimate private language game, and Deleuze/Guattari's account of the other as a 'possible world' reframes the frightened face on the cinema screen.
- ch. 20 "The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers" **·** Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, Francis Bacon — The Culture Industry; One-Dimensional Man; The Idols of the Mind — R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.
- ch. 21 "From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Herbert Marcuse — Perspectivism; One-Dimensional Man; Allegory of the Cave — Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
- ch. 22 "List of Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 23 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of David Cronenberg" *(front)*

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
