- ch. 9 "Premonitions of a Log Lady" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "I. I am one hundred percent sure that we’re not completely sure" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. Dream Investigations of Tree House Operations" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — The Rochas argue that Agent Cooper's grab-bag of methods—rock-throwing named for suspects, dream clues, Tibetan intuition, plus Albert's forensics and Truman's teamwork—exposes the fallacy of scientism, the over-application of scientific method to what it cannot settle. They stress that Cooper's dream-derived 'deductive technique' is not really deductive but intuitive guesswork, and that real crime-solving (like the PCAST critique of forensic matching) is a messy blend of induction, instinct, and luck rather than the certainty shows like CSI pretend to. The chapter is really about the limits of scientific certainty in knowledge of the world.
- ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" **·** David Hume, The Buddha, Socrates, Carl Jung — Bundle Theory of Self; Atman and Brahman; Non-Self (anatman); The Unexamined Life — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- ch. 13 "3. Laura Palmer—Madonna and Whore" **·** Sigmund Freud — Objectification; The Male Gaze; Feminism — Jones argues that Laura Palmer is trapped in Freud's Madonna-whore complex—the male inability to see a woman as both virtuous and sexual—with BOB voicing the cultural signals that brand her 'dirty and sleazy' for her sexuality. He reads the Fireman/Giant, who births Laura as a golden antidote to BOB, as a patriarchal 'nice guy' whose idealizing Madonna role is as much a trap as the whore role BOB imposes. The chapter uses Laura's dual life to expose how patriarchy forces women to choose between two reductive poles, both maintained by male power.
- ch. 14 "4. Special Epistemic Agent Dale Cooper" **·** Alvin Goldman, Edmund Gettier — Reliabilism; Philosophical Skepticism — Written as Cooper's dictations to Diane, Rard uses the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge and the internalism/externalism debate to ask whether Cooper is justified in trusting dreams and visions in a world with supernatural forces. Through the Invitation to Love Ouija-board example she shows how a reliable but unrecognized source yields externally justified belief (reliabilism); Cooper then earns internal justification the way one tests a hypothesis—treating the giant's predictions ('man in a smiling bag', 'the owls are not what they seem', 'without chemicals he points') as testable predictions that come true, making him a 'special epistemic agent.'
- ch. 15 "5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Deontology — The Phillipses argue that abrasive forensic agent Albert Rosenfield is a model Kantian: his refusal to lie to spare Truman's feelings follows the formula of universal law, and his insistence that Truman be punished for the assault treats Truman as an autonomous end. They run Gordon Cole's manipulative lying through the universalizability test (it fails, unlike wanting pie), distinguish hypothetical from categorical imperatives via Cooper's rebuff of Audrey, and read Albert's 'I love you, Sheriff Truman' and Gandhi/King nonviolence as respect for persons as ends in themselves—duty done for the right reason.
- ch. 16 "II. My log does not judge" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "6. But What Does It Mean" **·** Immanuel Kant, Bertrand Russell, W.V.O. Quine — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Sense and Reference — Kreider argues Twin Peaks is less about determinate meaning than about handing viewers incomplete, underdetermined content to complete themselves. He reads the opening sequence's waterfalls and trees through Kant's aesthetic 'purposiveness without purpose,' the swaying traffic light and 'the full blossom of the evening' as Russell's incomplete symbols, and the range of legitimate interpretations through Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence; Susanne Langer's Feeling and Form adds that film creates a dreamlike virtual present, so the Part 8 atomic-bomb sequence works exactly as a dream we must interpret.
- ch. 18 "7. The Art of Playing Along with Dancing Little People" **·** Aristotle, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Plato — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); Potentiality and Actuality; Allegory of the Cave — Luzecky and Elsby argue that Twin Peaks is genuine art because, against Plato's condemnation of mimetic art as confusing copies to be exiled, it fulfills Aristotle's Poetics: art's essential function is dramatic reversal, surprising and transfixing us (Dougie's absurd casino win, the dancing Man from Another Place). Drawing on Gadamer's 'Spiel' (play/game) and Ingarden's schematized, incomplete artworks, they contend the work of art exists only as an ongoing rhythmic 'to and fro' between image and viewer—so we complete the Red Room scene by participating in it, moving it from potentiality to actuality.
- ch. 19 "8. I Sure Feel Uncomfortable Being in This Situation with You" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Rosenbaum argues that Twin Peaks deliberately engineers audience discomfort to make its point about the limits of human understanding and the blurred lines between categories we prefer distinct. He analyzes its straddling of melodrama and cringe comedy, its ambiguously diegetic Badalamenti score (a Brecht-like estrangement effect that ruptures our absorption), and its 'behavioral uncanny valley' plus bathos—Cooper casually chewing gum mid-murder-talk—arguing the real horror is epistemic uncertainty about who and what the townspeople really are.
- ch. 20 "III. It’s like I’m having the most beautiful dream and the most terrible nightmare at once" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Isaiah Berlin, The Buddha — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); Dharma — Potter and Cobb argue that Twin Peaks is a Romantic refusal of resolution: mysteries live by not being solved, so Lynch and Frost break the rules that stories need authors, protagonists who solve problems, and endings. They read Cooper's entrapment in a time loop through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati (quoting The Gay Science and The Will to Power), tie Wally Brando's Dharma speech and Isaiah Berlin's Roots of Romanticism to the theme, and argue the real 'story' is the endless meta-narrative co-created between the show and each viewer—Life itself as process without endpoint.
- ch. 22 "10. The Miss Twin Peaks Award Goes To . ." **·** Objectification; Feminism — Rard (as her 'doppelganger') distinguishes 'power-over' (getting others, mostly men, to do your bidding through beauty and manipulation) from the more stable 'power-to' (skills, resources, ability to act for oneself). She traces Josie Packard, who lives by manipulating Harry and Pete and is destroyed when surrounded by people immune to her charms, against Audrey Horne, who begins with the Norwegian stunt and the perfume-counter blackmail but transitions to running her father's business—acquiring real power—while Lana Milford's near-total charm and Nadine's adrenaline strength mark the extremes.
- ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" **·** Hannah Arendt, Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Feminism; Objectification — Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.
- ch. 24 "12. It’s Not About BOB—It Never Was" **·** Socrates, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Aristotle — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Apollonian and the Dionysian — Huntingford argues Lynch reveres madness as the true source of insight, casting Cooper as the Romantic 'mad poet' and Socratic divinely-inspired Oracle (Phaedrus) whose dream-forays reveal Twin Peaks' buried truths while 'normal' is the real evil. She frames BOB—born from the atomic blast—and garmonbozia through Kant's Sublime as the fearful, irregular power behind nature that exceeds reason, and reads Cooper's tragic ka (via Stephen King's Dark Tower) and shadow-self confrontation, plus Rousseau's ethics of truth-seeking, as the show's message: some mysteries are not meant to be solved, and to embrace that madness is freedom.
- ch. 25 "IV. The owls are not what they seem" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "13. Reason and Catharsis" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Aristotle, Albert Camus — The Absurd; Existentialism; Theory of Forms — Elsby and Luzecky argue that we compulsively rationalize Twin Peaks (tulpas, pale-horse omens, Diane-as-tulpa) the way we abstract concepts to tame the contradictory sensible world (Plato's long-and-short finger), but Lynch—especially in Part 8—deliberately thwarts this, exposing what Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols calls the post-Socratic tyranny of rationality. They offer an alternative reading of Aristotelian catharsis (via Trela): because the fictional world is not ours, we can experience its irrationality and absurdity, emotions purged of their tie to reality, as freedom rather than the existential despair the absurd would cause in our own world.
- ch. 27 "14. Diane, I Am Now Upside Down" **·** Plato — Personal Identity — McMullen and Phillips take up the paradox of fiction (Radford's 'How Can We Be Moved by the Fate of Anna Karenina?'): how can Cooper, whom we know is not real, cause genuine emotion? Using the criterion that what exists has causal powers, they reject the forgetting, suspension-of-disbelief, and reminds-us-of-real-people explanations, and adopt Amie Thomasson's view (Fiction and Metaphysics) that characters are real abstract artifacts—like laws or the United States. This lets them explain our parasocial interaction with Cooper (treating him as a friend over coffee) and wishful identification (wanting to be him) as responses to something that genuinely, if abstractly, exists.
- ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" **·** Aristotle, Augustine of Hippo — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics; The Problem of Evil — Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.
- ch. 29 "16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Johann Fichte — Personal Identity; Authenticity; Existentialism — Bunce reads Twin Peaks' pervasive doubling as dramatizing self-loss versus self-mastery. Cooper is good because he integrates his rational and mystical sides into an authentic whole, while BOB is a parasitic, one-dimensional inhabiting spirit and Laura chooses death over becoming BOB. He explains self-loss through La Rochefoucauld and Rousseau on amour-propre and the modern craving for esteem (Josie's masks versus Norma's refusal to become a brand), and traces the doppelganger motif from Jean Paul's satire of Fichte's clear I/not-I distinction to Dostoyevsky's The Double—arguing that, unlike Jean Paul, Twin Peaks affirms an authentic, whole self one is responsible for.
- ch. 30 "17. Through Plastic Our Secrets Seen" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer — The World as Will; Authenticity; The Unexamined Life — Winters uses Schopenhauer's World as Will and Idea to argue that the townsfolk (Shelly, Leo, Ben, Josie, Ed, and Laura) do not freely choose the lives they despise but are driven by the blind will, and so live double lives whose secrets a single death exposes. Laura, unlike the others who mismanage their passions, was denied the chance to develop her own values, so she pursued danger, drugs, and prostitution to see herself through her own eyes; death, he argues, reveals true character (the townsfolk's rush to bury her, their guilt), turning Socrates' unexamined-life dictum uneasy—sometimes what examination reveals is a monster we would rather not see.
- ch. 31 "V. I have no idea where this will lead us, but I have a definite feeling it will be a place both wonderful and" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "18. Repeating Twin Peaks" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Søren Kierkegaard, Jacques Lacan — Eternal Recurrence; The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real — Komel argues repetition is both a structural principle of the TV series (every show repeats its pilot) and the key to Twin Peaks, invoking Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Kierkegaard, and Lacan/Žižek. Using Lacan's aim-versus-goal of desire and Žižek's 'coffee without milk' as a positive absence, he reads Laura Palmer as a 'positive absence' around which the series turns, and shows the murder repetitions are out of order—Maddy's on-screen death precedes and retroactively produces Laura's in Fire Walk with Me. Laura's final scream in The Return, unlike its predecessors, subversively rewrites the original, so 'The Return' is really 'The Repetition' that undoes its origin.
- ch. 33 "19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie" **·** René Descartes, Jean Baudrillard — Mind–Body Dualism; The Absurd; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'
- ch. 34 "Bibliography" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Bookhouse Gang" *(notes)*
- ch. 36 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Documentary Film

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "00_LaRocca_Prelims.html" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "01_LaRocca_Chapter_000.html" **·** Plato, Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — LaRocca's introduction frames the whole volume through Plato's ancient 'quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and his critique of mimesis (Republic Book X), arguing that documentary film is just another kind of poetic imitation whose truth-claims deserve philosophical scrutiny. Drawing on Cavell's 'film was as if made for philosophy,' Kiarostami's 'cinema is nothing but fakery,' Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and Flaherty's 'sometimes you have to lie to tell the truth,' he shows how documentary blurs fiction/nonfiction and courts fabrication. He reads the digital turn (Manovich, Rodowick) as pushing cinema toward Baudrillard's hyperreal simulacra, images that no longer index reality but simulate it.
- ch. 4 "02_LaRocca_Chapter_001.html" **·** René Descartes, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Martin Heidegger, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Cogito; Philosophical Skepticism — Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.
- ch. 5 "03_LaRocca_Chapter_002.html" **·** Scientific Realism vs Anti-Realism — Carroll offers a critical reconstruction of Andre Bazin's film theory, separating Bazin's lasting achievement as a historian of film style from his dubious metaphysical commitments. He shows how Bazin championed 'spatial realism'—deep-focus, long-take sequence shots as in Renoir's Rules of the Game and Welles's Citizen Kane—against Soviet and Hollywood montage, on the grounds that unedited homogeneous space imparts authenticity, grants the spectator freedom to discover meaning, and preserves the ambiguity of reality. Carroll treats Bazin's claim that recording realism is cinema's essential destiny as an anti-realist target to be demythologized, defending the study of film-realist style while rejecting the essentialist evolutionary scheme underneath it.
- ch. 6 "04_LaRocca_Chapter_003.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Currie defines documentary via the distinction between a trace (a causal, intention-independent record like a photograph, footprint, or death mask) and testimony (an intention-mediated representation like a painting or written history), placing simulations between them. A film is an ideal documentary when its images' 'trace content' coheres with its narrative, whereas Casablanca or All the President's Men has a separate 'narrative content' representing fictional characters. He grades real cases—Night Mail's faked mail-sorting, Roger and Me's rearranged chronology, Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will—by degree of coherence, and argues trace content is nonconceptual while narrative content is conceptual, so most docudramas are really fictions.
- ch. 7 "05_LaRocca_Chapter_004.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Plantinga attacks subjectivist theories that locate the fiction/nonfiction distinction solely 'in the mind of the audience,' using the fable of a naive student, Michael, who takes such theories literally and cites Star Wars and E.T. as sources in a history paper on space travel. Against Branigan and Eitzen ('When is a documentary?'), he argues you cannot legitimately comprehend a fiction film nonfictionally because that confuses a document with a documentary. He proposes a three-part account: the distinction resides in cultural convention, in the film's designed features, and in the viewer's reception, hinging on the filmmaker's 'assertive stance' versus 'fictive stance'—like the difference between a screwdriver and a hammer.
- ch. 8 "06_LaRocca_Chapter_005.html" **·** Martin Heidegger, Simone de Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Being-Toward-Death; Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology — Sobchack offers a semiotic phenomenology of how real death is represented in documentary, arguing that death itself always exceeds and confounds indexical representation—we never see death, only dying and the corpse. Using Aries on the modern taboo-ing of natural death, Barthes on the traumatic photograph, and the Zapruder assassination footage whose frame-by-frame scrutiny yields only mystification, she shows why violent, abrupt mortification of the lived body is the most effective cinematic sign of death. Drawing on Heidegger's Being-toward-death and its deferral, Beauvoir's 'no such thing as a natural death,' and Merleau-Ponty's lived body, she classifies documentary's ethical 'gazes' at death (accidental, helpless, endangered, interventional, humane, professional) as inscriptions of the filmmaker's moral stance in an embodied ethical space.
- ch. 9 "07_LaRocca_Chapter_006.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Tom Gunning argues that pre-WWI 'actuality' film is a distinct form from Griersonian 'documentary,' governed by what he calls the 'view' aesthetic: films (phantom rides, travelogs, 'process films' like D'ou Viennent les Faux Cheveux or A Day in the Life of an English Coal Miner) that mime the act of looking and display rather than embedding images in an argument. He locates the shift to documentary in WWI propaganda films such as Londen in Oorlogstijd, where images become evidence within a discursive claim. The essay is film historiography rather than an application of a named philosopher, so no taxonomy slug fits its core argument.
- ch. 10 "08_LaRocca_Chapter_007.html" **·** Anthropocentrism — Scott MacDonald contrasts Disney's True-Life Adventures (The Vanishing Prairie, The Living Desert), which anthropomorphize animals into 1950s middle-class nuclear families and naturalize Manifest Destiny, with Jean Painleve's science films (The Seahorse, Acera, The Vampire), which choose organisms precisely because their sexual and reproductive lives defy conventional human morality. Using Nichols's claim that nature film lacks documentary's 'voice,' MacDonald argues nature films always carry ideology, and that Microcosmos and the anti-anthropocentric attention to insects show the genre's untapped philosophical value against the humanities/sciences split dramatized in Su Friedrich's The Head of a Pin.
- ch. 11 "09_LaRocca_Chapter_008.html" *(no index entry yet)* — William Rothman reads Jean Rouch's ten-minute single-take The Drums of Yore: Tourou and Bitti (and the later Dogon films Funeral at Bongo and Ambara Dama) to argue that Rouch's 'cine-trance' and 'one take/one sequence' method fuse anthropology, philosophy and poetry, so that the camera's mere presence provokes the Songhay dancer's possession by the god Kure. Leaning wholly on Stanley Cavell's ontology of film (the world on film as 'skin of the world,' the photograph's object as its subject), Rothman claims filming itself possesses Rouch, revealing the invisible in the visible. Its governing philosopher, Cavell, is absent from the taxonomy.
- ch. 12 "10_LaRocca_Chapter_009.html" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); Transcendentalism — William Day argues that Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams, filming the 32,000-year-old Chauvet Cave paintings in 3D, works not by preserving a past but by transfiguring the present, placing the viewer in a 'mythological relation to time.' He reads three literary precursors to this cinematic 'doubleness'—Emerson's 'History' and 'The American Scholar' (the past made 'now'), Thoreau's spectator-self in Walden's 'Solitude,' and Weil's 'renunciation of time'—as antecedents to Cavell's ontology of film. The Fred Astaire shadow-dance from Swing Time, spliced into the cave footage, becomes Day's emblem of what becomes of things on film: the shadows dance on after Astaire stops.
- ch. 13 "11_LaRocca_Chapter_010.html" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Martin Heidegger, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Transcendentalism — Pederson and Zimmermann analyze Vincent Grenier's 'avant-doc' videos (Color Study: Slaterville New York, Watercolor: Fall Creek, Les Chaises, Armoire) as interventions in the philosophy of documentary landscape. They read his flattened tableau shots and digitally manipulated color fields against the Hudson River School and Ansel Adams's transcendentalist (Emersonian/Thoreauvian) American sublime, invoking Timothy Murray's Heideggerian poiesis of habitats and Baudrillard's simulation/simulacra to argue Grenier replaces representation of nature with simulation—e.g., the pigeon reacting to its mirror image in Armoire—dissolving the divide between the natural and the technological.
- ch. 14 "12_LaRocca_Chapter_011.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Ariella Azoulay reflects on her film Civil Alliances—Palestine 1947–48, built from Haganah-archive documents of over a hundred civil agreements between Jews and Arabs (such as the Deir Yassin/Givat Shaul good-neighbor pact) that historians erased to sustain a narrative of enduring national conflict. Filming twenty-five Arabs and Jews reciting these promises around a reconstructed 1947 map, she argues that 'sovereign citizenship' is a colonial historiographic tool and that these archival promises are not about the past but a renewable civil future. The argument is political and archival rather than an application of a taxonomy philosopher.
- ch. 15 "13_LaRocca_Chapter_012.html" **·** John Dewey — Experience and Education — Diana Allan traces a single 1948 photograph of the Palestinian fisherman Said Otruk—the basis of her video portrait Still Life—to examine the tension between the evidentiary and the affective in documentary photographs. Drawing on Dewey's Art as Experience distinction between 'perception' that is fresh and alive and 'recognition' arrested for another purpose, plus Bazin, Barthes's punctum, Berger and Cavell, she argues that when seeing is subordinated to political/national purpose the image's resolution is reduced, and that her own misremembering of the photo mirrors Said's, revealing memory's mediated, refracted temporality.
- ch. 16 "14_LaRocca_Chapter_013.html" **·** René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza, George Berkeley, Gilles Deleuze — The Cogito; Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Mind–Body Dualism — Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'
- ch. 17 "15_LaRocca_Chapter_014.html" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Henri Bergson — Duration (durée) — Bernadette Wegenstein examines her own cinema-verite practice in The Good Breast (and See You Soon Again), arguing that verite 'provokes' rather than merely produces truth through the filmmaker's participatory presence. She grounds this in Italian neorealism via Bazin (the real 'aimed at,' not re-presented) and Deleuze's Cinema II 'time-image'—a Bergsonian cinema 'of the seer' attuned to lived duration. Through her breast-cancer patient-characters (Doris, Carol, Debra, Shelia) and the surgeon Dr. Schnaper's trip to Saint Agatha's Catania, she shows how editing calls forth an 'alternate reality' and an existential (Kracauerian) realism.
- ch. 18 "16_LaRocca_Chapter_015.html" **·** Martin Heidegger, G.W.F. Hegel, Karl Marx, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Question Concerning Technology; The Dialectic; Allegory of the Cave — Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.
- ch. 19 "17_LaRocca_Chapter_016.html" **·** Karl Marx, Antonio Gramsci, G.W.F. Hegel — Alienation; Cultural Hegemony; Ideology and False Consciousness — Elan Gamaker analyzes Ken Loach's Cathy Come Home and Ken Russell's London Moods and Shelagh Delaney's Salford as British social-realist 'documentary style,' arguing that agency (in the Marxist sense of free choice against structure) is progressively eroded from funder to filmmaker to subject to viewer. He shows how Grierson's neo-Hegelian faith in state institutions turned documentary into 'good propaganda' that alienates the underclass it claims to serve, so the form reproduces cultural hegemony and false consciousness. Loach's stylization and Russell's ambiguity strip the depicted subjects of voice, though Gamaker holds that a later viewer's shifting interpretation can partly restore agency.
- ch. 20 "18_LaRocca_Chapter_017.html" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Baruch Spinoza, Henri Bergson — Duration (durée); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Phenomenology — Selmin Kara reads Victor Erice's Dream of Light (The Quince Tree Sun), about the painter Antonio Lopez trying to capture a quince tree in shifting autumn light, as a case for a 'new materialist' ontology of documentary against Bill Nichols-style representationalism. Drawing on Deleuze via De Landa's actual/virtual continuum, Spinoza's and Bergson's vital-matter lineage, and Bennett's 'vibrant matter,' she argues the film's dream sequence of the operator-less camera, dimmer and rotting fruit foregrounds the mediation rather than the mastery of light. She proposes updating Grierson's 'creative treatment of actuality' to 'the creative treatment of actuality and virtuality,' treating filmic and profilmic matter as intra-acting agents.
- ch. 21 "19_LaRocca_Chapter_018.html" **·** William of Ockham — Ockham's Razor; Theory of Forms — Rick Altman dismantles four and a half 'fallacies' that let film theory ignore sound: the historical fallacy (sound as a late add-on), the ontological fallacy (image alone is cinema), the reproductive fallacy (recording reproduces rather than represents sound), the nominalist fallacy, and the half-fallacy of indexicality. In the nominalist section he explicitly frames the dispute over whether the 'same' sound heard from different seats shares a real identity as the medieval realism-versus-nominalism debate, casting Plato and Augustine as the realists and William of Ockham as the nominalist, and warning that ultra-nominalism about sound jeopardizes shared understanding. He uses Peirce's index/icon/symbol distinction to argue electronics has desacralized cinema's indexicality.
- ch. 22 "20_LaRocca_Chapter_019.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg's DOGMA 95 manifesto and its 'Vow of Chastity' declare a rescue action against the 'individual film,' the auteur concept (dismissed as bourgeois romanticism) and the cinema of illusion and cosmetic trickery. The ten vows bind the director to location shooting, diegetic sound, handheld camera, no optical work, no superficial action or genre, the here-and-now, and no directorial credit, swearing off personal taste in order to 'force the truth out of' characters and settings. As a primary-source polemic it advances an anti-illusionist, anti-individualist ethic of documentary-adjacent truth-telling rather than applying any named philosopher.
- ch. 23 "21_LaRocca_Chapter_020.html" *(no index entry yet)* — Werner Herzog's Minnesota Declaration is a thirteen-point primary-source polemic attacking Cinema Verite as 'the truth of accountants' that confounds fact with truth and merely photographs the 'ancient ruins of facts.' Herzog insists on a deeper 'poetic, ecstatic truth' that is mysterious and reachable only through fabrication, imagination and stylization, illustrated by his own Lessons of Darkness. The aphorisms about indifferent nature, the merciless ocean and 'you can't legislate stupidity' assert that documentary illumination lies beyond mere factual accuracy, but the piece names no philosopher and applies no taxonomy concept directly.
- ch. 24 "22_LaRocca_Chapter_021.html" *(no index entry yet)* — V. F. Perkins performs a close reading of the final four-minute shot of Frederick Wiseman's High School, where principal Dr. Haller reads a soldier's letter from Vietnam ('I am only a body doing a job') and claims it proves the school's success. Against the critical consensus (Kael, Bordwell and Thompson) that fixes only on the 'body doing a job' line, Perkins recovers two overlooked features: the gendered, maternal significance of the female reader, and Wiseman's stealthy editorial dropping of the sound a half-second before the image fades, leaving the principal's triumphant smile 'hollowed out.' He argues film grades its effects so that meaning can register below conscious notice, and warns that pause-and-rewind analysis steals the filmmaker's control over time, so close reading must stay answerable to a true experience of the movie.
- ch. 25 "23_LaRocca_Chapter_022.html" **·** Thomas Nagel, Tom Regan — What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'
- ch. 26 "24_LaRocca_Chapter_023.html" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Keith Dromm argues against the 'assertoric view' of documentary (Carroll's presumptive assertion, Currie's photographic traces, Plantinga's asserted veridical representation), contending that documentary films aim less to make assertions than to promote understanding. Drawing on Elgin, Zagzebski and Kvanvig on understanding as a holistic, skill-like cognitive success, and on Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations account of how understanding is taught through examples, practice and 'perspicuous representation,' he shows how Resnais's Night and Fog, Ken Burns, Errol Morris and Frederick Wiseman convey an understanding of their subject through creative technique. He treats reenactments as scientific-model-like idealizations that serve understanding even when they depart from literal truth.
- ch. 27 "25_LaRocca_Chapter_024.html" **·** Aristotle, Gilles Deleuze, Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — K. L. Evans argues that Adam McKay's The Big Short is fiction that nonetheless borrows documentary's assertive stance to make true claims about the 2008 subprime crisis and to insist ordinary viewers are smart enough to 'read the signs.' Using Aristotle on fiction (concerned with meaning not fact), Auerbach and the Heraclitean maxim that 'a man's character is his fate,' she distinguishes real people from 'characters' (living images) like the film's Michael Burry and Billy Beane, arguing that casting Brad Pitt signals the fictive stance. She invokes Deleuze's question about the 'mode of existence' of whoever pronounces a proposition to explain how the unreliable narrator Vennett can still narrate reliably, and how the film embeds indigestible factual 'markers' to refute the idea that the crisis was too complex to understand.
- ch. 28 "26_LaRocca_Chapter_025.html" **·** Martin Buber, Frantz Fanon — I–Thou Relation — Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.
- ch. 29 "27_LaRocca_Chapter_026.html" **·** Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Dasein (being-there); Embodiment (the lived body) — Michael Fried reads Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno's Zidane: A Twenty-First Century Portrait, seventeen synchronized cameras trained on Zinedine Zidane through one Real Madrid match, as a portrait that lays bare a new relation between absorption and being-beheld. Set within Fried's own absorption/theatricality tradition, the film shows Zidane wholly absorbed yet acutely conscious of eighty thousand spectators ('you are never alone'), which Fried reads via Heidegger's notion that even this 'bare' absorbed consciousness discloses a shared world (underscored by the halftime global news montage). He then stages the film as evidence in the McDowell-Dreyfus dispute over whether perception is conceptual, arguing that Zidane's 'expert coping' looks 'permeated by mindedness' (McDowell) rather than the non-conceptual absorbed coping Dreyfus, following Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology, describes.
- ch. 30 "28_LaRocca_Chapter_027.html" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, George Berkeley, David Hume, John Locke — Language Games; Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Everything Flows / Logos — Hagberg argues that Grant Gee's documentary Patience (After Sebald) achieves a truthful portrait of W. G. Sebald not by static correspondence but by enacting his shifting, connection-making sensibility, as displayed in The Rings of Saturn. He deploys Wittgenstein's remarks on aspect-perception and 'seeing-as' (the duck-rabbit, the 'lighting up of an aspect') to show that perception is always already inflected by imagination, memory and language-games, dismantling the empiricist picture of Locke, Hume and Berkeley in which brute sensation precedes reflection. Borges's 'The Garden of Forking Paths' and 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' supply the model of a Heraclitean flux of forking, mind-dependent connections, and the film's darkroom-like fading images and layered soundtrack are read as mimetically faithful to how a human sensibility perceives and remembers.
- ch. 31 "29_LaRocca_Chapter_028.html" **·** Martin Heidegger — Phenomenology; Dasein (being-there) — Warren draws on Chantal Akerman's own remark that she makes no distinction between documentary and fiction ('they are all just films') to argue that every Akerman work fuses observation and transfiguration, extension and 'intension.' Reading Je tu il elle, Jeanne Dielman, News from Home and From the Other Side, he shows how documentation of the mundane (Delphine Seyrig molding meatloaf, the Mexico border fence as a blank projection screen) is always already a fashioning, so the real becomes itself only through being made into film. He links the strange, surreal wonder Akerman's border and night-train images provoke to Heidegger's pre-Socratic question of Being ('How is it that we are?') and to a phenomenological attentiveness to the everyday, following Rancière and Cavell on film's double nature.
- ch. 32 "30_LaRocca_Chapter_029.html" **·** Feminism; Objectification — Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.
- ch. 33 "31_LaRocca_Chapter_030.html" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Socrates — Subjectivity Is Truth; Socratic Method (elenchus) — Hoffman reads Sarah Polley's Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer's The Act of Killing through Kierkegaard's account of indirect communication and 'deceiving into the truth.' Like the Socratic maieutic teacher who removes his authority and lets pupils reach their own conclusions, both directors withhold voice-of-God assertion and instead present multiple, conflicting, sometimes ethically monstrous storytellers, indulging their delusions to expose them. Polley stages fake Super-8 home movies and rival accounts of her mother and paternity so that truth becomes subjective appropriation rather than objective fact; Oppenheimer lets Indonesian genocide perpetrators reenact their killings as Hollywood fantasies until Anwar Congo is 'deceived' into his own broken self-awareness, indicting the regime that still celebrates him.
- ch. 34 "32_LaRocca_Chapter_031.html" **·** Jean Baudrillard, G.W.F. Hegel — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Simulation Hypothesis — LaRocca argues that Casey Affleck's I'm Still Here, in which Joaquin Phoenix faked a drug-addled retirement and hip-hop career, is best understood as a 'hoax-verite' whose collapse of the boundary between real and represented turns it into a Baudrillardian simulacrum and hyperreal artifact, a documentary of images 'without an original referent.' Against Noel Carroll's account of documentary as a film of presumptive assertion and Plantinga's assertive stance, LaRocca shows how Affleck exploited audience faith (staged home movies, the David Letterman 'beat down') so that the film's metaphysical, epistemic and ethical status transformed once the fraud was confirmed. He invokes Hegel's remarks on abstract individuality and compares the case to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' Roth's and Kaufman's metafiction, to argue the deception paradoxically discloses deeper truths about what documentary is.
- ch. 35 "33_LaRocca_Chapter_032.html" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "34_LaRocca_Chapter_033.html" *(notes)*
- ch. 37 "35_LaRocca_Chapter_034.html" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Film Noir

- ch. 1 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Copyright Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Dedication" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Foreword" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, William James — The Death of God; Transcendentalism; Existentialism — Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer — Existentialism; The Death of God; The Meaning of Life; The Absurd — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- ch. 8 "Part 1 The Essence and Elements of Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, Plato, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Albert Camus — The Death of God; Theory of Forms; Everything Flows / Logos; Existentialism — Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.
- ch. 10 "A Darker Shade Realism in Neo-Noir" **·** G.E. Moore — The Naturalistic Fallacy; Moral Relativism — Jason Holt argues that realism, especially about the role values play in people's lives, is the underappreciated essence of noir, offering a working definition of noir as 'stylized crime realism.' Surveying neo-noir detectives (Harper, Chinatown's Gittes), revamped femmes fatales who get away with it (Body Heat's Matty, The Last Seduction's Bridget), morally ambiguous protagonists (To Live and Die in L.A., Manhunter), and Lynch and Tarantino, he shows how the post-Production-Code freedom lets endings ring true to life by letting the guilty escape justice. He coins the 'normativistic fallacy' as the inverse of Moore's naturalistic fallacy: inferring what is from what ought to be, arguing that mainstream cinema's poetic justice commits it while neo-noir's downbeat endings correct it, fulfilling the realism latent in classic noir.
- ch. 11 "Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Plato — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics; The Categorical Imperative; Moral Relativism — Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.
- ch. 12 "Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Carl Jung — The Death of God; Existentialism; Yin and Yang; Archetypes — Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.
- ch. 13 "From Sherlock Holmes to the Hard-Boiled Detective in Film Noir" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze, René Descartes — The Pragmatic Method; The Rhizome; The Death of God; Will to Power — Jerold Abrams argues that the noir detective inherits the Holmes/Dupin detective logic but inhabits a fundamentally different maze. Using Eco's three labyrinths, he maps the classical Greek maze (with faith as Ariadne's string) and the mannerist maze (with Cartesian/Kantian pure reason) onto the escapable world of classic detection, and the Deleuzian rhizomatic maze, born after Nietzsche dissolved reason into will to power, onto noir's inescapable world (The Third Man, Kiss Me Deadly, The Maltese Falcon's fake statue). He shows both detectives use Peircean abduction (the logic of guessing) rather than pure deduction, illustrating it with knife-wound examples and Calloway's trapdoor inference in The Third Man, while the noir femme fatale becomes the anti-Ariadne whose thread of clues leads only to the hangman's rope.
- ch. 14 "Part 2 Existentialism and Nihilism in Film Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Albert Camus, Thomas Nagel, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Meaning of Life; The Absurd; Philosophical Pessimism; Existentialism — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- ch. 16 "The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Death of God; The Unconscious; Rebellion and Revolt — Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.
- ch. 17 "Symbolism, Meaning, and Nihilism in Quentin TaranTino's Pulp Fiction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — The Death of God; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Conard reads Pulp Fiction as a study of American nihilism in Nietzsche's 'God is dead' sense: with no transcendent framework of value, Jules and Vincent orient their lives by transient pop-culture icons (Jack Rabbit Slim's, the Fonz) and by Marsellus Wallace's arbitrary power, so the mysterious briefcase has worth only because he wills it. He contrasts this void with Aristotelian ethics, where a thing's good lies in realizing its rational essence. Jules's transformation begins when he survives the misfired shots and reinterprets his Ezekiel 25:17 recitation as a call to be 'the Shepherd,' while Butch's choice of the samurai sword over the baseball bat signals a return to an objective warrior code beyond the empty pop icons.
- ch. 18 "Part 3 Six Classic Films Noirs" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Film Noir and the Frankfurt School America as Wasteland in Edgar Ulmer's Detour" **·** Theodor Adorno, Walter Benjamin, Herbert Marcuse — The Culture Industry; The Aura of the Artwork — Cantor argues that Ulmer's Detour deconstructs the American dream in a manner that closely parallels the Frankfurt school's culture critique. Al Roberts's westward journey toward success collapses into crime and doom, dramatizing Horkheimer and Adorno's claim in 'The Culture Industry' that Hollywood sells the masses an illusory lottery of hope (Haskell's horse 'Paradisical,' Sue's failed stardom) to reconcile them to capitalism. Cantor ties Roberts's disgust at jukebox music and his 'jazzing up' of Brahms directly to Adorno's polemics against mechanical reproduction and Benjamin's loss of the artwork's aura. He finally suggests both Ulmer and the émigré Marxists project a European elitist alienation onto an America they picture as an empty wasteland.
- ch. 20 "Knowledge, Morality, And Tragedy in The Killers and Out of the Past" **·** Aristotle — The Male Gaze — Jarvie tests whether The Killers and Out of the Past rise to tragedy in Aristotle's Poetics sense and answers no. Using Aristotle's demands for noble protagonists acting on principle, a fatal error, and a catharsis of pity and terror, he shows that Swede and Jeff are self-centered moral cowers ensnared by femmes fatales (Kitty, Kathie) whose only 'error' is sexual susceptibility, which is banal rather than tragic. He argues the films' 'personal morality' is incoherent because morality is social, and that their false-appearance mystery plots plus flippant normalizing codas (Reardon's insurance office, The Kid's lie to Ann) reassure audiences and encourage the puritanical 'sexy woman as succubus' myth instead of educing genuine catharsis.
- ch. 21 "Moral Man in the Dark City Film Noir, the Postwar Religious Revival, and The Accused" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Death Drive (Thanatos); The Male Gaze — Palmer nuances the 'dark mirror' theory of noir by recovering a redemptive subgroup, reading Dieterle's The Accused through the postwar religious revival and the writings of Reinhold Niebuhr and Erich Fromm. Where Lang's The Woman in the Window only chastens its professor via a dream, The Accused stages a genuinely penitential arc: repressed psychology professor Wilma Tuttle kills the aggressive student Bill in panic, then is therapeutically forced to relive the crime (at the prizefight and in the reenactment) until love with lawyer Warren Ford delivers her from 'separateness.' Palmer argues this patriarchal, therapeutic 'conversion'—glamorizing Loretta Young out of her mannish disguise—reconfigures Niebuhr's taming of passion and Fromm's account of love as a decision, heralding a coming 'culture of narcissism.'
- ch. 22 "On Reason and Passion in The Maltese Falcon" **·** Plato — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); The Male Gaze — Knight argues that Sam Spade is not the dispassionate reasoner philosophy since Plato has assumed the detective to be, defending instead cognitivism about the emotions (via Solomon, de Sousa, and Damasio's Phineas Gage case). Because the hard-boiled detective enters events in media res, Spade must work hermeneutically to reconstruct the real story behind Brigid O'Shaughnessy's lies, and his judgments of trust, confidence, and loyalty fuse reason with feeling. In the climax Spade sends Brigid over for murdering Miles Archer precisely because reason and emotion together tell him he cannot trust her, whereas Brigid—the film's true cold calculator—only feigned emotion to make him her sap; Knight contrasts her with the non-fatale Vivian Rutledge of The Big Sleep.
- ch. 23 "Ride the Pink Horse Money, Mischance, Murder, and the Monads of Film Noir" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Gottfried Leibniz, Plato — The World as Will; Ethics of Compassion; Monadology — Silver reads Robert Montgomery's Ride the Pink Horse as a prototypically noir embodiment of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. The revenge-driven Gagin, like Hugo, is enslaved to money and will—'a man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants'—and takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world, blind to the monads and Platonic-cave shadows of fate around him. Against him stand Pancho's suffering kindness and the Indian girl Pila's selfless compassion, which Silver aligns with Schopenhauer's dictum that 'compassion is the basis of all morality' and his prizing of aesthetic transcendence. The carousel (tío vivo) and the burning of Zozobra, the god of bad luck, become symbols of will's pointless circular striving from which only sacrifice and art offer escape.
- ch. 24 "Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 25 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Horror

- ch. 1 "Half Title" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Table of Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Gynaehorror as convention and challenge" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud — The Rhizome; Woman as the Other — This introductory chapter defines 'gynaehorror' as horror rooted in women's reproductive bodies (menstruation, virginity, pregnancy, motherhood, menopause), reading films like Inside, Vigil, Teeth, Alien, The Brood and Rosemary's Baby through it. It leverages Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome/becoming to reframe the monstrous female body not as a fixed molar 'being' but as a productive, boundary-breaching 'becoming', while positioning woman as the abject Other against which the male subject defines himself. It argues horror is simultaneously conservative (punishing women) and potentially radical.
- ch. 8 "Heteronormative horrors" **·** Judith Butler, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze — Heteronormativity; A Vindication of the Rights of Woman; Gender Performativity — Reading virgins and the vagina dentata as the dyad through which horror polices female sexuality, the chapter uses Irigaray's account of the virgin as prop to male subjectivity and Creed's femme castratrice to analyse Halloween's 'Final Girl', Teeth's toothed-vagina revenge on abstinence-only purity culture, Jennifer's Body and Haute Tension. It closes with Rich's 'compulsory heterosexuality' and Wittig's 'heterosexual contract' to argue horror naturalises heteronormativity by casting female sexuality as either contained (virgin) or monstrously open (vagina dentata).
- ch. 9 "‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze — Woman as the Other; The Problem of Evil — The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.
- ch. 10 "Brave new worlds cyborg futures and female subjectivity" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud — The Rhizome; Mind–Body Dualism; One Is Not Born a Woman — Examining 'reproductive technohorror' from Shelley's Frankenstein through Splice, The Unborn and The Machine, the chapter argues these films code science as masculine domination of feminised nature (via Bordo's Cartesian masculinisation and Merchant's Bacon) and eliminate the female body altogether so man can create life without woman. It contrasts this with Haraway's post-gender cyborg and Braidotti's Deleuzean metal-morphoses, using becoming-woman and the rhizome to imagine reproductive difference as productive rather than as the erasable 'female problem'.
- ch. 11 "Monstrous motherhood" **·** Michel Foucault, Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge; The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real — The chapter argues that horror films about mothers are not static representations but Foucauldian sites where 'discourses of motherhood' are produced, policed and contested; using Foucault's account of bodies disciplined through power/knowledge, it treats films as cultural artefacts that both enforce and challenge norms of 'essential' and 'ideal' motherhood. It reworks Sarah Arnold's Lacanian 'Good Mother/Bad Mother' schema (the mother who sacrifices herself so the child enters the Symbolic and submits to the Law of the Father) alongside popularised Freudian mother-blame (the 'refrigerator mother', 'tell me about your mother') to read Psycho's Norma(n), the phallic mothers of The Killing Kind and The Brood, and the doomed single mothers of The Ring, Silent Hill and Triangle. It coins the 'monstrous-maternal' to argue that motherhood is framed as always-already monstrous because no woman can meet the impossible, shifting criteria of ideal motherhood, illustrated through Grace's Vivian/Madeline generational clash and Serial Mom's Beverly Sutphin.
- ch. 12 "The ageing woman as (American) horror story" **·** Michel Foucault, Gilles Deleuze — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge; The Rhizome — The chapter theorises the 'abject barren body' — the menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal woman — connecting menarche as an upswell of feminine power (Carrie's telekinesis, Ginger Snaps, The Witch's Thomasin) to menopause's cultural construction as loss and 'living decay'. Drawing on Mary Douglas and Kristeva on pollution and abjection, and on Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' and bodies defined by capacities rather than fixed being, it argues that the female reproductive body is more often barren than fecund and that this state is another generative modality, not an absence. It reads the Western biomedical pathologisation of menopause (Wilson's Feminine Forever, HRT) as a Foucauldian disciplinary discourse, then tracks older women through Sunset Boulevard's Norma Desmond, the hagsploitation cycle (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, Strait-Jacket, Hush Hush Sweet Charlotte), and The Taking of Deborah Logan, concluding that Jessica Lange's American Horror Story roles offer the fullest, sexually frank rebuttal to the abjection and invisibility of the ageing woman.
- ch. 13 "Afterword monstrous miscarriages and uncanny births" *(no index entry yet)* — The afterword uses the anthology films The ABCs of Death and its sequel to argue that 'gynaehorror' can be either reactionary or radical. Recounting a female-fan viewing of the first anthology, it catalogues its 'matrix of misogyny' — pervasive objectification, sexual assault and the reductive 'M is for Miscarriage' punchline that renders the woman's reproductive body abject and disposable. Against this it champions the sequel's 'Z is for Zygote', in which an abandoned pregnant woman keeps her thirteen-year-old unborn inside her and is finally turned inside-out and reborn as a 'mother-skin', reading the short as a provocative, generative treatment of maternity, ageing and reproduction. It closes the book's argument that gynaehorror need not belittle women's bodies but can be monstrous in the productive sense of a zygote — new life and new possibilities.
- ch. 14 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 15 "288" *(front)*

## The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "THE PHILOSOPHY OF POPULAR CULTURE" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; The Absurd; Authenticity — Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.
- ch. 9 "Part One The Subject at War" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, René Descartes — The Absurd; Existentialism; Bad Faith — Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.
- ch. 11 "Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Heraclitus — Will to Power; Everything Flows / Logos; The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality — Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.
- ch. 12 "Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Aristotle — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Existentialism; Being-Toward-Death — Holt uses Paths of Glory to illustrate existential ethics, framing the doomed 701st Regiment as 'thrown' beings-toward-death who retain full freedom in how they meet their fate. He resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' (denying objective values while commanding authenticity) by treating authenticity as a formal, second-order virtue like integrity: Colonel Dax is sincere and consistent, General Mireau an inauthentic hypocrite acting in bad faith. Addressing weakness of will (Roget's cowardice) and the condemned Paris 'dying well' before the firing squad, Holt argues that courage—an Aristotelian character virtue—is the smuggled-in content that grounds any formalist existential ethics.
- ch. 13 "Part Two The Subject in Love" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" **·** Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard — Philosophy of Love; Moral Luck; Existentialism; The Categorical Imperative — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- ch. 15 "Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Socrates, Plato, Michel Foucault — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Existentialism; Pragmatism — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.
- ch. 16 "The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce — The Pragmatic Method; Personal Identity — Abrams argues Kubrick's and Nabokov's Lolita is a philosophical detective story descended from Poe's Dupin tales, and that Humbert fails as a detective because he lacks the right logic. Using Peirce's abduction (and Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative types), he shows Humbert excels at 'overcoded' guesses—spotting a nymphet at a glance—but cannot make the 'undercoded' abductions needed to see that Quilty is shadowing him, because he is all chess-like calculation and no playful 'musement' or acumen. Humbert (the resolvent) and Quilty (the creative) split Poe's 'bi-part' double-Dupin; Quilty the changeling-Minotaur controls the labyrinth and dies behind Lolita's portrait as a self without a unified identity.
- ch. 17 "Part Three The Subject and the Meaning of Life" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler" **·** David Hume, Karl Marx, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, G.W.F. Hegel, Seneca — Philosophical Skepticism; The Absurd; Existentialism; The Meaning of Life — Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).
- ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" **·** Aristotle, Seneca, John Stuart Mill — Stoicism; The Meaning of Life; Virtue Ethics; Fate and Foreknowledge — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- ch. 20 "Part Four The Subject in History" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden" **·** Plato, Plutarch — Tripartite Soul; Justice in the Republic — Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's rivalries onto to thymoeides, the soul's 'second' spirited part governed by philotimia (love of honor): Crassus's obsessive hamilla with Gracchus, and his skewed contest with Spartacus over Varinia and Antoninus. Reading Draba's trident-throw and Crassus's closing 'now I fear him' as the spirited part's competitiveness overrunning reason, Braden shows the gladiatorial paired combat mirroring republican politics on its way to the Principate.
- ch. 22 "The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska" **·** Thomas Nagel, Albert Camus — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Meaning of Life — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.
- ch. 23 "The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The End of Grand Narratives — Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.
- ch. 24 "Part Five The Subject of the Future" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — Free Will vs Determinism; Will to Power; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.
- ch. 26 "“Please Make Me a Real Boy” The Prayer of the Artificially Intelligent Jason T. Eberl" **·** Alan Turing, G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle, Boethius — The Turing Test; Master–Slave Dialectic; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Eberl argues that HAL 9000 in 2001 and David in A.I. present sufficient evidence of personhood, testing them against the Turing test, behaviorism, and Boethius's definition of a person as an individual substance of a rational nature. He uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their self-conscious creations, reading Bowman's disconnection of HAL and the Flesh Fair's destruction of Mechas as humans failing to recognize persons. Invoking Aristotle's telos and virtue, he claims the Flesh Fair's real moral crime is precluding Mechas from pursuing their own flourishing, while David's Pinocchio-like leap of faith marks him as person-like.
- ch. 27 "Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Nick Bostrom — The Übermensch; The Death of God; The Last Man; The Noble Lie — Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.
- ch. 28 "Filmography" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Contributors" *(notes)*
