## The Philosophy of Joss Whedon

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 4 "Photo Credits and Captions" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Introduction" *(no index entry yet)* — This introductory prospectus argues that fictional narrative films (and their makers) can 'do' philosophy, and proposes Joss Whedon's corpus as a surprising confirming instance of the film-as-philosophy thesis. It defines philosophy as an activity of asking universal questions and removing contradictions by argument, then chapter-by-chapter previews how Buffy, Angel, Firefly/Serenity, Dr. Horrible, Dollhouse, The Cabin in the Woods and the Avengers films will be read through Heidegger, Sartre, Socrates, Rawls, Plato, Aristotle, Locke, Kant, Mill, Parfit and others. It sets out the interpretive presuppositions (what counts as Whedon 'canon') that govern the whole book.
- ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Locke, Socrates, John Rawls, Plato, Derek Parfit — Authenticity; Existence Precedes Essence; Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Bad Faith — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, Plato, René Descartes, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Socrates, Thomas Hobbes, Nel Noddings — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Mind–Body Dualism; Utilitarianism; The Chinese Room — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- ch. 8 "Conclusion" **·** Derek Parfit, John Locke, Nel Noddings, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — Personal Identity; The Ethics of Care; Existentialism; The Meaning of Life — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- ch. 9 "Bibliography" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 11 "About the Author" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — Ethical Egoism; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Sanders reads Casino as a dramatization of ethical egoism, using the parasitic bond between Nicky Santoro and Ace Rothstein to ask whether an egoist who treats a friend as a mere instrument can have real friendship. He distinguishes 'maximizing' egoism (Nicky's ruinous take-everything drive, ending in his beating death) from a 'satisficing' egoism that restricts its own dispositions, arguing against Blum, Wilcox and an Aristotelian objection that only the maximizing version is truly incompatible with friendship. Aristotle's account of virtue and friendship supplies the standard the film's egoists fall short of.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** John Locke, Socrates — The Social Contract; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Skoble uses Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle to probe when vigilantism is justified, invoking Locke's claim that in civil society individuals delegate private vengeance to the state for objectivity. He argues Travis's rescue of the trapped child prostitute Iris is legitimate (the police won't help, she can't help herself) while his plan to assassinate Senator Palantine is madness, drawing the key line between correctly identifying a deserving target and mere perceived evil (contrasting Travis with Death Wish's Kersey, Batman, and Klan lynch mobs). He closes with Socrates' 'unexamined life' as the remedy: contemplating justice so we can confront real badness rather than turn away.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Tripartite Soul; Justice in the Republic — Kowalski likens Goodfellas' Henry Hill to Plato's Gyges: both act immorally with near-total impunity, posing Glaucon's challenge in the Republic of why one should be just when one can escape all consequences. He applies Plato's tripartite soul (appetitive, spirited, rational) to Henry (runaway appetite/cocaine), Tommy (overstretched spirit, killing Billy Batts and Spider out of wounded pride) and cool, untroubled Paulie, treating them as the disharmonious 'unbalanced self.' Against the objection that these gangsters seem happy, he deploys Plato's health/happiness analogy and the feeling-happy vs being-happy distinction to argue they suffer 'cancer of the soul' and cannot be truly happy.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Thomas Aquinas, Plato, Jean-Paul Sartre, Sigmund Freud — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Philosophical Pessimism; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Tripartite Soul — Conard uses Mean Streets' guilt-ridden Charlie to survey conceptions of unhappiness against three definitions of happiness: beatitude (Aquinas), pleasure (Mill's hedonism), and flourishing (Aristotle's eudaimonia). He reads Charlie as damned in his own Catholic eyes, then invokes Nietzsche's Genealogy that religion manufactures guilt from internalized instinct, Plato's disordered soul and akrasia to explain Charlie's conflicting desires, and Schopenhauer's and Freud's pessimism that suffering is our natural state. He argues Charlie reaches dysdaimonia by acquiring vices and pursuing an ignoble (gangster) life, closing with Plato's Symposium and Sartre's facticity/transcendence to cast unhappiness as an ontological lack at the heart of human desire.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Michel Foucault — Will to Power; The Übermensch; The Death of God — Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(no index entry yet)* — Knight opens by denying that fiction films (Scorsese's included) actually 'do' philosophy, arguing they raise philosophical themes rather than construct arguments or thought experiments, then reads The Age of Innocence for its themes. Her thesis is that Scorsese renders the 'social semiotics' of 1870s New York high society—flowers, cutlery, seating, hand-kissing, the yellow-versus-red roses—as a code that constrains individual desire, with the outsider Countess Olenska as the catalyst who exposes its rigidity. Newland Archer is trapped between belonging and fleeing, and society (via May and the van der Luydens) quietly conspires to ship Ellen back to Europe and preserve the status quo, the camera and omniscient narrator judging the judges.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; Bad Faith; The Look (hell is other people); The Myth of Sisyphus — McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Blaise Pascal, Plato, Immanuel Kant — Pascal's Wager; Ethical Egoism — Richard Greene analyzes The King of Comedy's Rupert Pupkin, who kidnaps talk-show host Jerry Landers to force his way onto TV and emerges a celebrity, calling this the 'Pupkin gambit' (harming others and oneself to secure an overwhelming personal payoff). Distinguishing internalist accounts of rationality (Plato's well-ordered soul, Kant's universalizable maxims) from an externalist one, Greene argues the gambit is irrational for a sane agent like the financier Michael Milken but rational for Pupkin via a Pascal's-wager structure: because Pupkin is delusional, even imagined success satisfies his desire, so the wager has huge upside and no real downside for him. He also invokes ethical egoism to show unethical acts can still be assessed for self-interested rationality.
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Bad Faith; Existentialism — Karen D. Hoffman reads The Last Temptation of Christ and Bringing Out the Dead through Sartre's distinction between the for-itself (transcendence) and the in-itself (immanence), arguing both reluctant saviors are tempted into bad faith. Scorsese's Jesus, tempted on the cross to abandon his mission and live as an ordinary husband and father, passively drifts toward a life of pure immanence that denies his human transcendence, until (following Kazantzakis's 'sprouting of wings' image via Judas) he reclaims his choice to be crucified. Frank Pierce inversely faces a false transcendence—the temptation to think of himself as God, or to escape via drugs, violence, or suicide—and resists it, allowing the vegetative Mr. Burke to die. Hoffman frames avoiding either exaggeration as the path to authentic Sartrean humanity and grace.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Adam Smith — The Invisible Hand — Paul A. Cantor argues that The Aviator, unusually for Hollywood, is a libertarian celebration of the entrepreneur, turning billionaire Howard Hughes into a Scorsese underdog battling the establishment. Drawing on Adam Smith and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, Cantor reads Hughes's willingness to risk his own money on Hell's Angels and TWA, his visionary anticipation of talkies and jets, and his Senate-hearing fight against the Pan Am/Senator Brewster monopoly as a dramatization of the true risk-taking entrepreneur versus the mere manager. The 'socialist dinner party' with the aristocratic Hepburns and Hughes's defeat of government-backed monopoly illustrate Smith's suspicion of merchants seeking privilege and his invisible-hand claim that self-interested competition, not those who 'trade for the publick good,' best serves the public.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Dewey, Emmanuel Levinas, Thomas Nagel, Michel Foucault — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Face of the Other — Richard Gilmore reads After Hours as a nocturnal katabasis in which office worker Paul Hackett is repeatedly offered, and repeatedly fails at, authentic encounter with the SoHo women and their artworks (Kiki's papier-mache man, the plaster-of-paris bagel). Using Levinas's totality-versus-infinity and the ethics of conversation, Kant's two worlds of interest and disinterested aesthetic judgment, and Dewey's Art as Experience, Gilmore argues that art and sex alike (per Picasso and Nagel's 'double reciprocal incarnation') demand abandoning one's 'logic of the same' to perceive the other. Foucault's disciplinary kronos-time versus kairos, and Zizek's anamorphic spot, frame Paul's entrapment in solipsism until, encased as a literal artwork and reborn at the office gates, he finally offers himself to June.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** The Buddha, Epictetus — The Four Noble Truths; Compassion (karuna); Impermanence (anicca) — Judith Barad explains the puzzling elements of Kundun—the compassion for enemies, the child taken from his parents, the swept-away sand mandala, the sky burial—through Tibetan Buddhist ethics, arguing it closely parallels Greek and Roman Stoicism. She reads the young Dalai Lama's growth into compassion and nonviolence toward Mao and the Chinese alongside Epictetus's teaching that only our own judgments, not others' acts, can harm us, and that we must restrain desire and attachment. The Four Noble Truths reframe the film: because all things (including the self) are impermanent and interconnected, the destruction of the mandala and the feeding of the father's corpse to vultures enact detachment, and true liberation via the Eightfold Path is self-won inner peace that China cannot seize.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson — Transcendentalism; Free Will vs Determinism — R. Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(notes)*
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Michael Mann

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche, Emmanuel Levinas, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, John Locke — Existentialism; Authenticity; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Sanders's introductory survey frames Mann's cinema as suffused with existentialist themes—alienation, freedom, authenticity, and existential choice—citing Sartre's 'condemned to be free' as the key to protagonists like Thief's Frank and Heat's Neil McCauley, who choose personal truth over surrender. It maps the volume's essays: Nietzschean will to power in the crime films, Levinas's ethics of the Other in Thief and Collateral, and Lockean/Rousseauian visions of nature in The Last of the Mohicans. Mann's outsiders repeatedly face the fateful, doom-laden choices (McCauley abandoning Eady to kill Waingro) that define existential man.
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Eternal Recurrence — Arnett reads Mann's 'modern crime films' through Nietzsche and Marc Augé's 'nonplace,' arguing Mann is a director-architect who exerts a will to power over institutional space (Atlanta's High Museum becomes Lecktor's prison in Manhunter; Neil's glass beach house in Heat). Mann's heroes are Nietzsche's 'godless' who refuse the herd, becoming Dionysian figures who redefine space—Neil and Vincent as Dionysian/Apollonian artists whose LAX showdown is a 'frenzy' of convergence. The endless recurrence of place-versus-nonplace, and Vincent killing Neil only to be trapped in supermodernity himself, dramatizes Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and Dionysian pessimism.
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Existentialism — Palmer casts the protagonists of The Jericho Mile and Thief as 'outsiders' in Colin Wilson's sense—men 'awakened to chaos'—read through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus. Rain Murphy, running endless meaningless laps and hurling away the timer, is Mann's Sisyphus: his fate belongs to him, the struggle itself filling his heart. Thief's Frank, who 'gets to where nothin' means nothin',' shreds his dream-collage and destroys everything rather than be owned by Leo, enacting the absurd hero's scorn for a Hobbesian 'war of all against all' where law lacks connection to justice.
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Existentialism — Sanders argues Mann's action serves existentialist ideas: identity, freedom, authenticity, and death. In Thief, Frank's insistence on 'the yield of my labor' and his self-immolating exit dramatize the individualist maximizer whose choice of principle—echoing Sartre's young man and Kierkegaard's 'purity of heart is to will one thing'—cannot be given from outside. The Miami Vice episode 'Heart of Darkness' is read as a morality play on authenticity: undercover agent Artie Lawson's flight into the fantasy persona is a bad-faith masquerade that ends in suicide, mirroring Crockett's own anxiety about his Sonny Burnett alter ego.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Will to Power; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Skoble examines evil in Manhunter through the film's Nietzsche epigraph—'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster'—as profiler Will Graham must 'become' Lecktor and Dollarhyde to catch them, risking his own psyche. Lecktor's claim that killing feels good because doing 'what God does' makes one godlike frames the killers' evil as a will to power. Skoble invokes the Socratic dictum that to know the good is to do the good, asking whether Dollarhyde's murderous 'becoming the Red Dragon' is a large-scale delusion, and warns that truly seeing the killer's fantasy risks adopting it.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze, Søren Kierkegaard — The Übermensch; Will to Power; The Rhizome — Sterritt reads Manhunter's Hannibal Lecktor as a perverse image of Nietzsche's Übermensch: hedonistic, ascetic, and expressing an overwhelming will to power, exercising superhuman self-control (his pulse never exceeding eighty-five while mutilating a nurse). Using Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming' and the body without organs, he contrasts the genuinely self-transforming Lecktor (a 'schizovivisectionist') with Dollarhyde, whose bogus becoming—trapped in Blake's 'mind-forg'd manacles' and the Red Dragon—makes him a pathetic tooth fairy rather than an overman, aligning both killers with Kierkegaard's demonic individual who stands above the universal.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Gilles Deleuze — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Rhizome — Ritzer argues Mann's aesthetics of horror in The Keep and Manhunter is an aestheticization of horror—the frightening transformed into the beautiful through mise-en-scène, color, and montage. Against Hegel's Lectures on Fine Art, which bans the purely negative and horrific from aesthetics, Ritzer marshals Schiller, De Quincey, and Auden to split the ethical from the aesthetic: Dollarhyde stages corpses as artworks and Graham reads crime scenes as an art critic. The Keep pushes further into Barthes's 'obtuse meaning' and Deleuze and Guattari's 'planes of immanence,' its stylized images referring to nothing but themselves—horror filmed solely for horror's sake.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Authenticity; Existentialism; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Rybin links Mann's style-versus-substance debate to the existential self-definition of his characters, focusing on Public Enemies. Dillinger, who tells Billie 'the only thing that's important is where somebody's going,' is not yet an icon but is 'becoming Dillinger' as the film unfolds. In the penultimate scene, watching Clark Gable in Manhattan Melodrama—'die the way you lived, all of a sudden'—Dillinger achieves authentic self-definition by claiming the gangster myth as his own identity, a Warshovian 'experience of art'; Mann's editing collapses the space between Dillinger and the screen just before Dillinger is gunned down, the cost of authentic selfhood.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Walter Benjamin — The Aura of the Artwork; Existentialism — Pomerance argues Public Enemies inverts the gangster genre's convention of the 'ecstatic' criminal viewed from law's judgmental exterior: Mann's handheld camera penetrates Dillinger's private, breathing, interior world (contrasting the mechanized, plan-driven Purvis), likening the film to Fantastic Voyage's journey inside a body. Drawing repeatedly on Walter Benjamin's Arcades Project—the flâneur who is 'utterly undiscoverable,' the bourgeois transformation of nature into interior—he reads the FBI's cataloging of Dillinger as modernity reducing an integrated person to a collectible 'public enemy,' culminating in the head shot that is both execution and publicity image.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Jean Baudrillard, Friedrich Nietzsche — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Aura of the Artwork — Paulus and Adriaensens argue that Mann's 'stylized realism' is best understood not as neobaroque spectacle but as mannerism: a self-conscious, image-conscious cinema in tension between classicism and anti-classicism. Reading Mann's green-screen shooting on Heat, the hyperreal night look of Collateral and the ultra-sharp digital of Public Enemies through Deleuze's letter to Daney on cinematic mannerism, they cast Mann as a Coppola-like 'bridge-builder' who offers a pedagogy of the image and gains Nietzsche's 'powers of the false.' Baudrillard's account of Apocalypse Now as excess of means and simulation frames the immersive spectacle Mann resists in favor of realism.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — The Categorical Imperative; The Golden Mean; Utilitarianism — LaRocca reads The Insider as a study of contracts, conscience and courage. He argues that when Jeffrey Wigand stops calculating consequences ('Fuck it. Let's go to court.') he becomes a Kantian: his testimony has moral worth because it is done from duty and the categorical imperative, not from the utilitarian hedonic calculus of Bentham and Mill that Bergman, Wallace and Scruggs press on him. Wigand's whistleblowing is then framed through Aristotle's account of courage as a mean between recklessness and cowardice, with Wigand as the 'citizen soldier' who acts from conscience while Mike Wallace exemplifies the coward who exceeds in fear.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Karl Marx, Thomas Hobbes — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Social Contract; Commodity Fetishism — Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Karl Marx — The Face of the Other; Existentialism — Skrodzka reads Thief and Collateral as exercises in deontology grounded in Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the Other. Frank's violent courtship of Jessie and his final destruction of his possessions, and Max's crashing of the cab after Vincent's interpellation, are staged as the self's annihilating opening to the face of the Other (glimpsed in the rearview mirror as Max's doppelganger). Using Bauman's account of liquid-modern disconnection and a leftist critique of late capitalism, she argues Mann grounds Levinasian ethics in physical labor, and defines Vincent's evil as that which is 'knowing but unknowable,' deaf to the Other's call.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Thomas Hobbes, Albert Camus — Natural Rights; The State of Nature; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** Harry Frankfurt, G.W.F. Hegel, Jean Baudrillard — On Bullshit; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Authenticity — Corne unpacks Vincent Hanna's tirade in Heat against his wife's ex-husband's 'dead-tech, postmodernistic, bullshit house.' He reads the smashing of the television and the headless sculpture through Bataille's Against Architecture (buildings as latent prisons of authority) and Jameson's diagnosis of postmodern depthlessness and the silence of affect. Using Hegel, Hugo and Ruskin on architecture's obligation to tell the truth, and especially Frankfurt's On Bullshit, Corne argues the house is 'bullshit' because it is indifferent to truth; Vincent's workaholism becomes a Frankfurtian discipline, and the film reflexively treats truth, authenticity and space as a problem.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" **·** James Rachels, Frank Jackson, Alvin Goldman — Moral Relativism; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Rodriguez-Ruiz treats Ali and The Insider as dramatizing the methodology of philosophy, especially conceptual analysis and the politics of defining social concepts. Ali's challenges to 'patriotism,' 'freedom' and his slave name, and the manipulation of 'confidential,' 'addictive' and 'tortious interference' in The Insider, show how much rides on contested definitions. Against cultural relativism, he deploys James Rachels's Elements of Moral Philosophy (there are moral facts; some rules are needed for any society to exist) and discusses conceptual analysis (Jackson, Goldman) and Schiappa's 'how ought we use X,' leaving both heroes committed to independent thinking over consensus.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Neo-Noir

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — Conard's editor's introduction defines film noir and neo-noir, cataloguing noir themes (moral ambivalence, alienation, pessimism, disorientation) across films like Blue Velvet, Angel Heart, L.A. Confidential, and The Usual Suspects, and previews the volume's thirteen essays. It argues neo-noir better embodies the noir outlook because its makers work self-consciously and can let criminals succeed. It closes by invoking Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living to justify philosophical reflection on these films.
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Personal Identity; The Absurd — Abrams argues that neo-noir differs from classic noir by replacing the search for an external villain in the city with the detective's search for his own divided self, structured through time (past, present, future noir). He reads Angel Heart and The Ninth Gate as theological past-noir, Blade Runner and Minority Report as high-tech future-noir where amnesia and precognition fracture identity, and Memento, The Bourne Identity, and Fight Club as present-noir where the sleuth must reconstruct himself from bodily clues; Leonard Shelby becomes a 'Sisyphus of memory' whose total self-consciousness recedes indefinitely.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, René Descartes, Alan Turing — Existence Precedes Essence; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; The Turing Test; The Cogito — Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Smith reads Memento as a test of Locke's memory theory of personal identity. He explains Locke's view that consciousness of past actions (not soul or body) constitutes the self, rehearses Reid's transitivity objection and the circularity objection, and uses Parfit's account of memory and fusion to defend a survival-not-identity reading. He distinguishes 'Leonard 1' (anterograde amnesiac who returns each cycle) from 'Leonard 2b', a person fused from his own memories and those projected onto Sammy Jankis, arguing we too are 'fused' survivors who reinterpret hazy pasts, complicating responsibility and concern for our futures.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existentialism; Personal Identity; The Absurd — Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Immanuel Kant, Arthur Schopenhauer, Socrates — The Categorical Imperative; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Deontology — Berger uses Harold Becker's The Onion Field to challenge Kant's moral idealism. Kant held that any rational being can deduce categorical imperatives and that conscience necessarily convicts the guilty and vindicates the innocent. Yet the killers Powell and Smith feel no guilt for murdering Kant-admiring cop Ian Campbell (Smith calls guilt a trick 'rich white guys dreamed up'), while the innocent, blameless Hettinger is destroyed by shame, thievery, and near-suicide. Berger weighs Schopenhauer's 'evil genius' objection and the sociopathy explanation, concluding Hettinger's guilt is a doomed attempt to preserve moral meaning.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Plato — Justice in the Republic; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Tripartite Soul — Skoble argues that A Simple Plan dramatizes Plato's Republic almost exactly: justice as psychological harmony among the parts of the soul, and injustice as self-destructive disharmony. When Hank, Jacob, and Lou keep found money, they enact Thrasymachus's and the Ring of Gyges challenge (would you be unjust if you'd never be caught?). Hank miscalculates his own self-interest, mistaking wealth for happiness; the deception, distrust, and murders that follow (including Hank killing Jacob) show that even the criminal who evades capture is ruined by his corrupted character, exactly as Plato predicts.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Forgiveness; Moral Relativism; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — D'Aries and Hirsch read Paul Thomas Anderson's Hard Eight as a neo-noir moral inversion: the aging criminal Sydney seeks atonement not through religious penance but through selfless love, rescuing John and Clementine while removing the loathsome Jimmy (who knows Sydney killed John's father). They contrast him with Melville's Bob le flambeur and Besson's The Professional, where convention demands the criminal be punished. Sydney escapes formal justice but is sentenced to a 'prison without bars' of self-loathing (the bloodstained cuff), and the authors warn that such sympathy-for-the-devil inversions verge on nihilistic moral relativism.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Jean-François Lyotard, Richard Rorty, Friedrich Nietzsche — The End of Grand Narratives; Moral Relativism; Truth as What Works — Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Sigmund Freud, Aristotle, Friedrich Nietzsche — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Unconscious; Existentialism — Gilmore reads Chinatown as neo-noir that is itself a kind of philosophy, engaging the hermeneutics of suspicion (Nietzsche, Freud, Marx) and existentialist alienation. Curly eating the venetian blinds signals a desire to recover a less painful blindness; Jake Gittes's 'conceptual scotomas' (Dennett) and hubris make him miss counternarratives, paralleling Oedipus as detective. Using Freud on the uncanny and doppelgangers (Jake doubled with Hollis Mulwray and Noah Cross) and Aristotle's Poetics on catharsis and the sublime, Gilmore argues 'Chinatown' names the abyss where every narrative is undone, and that facing this dark sublimity is the way of wisdom.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Hannah Arendt — The Last Man; Master and Slave Morality; The Banality of Evil — Hibbs argues that nihilism, a working assumption in neo-noir, turns the noir protagonist's quests pointless, absurd, and thus comic, and that the Coen brothers exemplify this comic response. Using Nietzsche on nihilism, the 'last man', the 'pathos of distance', and aristocratic self-creation, he reads films like The Silence of the Lambs and Cape Fear as celebrating the 'super-antihero'. The Big Lebowski comically levels nihilism (Walter: the German nihilists are 'cowards'; nihilism cannot be lived), while Fargo and Raising Arizona affirm family and fertility, a 'banality of goodness' answering Arendt's banality of evil, letting nature's comedy perpetuate itself.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Philosophical Skepticism; The Absurd; The End of Grand Narratives — Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Karl Marx, Plato, G.W.F. Hegel — Commodity Fetishism; Justice in the Republic; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Schuler and Murray read Chinatown through Marx and Plato as a critique of capitalism's compulsions. Drawing on Marx and Engels on capital's Promethean transformation of nature and Hegel on art embodying abstractions, they argue neo-noir's centrifugal Los Angeles makes water, not diamonds, the object of desire, with wealth taking the abstract form of value. Plato's Republic warns that the boundless love of money (linked to Gyges, invisibility, and tyranny) destroys justice as reasonable self-limitation; Noah Cross's incest mirrors the 'rape of the Owens Valley', and Jake's defeat ('Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown') marks the exhaustion of the postwar golden age.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Perspectivism; Personal Identity; Philosophical Skepticism — Sanders coins 'sunshine noir' for Miami Vice as postmodern neo-noir, defining postmodernism via antirealism, skepticism about knowledge, and enigmas of personal identity, anticipated by Nietzsche's perspectivism. He analyzes three episodes: 'Heart of Darkness', where undercover agent Artie Rollins is consumed by his fantasy self (mirroring Crockett's Sonny Burnett) and hangs himself; 'Shadow in the Dark', where Crockett adopts the burglar's mind-set (Dilthey's Verstehen) in a dreamlike, glass-imagery structure that undermines the realist camera; and 'Lend Me an Ear', where the surveillance expert Duddy, echoing The Conversation, collapses into paranoid moral solipsism.
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(notes)*
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film

- ch. 1 "Cover Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Preface and Acknowledgments" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science Fiction Film" **·** Martin Heidegger, David Hume, Plato, René Descartes — Personal Identity; The Hard Problem of Consciousness; The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Sanders's editorial introduction surveys the twelve essays, arguing that science fiction film and philosophy are thematically interdependent, and previews each film's problem: Deckard's possible replicant status in Blade Runner, Biderman's existential reading of Quaid in Total Recall, his own paranoia interpretation of Invasion of the Body Snatchers, McMahon's Heideggerian being-toward-death in Frankenstein. He raises critical objections of his own, e.g. that the 'Deckard is an android' inference is logically invalid and that equating computer rationality with value-free computability (2001, Colossus) cannot yield normative judgment.
- ch. 8 "Part 1 Enigmas of Identity and Agency" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "What Is It to Be Human Blade Runner and Dark City" **·** John Locke, David Hume — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — Knight and McKnight read Blade Runner and Dark City as noir-influenced cyberpunk that asks what it is to be human. They argue that Deckard's replicant status (the origami unicorn, the shared family photo) and Murdoch's serially reprogrammed memory show memory to be unreliable, invoking Locke's prince-and-cobbler thought experiment and the problem of new brains in one body. Their conclusion is that it is emotion and relationship, not memory, that ground agency and personhood: Roy's empathy in dying and Deckard's love for Rachael, Murdoch's love for Emma/Anna, are what mark the characters as human.
- ch. 10 "Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, David Hume, John Locke, Martin Heidegger, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Jacques Derrida — Personal Identity; Existence Precedes Essence; Bundle Theory of Self; Bad Faith — Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.
- ch. 11 "Picturing Paranoia Interpreting Invasion of the Body Snatchers" **·** David Hume — Philosophical Skepticism; Personal Identity — Sanders rejects the standard Cold War-allegory and feminist readings of Invasion of the Body Snatchers and argues the film is best understood as film noir dramatizing paranoia. He shows that the mechanics of pod duplication are riddled with incoherence (multiple duplicates, location, timing, matching), then reads the frame story as evidence that Miles's whole account is a delusional psychosis. Dr. Hill's acceptance of the wild story on flimsy evidence violates Hume's maxim that a rational person proportions belief to evidence, making the film an ironic meditation on the philosophical significance of paranoia and lost humanity.
- ch. 12 "The Existential Frankenstein" **·** Martin Heidegger — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Existentialism; The They-Self (das Man) — McMahon gives an existential reading of Whale's Frankenstein and Shelley's novel through Heidegger's being-toward-death and Ernest Becker's denial of death. Victor Frankenstein exemplifies Becker's 'defiant Promethianism,' the offensive denial that seeks to conquer death, and the monster personifies death itself. She argues his obsession erodes his humanity, estranges him from others, and generates moral dilemmas, illustrating Heidegger's claim that only authentic acceptance of mortality restores individuality and genuine community, so that mastering death would make us monsters.
- ch. 13 "Part 2 Extraterrestrial Visitation, Time Travel, and Artificial Intelligence" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Technology and Ethics in The Day the Earth Stood Still" **·** John Stuart Mill, Thomas Hobbes — The Harm Principle; The Social Contract; Just War Theory; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Skoble reads The Day the Earth Stood Still as an allegory about the ethics of force and technology. He argues Klaatu's ultimatum extends Mill's harm principle to the interplanetary level: societies may fight among themselves but not threaten others, so Gort's robot police enforce a right to peace that no one has a right to violate. He distinguishes the robots' narrow, non-paternalistic authority from Hobbes's absolute sovereign, defends the ultimatum as preemptive self-defense rather than a rights violation, and contrasts the film's trust in machines with the later technophobia of Colossus and The Terminator.
- ch. 15 "Some Paradoxes of Time Travel in The Terminator and 12 Monkeys" **·** David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds; Personal Identity — Devlin uses The Terminator and 12 Monkeys to work through time-travel paradoxes with David Lewis's framework. He resolves the personal-identity paradox of the two James Coles at the airport via Lewis's distinction between personal and external time, and treats the grandfather paradox differently for each film: 12 Monkeys holds a possibilist growing-universe model in which the fixed past cannot be changed (Cole cannot kill his younger self), while The Terminator adopts a branching-universe model allowing the past to change into an alternate timeline. He closes on the causal loop of the Army of the 12 Monkeys message, which lacks an origin unless uncaused causes are allowed.
- ch. 16 "2001 A Philosophical Odyssey" **·** Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Edmund Husserl — Dasein (being-there); Embodiment (the lived body); The Question Concerning Technology; Theory of Forms — Stoehr interprets Kubrick's 2001 as inducing a feeling of disembodied presence through unrooted camerawork (contrasted with Ford's The Searchers), matching its theme of technology severing us from the natural world and our bodies. Drawing on Heidegger's Dasein and Hubert Dreyfus's On the Internet, he argues there are no context-free Archimedean standpoints and stages the Plato-versus-Nietzsche debate over the body: Plato's Phaedo prizes the soul's escape from the body, while Nietzsche's Zarathustra affirms embodied, situated existence. HAL's seeming humanity underscores that machines lacking bodies cannot fully replicate human intelligence.
- ch. 17 "Terminator-Fear and the Paradox of Fiction" **·** Thomas Nagel, John Searle — The Hard Problem of Consciousness; What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; The Turing Test — Holt uses the Terminator's first-person infrared POV shots (evoking Nagel's 'what is it like' question about an alien artificial consciousness) to frame the paradox of fiction: how we feel fear toward things we know do not exist. He offers a contextual divide-and-conquer solution, arguing higher emotions like pity and admiration for Sarah and Reese are largely make-believe, while lower emotions like Terminator-fear are genuine and need no existential belief (thought and mere possibility suffice). He adds that such fear is more rational for a naturalist who admits artificial intelligence is possible than for a dualist, and speculates the Terminator functions as an archetype embodying tech-noir dread.
- ch. 18 "Part 3 Brave Newer World Science Fiction Futurism" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Dialectic of Enlightenment in Metropolis" **·** Theodor Adorno, Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel, Immanuel Kant — The Culture Industry; Totalitarianism; Will to Power; The Dialectic — Abrams reads Fritz Lang's Metropolis as anticipating Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment by two decades. He maps the film's arc—from the Christian mythology of the catacombs, through Joh's technototalitarian rational city and the human-machine fusion of Rotwang's false Maria, back into ancient myth (the M-Machine as Moloch, the whore of Babylon, the Tower of Babel)—onto their thesis that Enlightenment reason turns totalitarian and reverts to mythology and madness. He ties reason's self-destruction to Nietzsche's will to power and contrasts the descent into 'absolute madness' with Hegel's progress toward absolute mind.
- ch. 20 "Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984" **·** Hannah Arendt, Jean-François Lyotard — Utopia and Dystopia; Totalitarianism; The End of Grand Narratives — Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.
- ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" **·** Henri Bergson, Theodor Adorno, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche — Duration (durée); The Absurd; The Culture Industry; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- ch. 22 "The Matrix, the Cave, and the Cogito" **·** Plato, René Descartes — Allegory of the Cave; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito; Theory of Forms — Conard argues that The Matrix alludes to Plato's cave (the pod-bound humans mistaking the program for reality, Neo's painful ascent) and to Descartes' dream argument and evil-genius doubt (the singular consciousness generating the Matrix), but betrays their spirit by rejecting transcendence and the a priori. Because the film is 'Christianity without God'—Neo can only remake the shadow-world of the Matrix, not touch ultimate reality—it grounds knowledge in a subjective gut feeling ('being the One is just like being in love') rather than Descartes' intellectual intuition of God or Plato's rational grasp of the Forms, leaving no answer to whether life outside the Matrix is itself another illusion.
- ch. 23 "List of Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 24 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes

- ch. 1 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Copyright Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Sherlock Holmes as Epistemologist" **·** William James — Philosophical Skepticism; Feminism — Baggett reconstructs Holmes's detective practice as an expansive epistemology built on observation, background knowledge, and abductive inference-to-the-best-explanation, using cases like 'The Blue Carbuncle' hat and the 'eliminate the impossible' maxim. He argues Holmes's boldness in drawing inferences is intellectual courage rather than hubris, invoking William James on the risk of losing truth by excessive caution. He then tests Holmes against feminist epistemologists who fault his cult of cold objectivity and mistrust of women (the Mary Morstan and Irene Adler episodes), concluding Holmes is partly vindicated by his imagination, intuition, and passion but still too fragmented between reason and emotion.
- ch. 6 "Not the Crime, but the Man Sherlock Holmes and Charles Augustus Milverton" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Immanuel Kant — Virtue Ethics; Virtue Ethics (arete); Consequentialism — Rozema examines 'The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton,' in which Holmes burgles a blackmailer's house, feigns an engagement to the maid, and watches Milverton's murder without intervening. He argues that Kantian deontology (too abstract to judge rectification) and consequentialism (paralyzed by unpredictable outcomes) both fail to assess Holmes's acts, whereas Plato and Aristotle's virtue ethics fits: judging the man's character over the isolated act. Citing Plato's 'true falsehood' vs. 'falsehood in words' and Aristotle on voluntary acts and the storm-tossed captain jettisoning cargo, he concludes a virtuous person may rightly do what is normally forbidden against a vicious foe like Milverton.
- ch. 7 "A Case of Insincerity What does it Mean to Deceive Someone" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Kinghorn builds a definition of deception by successively refining it against Holmes cases: honest error ('A Scandal in Bohemia'), double-bluffing ('The Empty House' wax bust), deceiving about a different proposition (the Windibank/'Hosmer Angel' interview), and non-deceptive manipulation (the drug-induced 'Creeping Man'). Invoking Wittgenstein on language as a public practice learned by trusting others' sincerity, he argues deception requires the target's mistaken reliance on someone's assumed sincerity. The surprising upshot: because Holmes and Moriarty mutually presume insincerity in their game, Holmes never truly deceives Moriarty.
- ch. 8 "Sherlock's Reasoning Toolbox" **·** David Hume, Karl Popper, René Descartes, John Stuart Mill, Aristotle — Problem of Induction; Falsificationism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Pigliucci shows that Holmes's celebrated 'deduction' is really a mix of induction and abduction, contrasting Aristotelian syllogism and Cartesian rationalism (with its failed Cartesian circle) against the fallibility of real investigation. He walks through Hume's problem of induction (Russell's inductivist chicken), the Mill-Whewell 'great induction debate,' and Popper's falsificationism—qualified by the Neptune/Uranus episode where scientists shielded Newton. Using 'Thor Bridge' and 'The Three Students,' he concludes Holmes is a pragmatic scientist wielding a whole toolbox, since there is no single scientific method.
- ch. 9 "Watsons, Adlers, Lestrades, and Moriarties On the Nature of Friends and Enemies" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics — Tallon applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics taxonomy of friendship—of use, of pleasure, and of virtue—to Holmes's relationships, plus Aquinas on friends helping each other flourish. The Baker Street Irregulars and Mrs. Hudson are friends of use; Holmes has few friends of pleasure; Watson is the friend of virtue, an 'other self' sharing virtue, support, and activity (getting Holmes off cocaine, taking a bullet). Inverting the account, he classifies Holmes's enemies as competitor (Irene Adler), rival/'frenemy' (Lestrade and Gregson), and foe (Moriarty), arguing a foe—an anti-self—can never become a friend.
- ch. 10 "Eliminating the Impossible Sherlock Holmes and the Supernatural" **·** David Hume, Alvin Plantinga — On Miracles; Scientific Realism vs Anti-Realism — Blanchette uses the Guy Ritchie film's Lord Blackwood 'resurrection' and 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' to ask whether a supernatural explanation is ever admissible. Drawing on Draper's definition of nature vs. the supernatural, Plantinga's natural-vs-logical necessity distinction, and Hume on miracles, he argues miracles are naturally impossible but not logically impossible unless nature is proven a closed system. He defends a truth-aimed methodology (pursue natural causes until the best explanation of failure is that none exists), showing Holmes rightly debunks both cases while thought experiments reveal conditions under which a supernatural verdict would become the rational inference.
- ch. 11 "Was it Morally Wrong to Kill Off Sherlock Holmes" **·** John Locke, Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx — Labor Theory of Property; Humanity as an End in Itself; Consequentialism — Terjesen asks whether Conan Doyle acted immorally in killing Holmes in 'The Final Problem,' framing it through property theory. He runs Locke's labor theory (illustrated via 'The Blue Carbuncle' gem), Proudhon and Marx's critiques, and both consequentialist and Kantian (respect-for-persons) justifications of intellectual property. He argues Conan Doyle's ownership of the iconic Holmes weakened as Paget, Gillette, Rathbone, and Dr. Joseph Bell co-authored the figure, so property rights alone can't justify the killing—but Conan Doyle's authorial dignity plus the narrative fitness of 'The Final Problem' and 'His Last Bow' make the send-off defensible.
- ch. 12 "Sherlock Holmes Artist of Reason" **·** Aristotle — The Meaning of Life; The Four Causes — McInerny argues Holmes is not a bloodless reasoning machine but an 'artist of reason' who fuses intellect with imagination ('the scientific use of imagination'). He lays out Holmes's four-stage method—fact-gathering interview and investigation, deep-thought hypothesis framing, denouement, and post-factum briefing—and notes his use of reasoning backward, reductio ad absurdum, and hypotheses over guesses. Finally he casts Holmes as a metaphysician who assumes a purposive, intelligible cosmos ('What is the meaning of it, Watson?'), a teleological order akin to Aristotle's Final End that grounds the local intelligibility Holmes exploits.
- ch. 13 "Sherlock Holmes and the Ethics of Hyperspecialization" **·** Socrates, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Alasdair MacIntyre — The Unexamined Life; Consequentialism; Deontology; Virtue Ethics — Costello and Bassham critique Holmes's 'brain-attic' theory from 'A Study in Scarlet'—that the mind has fixed capacity and should hold only vocationally useful knowledge. Cognitive science (interference and schema theory) and the sociology of social/cultural capital show useless knowledge is often useful, as when Holmes trades boxing lore or reads cultural cues. They then argue for a duty of self-improvement grounded in consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, and virtue ethics (Aristotle, Aquinas, MacIntyre) plus Socratic care of the soul, concluding that Holmes—an omnivorous reader who quotes Goethe and Hafiz—doesn't practice what he preaches and took specialization too far.
- ch. 14 "Passionate Objectivity in Sherlock Holmes" **·** Bernard Williams, Susan Wolf — Integrity Against Utilitarianism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Taliaferro and Le Gall pose the ethical clash between impartial detachment and partial loyalty, situating Holmes between Simon Keller (loyalty as a threat to being a 'good believer,' echoed by Holmes's 'Sign of Four' rejection of emotion) and Bernard Williams and Susan Wolf (who defend priority for loved ones—Williams's 'one thought too many'). Using Watson's shooting in 'The Three Garridebs,' Holmes's weaning off drugs, and 'perverted love' in the Sussex Vampire and Thor Bridge cases, they argue loyalty rightly understood as seeking the friend's good aids clear reasoning, and that Holmes exhibits a 'passionate objectivity' in which some acquaintance with passion is essential to being genuinely objective.
- ch. 15 "The Industrious Sherlock Holmes" **·** Henry David Thoreau — Walden (deliberate living); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Bassham diagnoses Holmes as a workaholic against clinical criteria (obsessive work, few relationships, perfectionism, health neglect through fasting and cocaine), then traces the rise of the Protestant work ethic (Calvin, Weber, Carlyle) and its modern decline. Drawing on Thoreau's Walden critique of 'lives of quiet desperation,' Pieper on leisure, and the 'affluenza' literature, he distinguishes pathological from benign workaholism by warning signs and by motivation. He concludes Holmes is a pathological workaholic in his symptoms but redeemed by his noble, non-materialistic motive of fighting crime and achieving justice.
- ch. 16 "The Dog that did not Bark Learning how to Read “The Book of Life”" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Aristotle — The Pragmatic Method; Self-Reliance; Virtue Ethics — Biondi uses the silent dog of 'Silver Blaze' to teach reasoning from absence, arguing Holmes's 'imagination' is a cultivable art—Peircean abduction combining observation, background knowledge, and the virtues of independence, courage, patience, and impartiality. She traces how Holmes finds Silver Blaze at Mapleton and unmasks Straker as the horse's would-be nobbler by consulting 'the book of life.' Framed by Emerson's 'study nature' and 'know thyself' (and Aristotle on what holds 'for the most part'), she uses the Irene Adler and 'Norbury'/Yellow Face failures to show how prejudice and overconfidence blind even Holmes to alternative hypotheses.
- ch. 17 "Aristotle on Detective Fiction" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes; Virtue Ethics — Sayers's 1935 essay reads Aristotle's Poetics as the finest guide to writing detective fiction, mapping tragedy onto the mystery: primacy of plot over character, unity of action, appropriate length, catharsis, and the parts of Peripety, Discovery, and Suffering with the criminal's hamartia. Its centerpiece is 'paralogismos'—the art of framing lies rightly by stating true consequents (B) so the reader infers a false antecedent (A) himself, illustrated by the Jones/Smith gramophone bluff, Knox's Viaduct Murder double bluff, and the 'Watsonity' fallacy behind Roger Ackroyd. She invokes 'The Hound of the Baskervilles,' 'The Speckled Band,' and 'The Copper Beeches' as Aristotelian exemplars.
- ch. 18 "The Grim Reaper on Baker Street" **·** Epicurus, Søren Kierkegaard, William James — Death Is Nothing to Us; Immortality and the Soul; The Meaning of Life — Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.

## The Philosophy of Spike Lee

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Preface" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "I. Justice, Value, and the Nature of Evil" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Symbolism of Blood in Clockers" *(no index entry yet)* — McFarland reads Lee's Clockers through Paul Ricoeur's account of defilement and Greek tragedy, arguing the film treats spilt blood as an 'unspeakable' evil that resists narrative and legal containment. He compares the ulcer-ridden, cleanliness-obsessed dealer Strike to Philoctetes and Oedipus, tracing how bloodstain passes through family lines (Rodney, Errol, Tyrone, Victor) and how detective Rocco's law fails to purge the contagion. The final train-into-the-desert shot leaves Strike, like an exiled tragic figure, neither cleansed nor at home.
- ch. 10 "The Prostitution Trap of Elite Sport in He Got Game" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Karl Marx — Commodity Fetishism; Alienation; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Holt and Pitter argue that Lee's He Got Game exposes a 'prostitution trap' in which elite athletes, like literal prostitutes, become commodified bodies alienated from themselves. They read the parallel plots of star recruit Jesus Shuttlesworth, his father Jake pressured to broker a signing, and the prostitute Dakota as three versions of the same trap, invoking MacIntyre's internal-versus-external goods and Deci/Ryan's intrinsic-versus-extrinsic rewards to show how coercive money threatens Jesus's love of the game. Jesus escapes by exercising autonomy, negotiating on his own terms and skipping the press conference to reach an 'authentic realism.'
- ch. 11 "Aristotle and MacIntyre on Justice in 25th Hour" **·** Aristotle, Alasdair MacIntyre — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Conard uses Lee's 25th Hour to test Aristotle's claim that justice is inseparable from community and necessary for eudaimonia, and MacIntyre's charge that liberal individualist society lacks any common good. Comparing the greedy Wall Street broker Frank (an Aristotelian overreacher driven by pleonexia) with the drug dealer Monty (fairer, though convicted under unjust Rockefeller laws), he argues Monty is not unjust yet still cannot flourish in a fragmented New York. Monty's profane bathroom 'fuck you' soliloquy dramatizes the city's incommensurable values, while the post-9/11 fellow-feeling offers a fleeting glimpse of the shared good MacIntyre says modern society lacks.
- ch. 12 "We Can’t Get Off the Bus A Commentary on Spike Lee and Moral Motivation" **·** Michael Sandel, Alasdair MacIntyre — Communitarianism; Double Consciousness — Beckles-Raymond reads Lee's Get on the Bus to defend a communitarian 'encumbered self' against the liberal 'unencumbered self,' arguing the Million Man March riders' racial identity is inseparable from their moral motivation. Drawing on Charles Taylor's strong evaluations and critiquing Tommie Shelby's thin-blackness solidarity, she shows each rider (George, Evan Sr., Jay, Jeremiah, Jamal, Xavier, Gary, Kyle, Randall) attends because being a good man is bound to being black, while the ejection of the self-hating Wendell marks the limits of thin identity. The film argues raced persons 'cannot get off the bus.'
- ch. 13 "Monsters and Moralism in Summer of Sam" **·** The Banality of Evil — Palmer argues Lee's Summer of Sam is less ethnography than moralism about the diffuse 'evil energy' that spreads through an Italian American Bronx enclave during the 1977 Son of Sam killings. Against Dan Flory's reading of the film as a veiled lynching parable, he contends Lee dismantles any clean line between the psychopath Berkowitz and his supposed innocent victims: the vigilantes become victimizers, punk outsider Richie doubles the killer through his violent stage act, and Vinny destroys himself through compulsive infidelity. Evil is shown as symptomatic of a whole social order in decline rather than located in one monster.
- ch. 14 "II. Race, Sexuality, and Community" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "(Still) Fighting the Power Public Space and the Unspeakable Privacy of the Other in Do the Right Thing" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Hannah Arendt, Charles W. Mills — The Private Language Argument; Philosophical Skepticism; The Public Sphere — Finnegan reads Do the Right Thing as a dramatization of philosophical skepticism and the 'problem of other minds,' using Wittgenstein's private-language argument, Austin's speech acts, and Cavell to argue that racism is not an epistemic failure to 'know' the Other but an ethical refusal to acknowledge. She shows Lee's split cinematic style (naturalistic interiority for the Italian Americans, alienating canted wide-angle shots for Radio Raheem and the black characters) enacts what being 'othered' looks like, while the Racial Slur Montage stages words as perlocutionary acts and Arendt's 'space of appearances' explains the black characters' exclusion. Mookie's thrown trash can and Sal's Wall of Fame register powerlessness rather than resolution.
- ch. 16 "Coworking in the Kingdom of Culture Identity and Community in the Films of Spike Lee" **·** W.E.B. Du Bois — Double Consciousness — Peterson uses W.E.B. Du Bois's 'Of Our Spiritual Strivings' and its 'co-worker in the kingdom of culture' to read Lee's New York films as studies of hyphenated identity and the making of American community. He traces how the Italian Americans of Do the Right Thing and Jungle Fever secure a fragile 'whiteness' only in negation of blackness (Sal, Pino, Frankie's egg-cream lament), how Summer of Sam's enclave turns on the difference embodied by punk Richie, and how 25th Hour's post-9/11 New York is disaggregated in Monty's mirror monologue. Lee's vision is a heteroglot city with 'many gates to the Kingdom of Culture.'
- ch. 17 "Feminists and “Freaks” She’s Gotta Have It and Girl 6" **·** bell hooks, Judith Butler, Simone de Beauvoir — Gender Performativity; Objectification; The Male Gaze — Hoffman assesses whether Lee's She's Gotta Have It and Girl 6 offer liberated female sexuality, drawing on second- and third-wave feminism and bell hooks. She argues Nola Darling only appears empowered before the rape scene and her submission ('Yours') reveal her as an underdeveloped object of the male gaze, whereas Girl 6, as a phone-sex worker consciously performing gender for callers, better exposes gender as socially constructed in a Butler-like sense. Even so, Girl 6's real feminist force lies not in its heroine but in its exposure of oppressive industries, especially the opening Tarantino audition where only the director's gaze counts.
- ch. 18 "The Dialectic of King and X in Do the Right Thing" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Mahatma Gandhi, Karl Marx — Just War Theory; Deontology; Ahimsa (nonviolence) — Silberstein reads Do the Right Thing as staging the ideological dialectic between Martin Luther King Jr.'s absolute nonviolence and Malcolm X's defense of retaliatory self-defense, both grounded in a theologically informed natural-law view of rights (King's Christian imago dei, X's Islamic tradition). He argues King mixes a deontological ethic (violence is always wrong) with a Gandhian consequentialist claim that violence begets violence, while X frames a race war as a just holy war. The film's Radio Raheem (LOVE/HATE knuckles), Buggin' Out's boycott of Sal's Wall of Fame, the Racial Slur Montage, and Mookie throwing the trash can dramatize whether ends justify means; the closing Sal-Mookie money exchange reframes racism as symptom of a deeper capitalist greed both King and X came to critique.
- ch. 19 "Fevered Desires and Interracial Intimacies in Jungle Fever" **·** John Stuart Mill, Frantz Fanon — Objectification; On Liberty; Black Skin, White Masks — Sundstrom uses Jungle Fever to dismantle the taboo (white and black versions) against interracial intimacy, treating Flipper and Angie's affair and the War Council's objections as a debate about black solidarity, loyalty, and self-hatred. He answers the War Council by invoking Mill's On Liberty and the tyranny of public opinion to defend sexual autonomy, and argues that demanding partners for political solidarity reduces them to props (objectification). He reads the psychoanalytic charge that interracial love is 'fevered' racial pathology as derived from Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks but ultimately baseless, and criticizes Lee for a puritanical ending that hides Orin and Paulie while exposing Flipper and Drew, failing to show interracial love as ordinary.
- ch. 20 "Bamboozled Philosophy through Blackface" **·** Charles W. Mills, Aristotle, Frantz Fanon — The Racial Contract; Moral Relativism; The Golden Mean — Flory argues Bamboozled deliberately makes its own audience laugh at Mantan's blackface coon routines to force self-reflection on how minstrel stereotypes still shape perceptions of African Americans. He reads Pierre Delacroix's shifting defenses of the show (free speech, art, 'get over slavery,' a simple-minded 'who is to judge' moral relativism) through Charles Mills's Racial Contract and 'epistemology of ignorance,' and his self-loathing through Fanon's struggle with racialization. Flory frames Lee as an Aristotelian gadfly: like Socrates, Lee arouses appropriately proportioned righteous anger (the Golden Mean) at injustice and goads viewers to philosophize, punishing Delacroix, Manray, and the Maumaus in a Manichaean moral structure to drive home minstrelsy's dehumanizing harm.
- ch. 21 "III. Time, the Subject, and Transcendence" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Transcendence and Sublimity in Spike Lee’s Signature Shot" **·** Martin Heidegger, Immanuel Kant — Phenomenology; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Abrams analyzes Lee's 'signature shot'—a character silently gliding forward toward the viewer—as a phenomenological device that ejects the immersed viewer back into self-aware spectatorship, drawing on Heidegger's account of anticipation and being futural in Being and Time and Danto's claim that a self-conscious camera makes the film about being viewed. He tracks the shot in Malcolm X (levitating before his assassination), 25th Hour (Mary floating on Ecstasy), and Inside Man (Frazier's superhuman, robotic rush after the staged execution). He then argues the shot is aesthetically sublime in Longinus's and Kant's sense: it renders characters superhuman and elevated off the ground, an objective image of subjective transcendence that signs Lee as both filmmaker and philosopher.
- ch. 23 "Economies of Time in Clockers" **·** W.E.B. Du Bois, Charles Sanders Peirce, Karl Marx, Richard Rorty — Double Consciousness; Commodity Fetishism; Thrownness (Geworfenheit) — Gilmore reads Clockers through DuBois's double-consciousness, arguing the film's dualities—the clockers' street dealing mirroring capitalist 'logic of maximum performance,' kronos versus kairos time, Hyde's commodity versus gift economies, systemic versus personal racism—make white and black viewers alike feel the anguish of Strike and Victor. The Gran Fury as predatory law, the slave-block-style police shakedown watched by Strike's mother, and Rocco seeing only his own reflection in Victor's eye illustrate Heideggerian thrownness and self-love-as-racism. Invoking Peirce's 'evolutionary love' (Radio Raheem's Right Hand/Left Hand speech), Rorty's renarrativization of who counts as 'white,' and Dewey's 'art is more moral than moralities,' Gilmore casts Lee as a pragmatist renarrativizing hate into love.
- ch. 24 "Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X" **·** John Locke, David Hume, René Descartes, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Bundle Theory of Self — LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.
- ch. 25 "List of Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 26 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; The Absurd; Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity — Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, René Descartes — The Absurd; Existentialism; Bad Faith — Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos; Will to Power; The Death of God — Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos.
