Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Aristotle — Authenticity; Existentialism; Bad Faith; Being-Toward-Death — Holt reads Paths of Glory as an illustration of existential ethics. The doomed men of the 701st are 'thrown' (Heidegger) into a suicidal attack on the Ant Hill, and the film contrasts the authentic Colonel Dax - sincere, consistent, refusing Mireau's command out of integrity - with the inauthentic, bad-faith General Mireau. Holt resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' by treating 'be authentic' as a formal meta-value, and argues that authenticity ultimately rests on the Aristotelian virtue of courage, shown when Paris 'dies well' before the firing squad despite an earlier failure of nerve.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard — Humanity as an End in Itself; Moral Luck; Philosophy of Love — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Jean-Paul Sartre, Michel Foucault, John Dewey — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Pragmatism — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (with 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and Eyes Wide Shut) to recover the philosophy of the body against the Socratic-Platonic-Cartesian denigration of the somatic. Using Merleau-Ponty's existential phenomenology ('I am my body') and pragmatists like Shusterman and Sullivan, he shows Kubrick's obsessive use of space, contingency, and the visceral - Davy's boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight, the weightless bodies of 2001, the Ludovico brainwashing of Alex, and the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut - to argue that subjectivity is corporeal and that anonymity of bodies can fund Foucauldian domination rather than liberation.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce — The Pragmatic Method; Pragmatism — Abrams reads Kubrick's Lolita as a parody of Poe's Dupin detective story, arguing that Humbert Humbert's method is not deduction but Peirce's logic of abduction (guessing). Humbert is the 'resolvent' half of Poe's double-Dupin - all calculation and chess - and excels only at overcoded abductions (spotting a nymphet) while failing the creative, undercoded abductions needed to see that Clare Quilty, the 'creative' double, is manipulating him. Abrams maps the film onto Poe's game-analysis (chess vs. cards) and the myth of the labyrinth, with Quilty as the ever-changing Minotaur whom Nabokov and Kubrick use for authorial 'involution.'
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Karl Marx, David Hume, Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, G.W.F. Hegel — Philosophical Skepticism; The Absurd; The Meaning of Life; Stoicism — Murray and Schuler argue that Kubrick's unifying vision is a dogmatic skepticism - the 'banality of the good' - in which good characters (Dax, Alice, Alex's parents) are flat and helpless while the wicked have sass, and irony rules. Drawing on Hume's essay 'The Sceptic' and Marx's dissertation on Epicurus's swerving atom, they read Kubrick as a 'rebel without a cause' whose skeptical tropes of cosmic insignificance, present pleasure, and the veneer over the ape (Dr. Strangelove, The Killing, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) accommodate rather than comprehend capitalist modernity. They contend Kubrick's Sartrean 'make your own meaning' answer is a false door, since projecting value either really transforms the world (refuting the claim it is indifferent) or projects nothing at all.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer, John Stuart Mill — Stoicism; The Meaning of Life; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a member of the 'cult of the cool' whose reticence and final resigned 'What's the difference?' surrender embody apatheia and acceptance of fate/logos. He tests Spencer Selby's claim that Clay and the sharpshooter Nikki must fail because their motives are immoral, arguing instead via an Aristotelian principle (virtues are stable dispositions) that their sudden lapses—the flimsy suitcase, Nikki's racial slur that loses him the lucky horseshoe—are Kubrick stacking the deck rather than genuine character. He closes by weighing Clay's life against models of a meaningful life (exuberance/romanticism vs. rationalism/self-fulfillment), faulting Clay for never subjecting his chosen ends to self-critical reason.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Plato, Plutarch — Tripartite Soul — Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's gladiatorial paria and the Crassus–Gracchus rivalry onto to thymoeides, the spirited/competitive middle part of the soul that Plutarch renders as philotimia (love of honor) driving the alpha males of classical history. The central thesis is that Crassus (Laurence Olivier) is ruled by this competitive second part: his skewed hamilla with Spartacus plays out not just on the battlefield but through the erotic triangle over Varinia and Antoninus ('he steals my boy, I steal his girl'), so the Republic falls to a coup driven by the restless, honor-seeking part of the soul.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Thomas Nagel, Albert Camus — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Thomas Nagel's essay 'The Absurd' (built on Camus's Sisyphus), distinguishing conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) from philosophical absurdity (the collision of the engaged participant perspective with the detached external one). He argues Kubrick's three signature devices—the painterly aesthetic that renders eighteenth-century rituals AS rituals, the slow reverse zoom that literally moves from close-up participant view to overwhelming long-shot external view, and the ironic omniscient narrator—make viewers see Barry's conventional absurdity and then confront their own inescapable philosophical absurdity. He notes Kubrick laments this predicament pessimistically where Nagel counsels irony.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Friedrich Nietzsche — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Death of God; Ressentiment — Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — Free Will vs Determinism; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.
- ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Alan Turing, G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle — The Turing Test; Master–Slave Dialectic; Personal Identity — Eberl compares HAL in 2001 and David in A.I. to ask whether an artificially created being can be a person meriting respect and rights. He runs both through criteria of personhood—self-consciousness, rationality, social activity, autonomy—and Turing's imitation game/behaviorism, concluding their responses give sufficient evidence of personhood even if the soul question is open. He uses Hegel's master–slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their creations (Bowman disconnecting HAL; the Flesh Fair destroying Mechas), warning against a moral crime of 'biological supremacy,' and invokes Aristotle's telos/virtue to argue Flesh Fairs wrongly preclude Mechas from fulfilling their function, while David's Pinocchio 'leap of faith' and cry 'I'm special, I'm David!' mark his approach to personhood.
- ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — The Übermensch; The Death of God; The Last Man — Abrams argues that 2001 films the whole evolutionary arc of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, from ape-men through humanity to the Star Child as the overman/posthuman. He maps the moon monolith's discovery onto the death of God (science debunking the creation myth, guarded by a Platonic 'noble lie' cover-up), the astronauts Bowman/Poole/Floyd onto the Enlightenment 'higher men,' and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus his and Poole's fatal spacewalks onto the last man and the falling tightrope walker whom Zarathustra carries. He then extends the vision toward Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's 'mind children,' while criticizing Kubrick for replacing Nietzsche's godless self-overcoming with alien 'replacement gods' that thin out the death-of-God insight.
- ch. 27 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Henri Bergson, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre, Augustine of Hippo, Jean Baudrillard — Philosophical Skepticism; Personal Identity; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** René Descartes, Plato, Daniel Dennett, Protagoras — Philosophical Skepticism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Moral Relativism — Rodriguez-Ruiz argues that Schizopolis and sex, lies, and videotape function as everyday 'thought experiments' about knowledge, contrasting them with Descartes's evil-genius and dream arguments and Dretske's disguised-zebra case. Fletcher must literally become his wife's lover's double to know she is cheating, and Ann pieces together John's affair from a stray earring, dramatizing how high the bar for knowledge of others is and how much depends on lucky accident. The trashcan-music scene stages the problem of induction and Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp. Soderbergh's boss's 'confirm nor deny' speech and Lester's preventable death show the films endorse a moderate skepticism that still affirms nature and power as real, rejecting full relativism and dogmatism.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Jean-François Lyotard, Jean Baudrillard — The End of Grand Narratives; Language Games; Personal Identity — Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Walter Benjamin — The Aura of the Artwork; Objectification — Pomerance combines philosophy of sex and philosophy of language to argue that sex, lies, and videotape is less about sex than about speaking sex and being watched speaking it. He analyzes Cynthia's videotaped confession about her first encounter, showing how her circumlocutions ('smooth like a test tube,' 'Ladies first') tease and withhold, and how Graham as silent 'priest of carnality' becomes an absent audience. Videotape 'amplifies' situated speech to a diffuse mass audience, so Cynthia's sexuality becomes a 'television personality,' pornographic in form and effacing her individuality in the manner of Benjamin's mechanical reproduction. The face and presence-in-time make every filmed performance both erotic and a kind of illuminating lie.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Henri Bergson, Gilles Deleuze, Thomas Hobbes — Duration (durée); Matter and Memory; Personal Identity — Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Henri Bergson, Gilles Deleuze, Thomas Hobbes — Duration (durée); Personal Identity; Matter and Memory — King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Walter Benjamin, Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Aura of the Artwork; The End of Grand Narratives — de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Baker uses Noel Carroll's aesthetic claim that film art requires 'sufficient' creative control ('no control, no style, no art') to defend Soderbergh's authorship across four remakes. The Underneath swaps noir shadow for suburban banality and green/blue color symbolism to externalize Michael's alienation; Traffic adapts a BBC series to indict NAFTA-era globalization and the treatment-starved drug war; Ocean's Eleven rewrites the Rat Pack ending so the thieves keep $150 million, an allegory of American wealth consolidation embodied by casino owner Benedict; Solaris strips science fiction to introspective desire. Baker further argues Soderbergh harnesses star images (Roberts, Douglas, Clooney) yet pushes them past type, synthesizing Hollywood's utopianism (per Dyer) with art-cinema social critique.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Jacques Lacan, Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The End of Grand Narratives; Personal Identity — Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Jacques Derrida, Friedrich Nietzsche — Binary Oppositions; Deconstruction — Nelson argues that critics forget Soderbergh directed Erin Brockovich because they file his career under the art/commerce binary, and he uses Nietzsche's attack on the 'faith in antithetical values' and Derrida's deconstruction to expose such binaries (art/entertainment, independent/mainstream, activity/passivity) as gendered, hierarchical, and unstable. He then shows the film's real signature is a 'self-centered narration' totally focalized through Julia Roberts's Erin, so that a tension between the movie's altruistic content and its Erin-fixated form never resolves. The chapter treats the binary as a rhetorically useful but collapsing tool rather than a real opposition.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Morton reads Schizopolis as Soderbergh's philosophical autobiography of identity, quoting Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding on memory as the ground of personal continuity to interpret Fletcher Munson's 'transmigration' into the doppelganger Dr. Korchek. Because Fletcher carries his own memory and nature into Korchek, he cannot escape his failed marriage (Korchek is sleeping with Fletcher's wife), confirming Lockean continuity: he 'cannot escape his own nature.' Morton ties the film's decayed language games and Elmo Oxygen's gibberish to a view that language masks action, and reads Fletcher's fate-frozen ending as identity surrendered to outside forces.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Sanders reads Soderbergh's HBO series K Street as a paranoid meditation on appearance and reality set in a Washington lobbying firm, where James Carville and Mary Matalin play fictionalized versions of themselves and the reclusive owner Richard Bergstrom manipulates everyone from afar while endlessly rewatching Mildred Pierce. Through three unresolved mysteries and a 'house of mirrors' structure, the show dramatizes the characters' skepticism about their capacity to know reality and Bergstrom's moral solipsism. Sanders argues Soderbergh's run-and-gun docudrama form itself enacts the epistemic uncertainty, leaving the text radically underdetermined about whether Bergstrom is a con man, a pawn, or a phantom-chasing paranoid.
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Gilles Deleuze, William James, Socrates, Henri Bergson — The Rhizome; The Unexamined Life; Pragmatism — Sterritt 'schizoanalyzes' The Informant! by arguing that its lying protagonist Mark Whitacre, an ADM executive turned FBI informant, is a nut psychoanalysis cannot crack because he has no unconscious depth: his self is Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomatic, depthless flow of desire with 'nothing behind it' (echoing Warhol). He reads Mark's compulsive fabrication as deterritorialization against the corporation-as-psychopath, links the film to the Socratic unexamined life and to William James's open, flux-embracing empiricism (via Cassavetes), and interprets the climactic collision of Mark's voiceover and dialogue as the film itself intervening as the ultimate informant.
- ch. 25 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Karl Marx — Utopia and Dystopia; Class Struggle; Commodity Fetishism — Tait gives a Fredric Jameson-derived Marxist reading of Ocean's Eleven, treating Danny Ocean's heist crew as a utopian 'figure of collectivity' whose diverse, cross-class, pan-American membership recalls the WWII combat film and rallies against Terry Benedict as the polysemous 'monster' (Jameson's shark in Jaws) standing for globalized capital displacing nostalgic American Las Vegas. He argues the victimless heist allegorizes a competing value system in which love, solidarity, and friendship trump money, restaging class conflict from Asphalt Jungle, Rififi, and Big Deal on Madonna Street. The film's utopian happy ending imagines redistributing wealth and 'beating the house' within the very system of late capital it critiques.
- ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Categorical Imperative; Deontology; Existentialism — Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.
- ch. 27 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Plato, Søren Kierkegaard, Gilles Deleuze, Augustine of Hippo — Allegory of the Cave; Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Augustine on Time — McFarland reads Soderbergh's Solaris as a meditation on recollection, recognition, and repetition, grounding it in Platonic recollection (the Phaedo, the cave, and the Symposium's love as desire) and Augustine's Confessions, where memory strains toward an elusive beloved-as-God, the 'cruel miracle' of present absence. When Solaris materializes Rheya, Chris Kelvin first jettisons the 'bad copy' but then, tempted by Snow, embraces Deleuze's endless degraded repetition of copies to erase his guilt over her suicide. Against this, Gibarian voices a Kierkegaardian call (Repetition, Either/Or) that there are 'only choices'; McFarland faults Chris, like Odysseus choosing Kalypso's island, for choosing the deathless eternal present over the human world of forward-moving choice.
- ch. 29 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The End of Grand Narratives — Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.
- ch. 30 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Tim Burton

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Personal Identity — The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Walter Benjamin, David Hume, René Descartes — Personal Identity; Bundle Theory of Self; The Cogito — Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir — Bad Faith; Woman as the Other; Authenticity — Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Despair (sickness unto death); Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Daniel Sullivan argues that Burton and Poe channel childhood 'ontological insecurity' (R. D. Laing) into horror fantasy, using Burton's short Vincent as case study. Seven-year-old Vincent Malloy, imagining himself as Vincent Price, escapes 'necessity's despair' into fantastic possibility but slides into what Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death calls defiant then demonic despair, clinging to a self-as-victim identity until he collapses. Sullivan reads fantasy as both consolation and danger—the flight into possibility further isolates the insecure child—and extends the possibility/necessity dialectic and Otto Rank's life/creation dialectic to Nightmare Before Christmas, Edward Scissorhands, and Big Fish.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Sigmund Freud — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Thomas Hobbes — Democracy; The Social Contract — Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill, John Dewey, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Aristotle, Martha Nussbaum — The Philosopher King; Democracy; On Liberty — Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Martin Heidegger, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Friedrich Nietzsche — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); Dasein (being-there); The Übermensch; The They-Self (das Man) — Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Immanuel Kant, Plato, Thomas Nagel — Phenomena and Noumena; What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Theory of Forms — Baltzer-Jaray uses Kant's phenomena/noumena split, Plato's Forms, and Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to ask whether Jack Skellington can know the essence of Christmas and whether Vincent Malloy can know what it is to BE Vincent Price. She argues Jack's lab-experiments on presents and snowflakes ('Jack's Obsession') can only yield phenomena, never the noumenal essence, so Kant would permit belief but not knowledge; Vincent, watching only Price's horror roles, grasps a mere phenomenal fragment. Via Nagel she concludes neither can occupy another's subjective viewpoint, so the lesson of both films is to celebrate otherness through communication rather than trying to be someone else.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(no index entry yet)* — Jenkins reads Burton's 'Sweeney Todd' (2007) through Edmund Burke's theory of the sublime and the device of synesthesia. She argues Burton relocates Burke's sublime from nature to the man-made, consuming city, staging beauty (Johanna, the flower-market flashbacks, saturated color) in losing tension with the 'dark and gloomy' urban sublime (desaturated Fleet Street, 'Epiphany'). Drawing on German Expressionist visual style (Caligari, Nosferatu) and the raindrop-to-blood credit sequence, she shows how sight, sound and represented taste (Mrs. Lovett's cannibal pies, the jugular-spray 'shooting star' during 'Johanna') mix the senses to force the queasy Burkean confrontation of terror and delight, ending in Burke's nihilistic darkness rather than redemption.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(no index entry yet)* — Knight and McKnight apply Tzvetan Todorov's categories of 'the fantastic,' 'the uncanny,' and 'the marvelous' to the eight Burton films starring Johnny Depp, arguing that Burton treats the fantastic not as a genre but as a transgeneric film MODE that sustains the viewer's hesitation between natural and supernatural explanation. Using Wayne Booth's notion of the authorial 'second self,' they cast Depp as Burton's persona/surrogate who realizes and sustains that uncertainty (Edward, Ed Wood, Ichabod Crane, Willy Wonka, Sweeney, the Hatter). They classify 'Ed Wood' and 'Edward Scissorhands' as resolving into the uncanny (rationally explicable) and 'Sleepy Hollow,' 'Corpse Bride,' 'Alice in Wonderland,' and 'Dark Shadows' as passing into the marvelous, where new laws of nature must be accepted.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Martin Heidegger, Sigmund Freud, Robert Nozick — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; The Experience Machine — McMahon argues Burton's death-saturated corpus functions as modern memento mori that fosters Heideggerian authenticity by arousing the uncanny and honest awareness of being-toward-death. She supplements Freud's account of the unheimliche (which she says wrongly substitutes castration anxiety for the primal fear of death) with Heidegger's link of angst, uncanniness, and finitude in 'Being and Time,' plus Terror Management Theory. Reading 'The Nightmare Before Christmas,' 'Corpse Bride,' and 'Dark Shadows,' she shows Jack, Bonejangles's Dance of Death, Emily, and vampire Barnabas use animation, comedy, and romance to make death palatable, and contrasts these films with Nozick's escapist experience machine—Burton supplements reality rather than replacing it.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Plato — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Allegory of the Cave — LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" **·** Karl Marx, bell hooks, Jacques Lacan — Commodity Fetishism; The Culture Industry — Olson argues Burton's signature saturated-versus-drab color palette in 'The Nightmare Before Christmas' and 'Corpse Bride' operates as a marketing strategy that commodifies childhood, conditioning children as future consumers who associate the films' colors with a utopian fantasy world to be bought back. She reads Jack's craving for the color of Christmas Town ('I want it for my own') through Lacan's objet petit a and through bell hooks's 'commodification of difference' (the Other consumed while its meaning is stripped away), and treats the Disney/Burton fairy-tale film as a Fordist commodity whose color palette—echoed on store shelves—drives product loyalty and nostalgic desire.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(notes)*
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(notes)*
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings

- ch. 1 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — The editors' introduction argues that The Lord of the Rings, though written by a philologist rather than a philosopher, dramatizes perennial questions Tolkien cared about as a Catholic: whether power always corrupts, whether death can be a gift, and the tension of fate versus free will. It frames the volume's method by invoking Socrates, who drew on art, sport, and music his listeners already knew to provoke examination of their lives, presenting Tolkien's fiction as the same kind of popular-culture doorway into the great questions.
- ch. 11 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Socrates — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic — Eric Katz reads the One Ring as a variation on Plato's Ring of Gyges from the Republic: both grant impunity, and both pose the question of whether anyone would stay moral if able to act without consequence. Where Plato only argues that unchecked power corrupts the soul, Tolkien shows it through Gollum's ruin, Boromir's fall, and Frodo's final failure at the Cracks of Doom, while Galadriel, Bombadil, and Sam refuse the Ring by knowing who they are. Katz concludes Tolkien answers Plato's 'why be moral?' with 'to be yourself.'
- ch. 13 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Nick Bostrom — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Existential Risk — Theodore Schick treats the Rings of Power as an allegory-free meditation on externalized 'potency,' applying it to emerging genetics, nanotechnology, and robotics. He contrasts the Council of Elrond's choice to destroy the Ring with Boromir's wish to wield it, and with Bill Joy's call to relinquish dangerous research versus Drexler's promise that nanotech could end poverty and disease. Schick argues our situation differs from Middle-earth because the knowledge cannot be un-forged, so grassroots social taming, not destruction of a single artifact, is the realistic response to knowledge-enabled mass destruction.
- ch. 14 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Sigmund Freud, Karl Marx, Martin Heidegger — Commodity Fetishism; Alienation; The Unconscious — Alison Milbank reads the One Ring as a fetish in both Freud's sexual sense (an object severed from the whole, twice literally cut from a finger, warding off the castrating maternal power figured in Shelob) and Marx's economic sense (a commodity that estranges makers from things and reduces persons to hoarders like Smaug). Against fetishism she sets Tolkien's gift-economy, embodied by Bombadil tossing the Ring in the air and by Sam's elvish rope, and Heidegger's older sense of the 'thing' as a gathering, so the novel teaches us to receive the world back as gift rather than possession.
- ch. 15 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Epicurus, Henry David Thoreau — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Gregory Bassham mines the happy communities of the Shire, Rivendell, and Lothlorien for six keys to happiness: delight in simple things (linked to Epicurus's natural pleasures and Thoreau's Walden simplicity), making light of troubles, close friendship (grounded in Aristotle's claim that friendship is the greatest external good), good character, cherishing beauty and creativity, and recovering wonder. He argues Tolkien's hobbits and elves illustrate what modern happiness research confirms, so Tolkien functions as a philosophical guide to a more joy-filled life.
- ch. 17 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Jorge Gracia contrasts Sam and Gollum, two hobbits of shared nature and culture who both pursue happiness but reach opposite ends. Gollum's happiness is possession of the Precious, a thing, sought in isolation and won by murdering Deagol, which destroys him; Sam's happiness is fellowship in the Shire with Frodo and Rosie, and his love for Frodo lets him surrender the Ring where Gollum cannot. Drawing on Aristotle's tie between happiness, one's nature, and friendship, Gracia concludes that for ordinary beings happiness is achievable only in a social context whose key is love expressed as loyalty and sharing.
- ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Hannah Arendt, Albert Camus — Amor Fati (love of fate); Existentialism — Eric Bronson reads the elves of Rivendell and especially Lothlorien through the 'merrier' existentialists, arguing that lasting joy requires facing the abyss and still affirming life, and knowing, as Nietzsche urged, what to remember and what to forget. Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.
- ch. 19 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power; The Übermensch; The Death of God — Douglas Blount casts Sauron as a candidate for Nietzsche's Ubermensch, embodying the unabashed will to power in a world where God is dead, life is meaningless, and taste rather than reason or morality guides the self-created life. Tolkien answers this not by argument but by a rival portrait whose beauty lies in community, humility, love, and self-sacrifice: Gandalf dying on the bridge, Frodo's mercy to Gollum, and Sam refusing the Ring's vision of 'Samwise the Strong.' Blount argues that on Nietzsche's own criterion of taste, Tolkien's picture of abnegation is the more compelling vision of a life lived well.
- ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo — The Problem of Evil; Free Will vs Determinism — Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'
- ch. 22 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Virtue Ethics; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Golden Mean — Aeon Skoble uses the characters to argue for Aristotelian virtue ethics over Kantian duty and utilitarian consequence, since right action flows from developed character and practical reason rather than rule-following. He reads Sam's loyalty and Aragorn's temperance as genuine virtue, Boromir as flawed-but-decent (undone by resentment and pride), and Smeagol's swift murder of Deagol as proof the Ring's corrupting power depends partly on prior character. Skoble contends Kant's rules would make Sam's loyalty no better than a Ringwraith's, and utilitarianism's demand for foreknowledge suits only Galadriel, so virtue ethics best fits Tolkien's flawed, developing heroes.
- ch. 23 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Epicurus, Lucretius, Boethius, Aristotle — Death Is Nothing to Us; Immortality and the Soul; Personal Identity — Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.
- ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Marx, Alasdair MacIntyre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; The Death of God — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.
- ch. 26 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Anthropocentrism; Deep Ecology; Wilderness and Nature Aesthetics — Andrew Light resists reading the peoples of Middle-earth as simple stand-ins for parts of nature, noting that the ents, not the elves, truly speak for the forest, so nature is animated to stand and speak for itself. His central idea is 'green time': through Tom Bombadil and the ents, Tolkien represents a naturally scaled, ecosystemic, near-indifferent temporal perspective, seen when Bombadil is unconcerned with the Ring and the ents ignore the riders of Rohan. Light argues this indifference should not make us indifferent to nature but should teach humility and long-term responsibility for problems like global warming, imagining what it is to care for things as a process beyond our own lifespan.
- ch. 27 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Immanuel Kant — The Problem of Evil; Free Will vs Determinism; Fate and Foreknowledge — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Dogen, Laozi, The Buddha — Buddhism; Taoism (Daoism); Yin and Yang; Zen Buddhism — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.
- ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Plato, René Descartes, Augustine of Hippo — Allegory of the Cave; The Cogito; Existentialism — J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.
- ch. 31 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — The Meaning of Life; The Leap of Faith — John Davenport argues The Lord of the Rings is religious not as Christian allegory but as an epic fairy tale in Tolkien's sense from 'On Fairy-stories,' delivering 'eucatastrophe,' the sudden joyous turn that, like Kierkegaard's faith in a salvation beyond our own power, hints at eschatological hope. Using Sir Gawain and the Green Knight as Tolkien's model for Frodo (both accept an impossible burden, both fail and bear a scar of mortality), he identifies the destruction of the Ring via Gollum, Eowyn's healing, and the sapling of Nimloth as eucatastrophic 'turns.' Davenport concludes the veiled religious message is that evil cannot stand forever, yet deliverance requires our sacrifice and faith beyond rational hope that 'day shall come again.'
- ch. 32 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 34 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" *(front)*

## The Philosophy of War Films

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Sigmund Freud, Michel Foucault, Heraclitus, Isaiah Berlin — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The Death Drive (Thanatos) — LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.
- ch. 7 "Part 1. The Aesthetics of War On-Screen" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "War and Representation" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Gilles Deleuze, G.W.F. Hegel, Theodor Adorno — The Rhizome — Jameson contends that war poses the 'nominalist dilemma'—the gap between abstract totality and sensory immediacy—making it ultimately unrepresentable, and enumerates eight recurring narrative situations (existential, collective, leaders, technology, landscape, atrocity, homeland attack, occupation). Using Burke's dramatistic pentad he argues the war narrative drifts from 'act/agent' toward 'scene,' where the anthropomorphic dissolves; Sartre's 'groups-in-fusion' and Deleuze's nomadic war machine model the collective buddy-squad, whose division of labor he compares to the heist film. Reading Grimmelshausen's Simplicissimus and Döblin's Wallenstein against Kluge's Stalingrad and Halberstadt collages, he shows war (from the Thirty Years' War to WWII aerial bombing) generating a rhizomatic, nonnarrative flow that defeats stable narrative convention.
- ch. 9 "War Pictures Digital Surveillance from Foreign Theater to Homeland Security Front" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Michel Foucault — The Panopticon (surveillance) — Stewart argues that War on Terror films (Redacted, Battle for Haditha, The Situation, In the Valley of Elah, Waltz with Bashir) depict 'a soldiery without a genre' because digital surveillance has fused sighting and triggering, so combat is nowhere and everywhere and the classic movement-image spectacle collapses. Drawing on Deleuze's movement-image/time-image distinction, he recasts the soldier as spectator (SSS' rather than SAS'), watching under the panoptic drone eye rather than acting, and shows sci-fi 'temportation' thrillers (Déjà Vu, Source Code, Eagle Eye) travestying the time-image into computerized wish-fulfillment. The Hurt Locker succeeds precisely by reverting to a man-vs-machine 'duel,' while Waltz with Bashir alone achieves genuine political reframing by breaking from animation into archival massacre footage.
- ch. 10 "Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Peebles defends the 'digital vérité' of Iraq War films (Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, The Battle for Haditha, Redacted, Standard Operating Procedure) against Garrett Stewart's charge that grainy embedded footage elides critique, arguing instead that the multiplying lenses close the distance between soldier and viewer to build empathy. She invokes Baudrillard's 'the Gulf War did not take place' to show how CNN's video-game-like distance erased the common soldier, which the up-close soldier-shot cell-phone image corrects. Reading Hank Deerfield's reconstruction of his son's fatal Humvee incident in Elah and Errol Morris's reframing of the Abu Ghraib photos in Standard Operating Procedure, she argues each frame is 'both an aperture and a restriction,' and that these tragedies are inherently antiwar.
- ch. 11 "Beyond Panopticism The Biopolitical Labor of Surveillance and War in Contemporary Film" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Michel Foucault, Karl Marx, Immanuel Kant, Walter Benjamin — The Panopticon (surveillance); Discipline and Docile Bodies; Class Struggle — Gooch argues that the post-2005 surveillance film cycle moves 'beyond panopticism': Foucault's disciplinary gaze gives way to Deleuze's 'societies of control,' and the surveiling gaze becomes direct domination and a form of biopolitical labor (Hardt and Negri) rather than an impersonal structure. He reads the prestige dramas (Redacted, Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, Lions for Lambs) as exposing the soldier's proletarianization and self-surveillance, and the thrillers/blockbusters (Déjà Vu, The Kingdom, Body of Lies, The Bourne Ultimatum, Eagle Eye, Burn after Reading) as staging a Marxist antagonism between living labor (the watching hero) and the fixed capital of surveillance technology. Using Deleuze's 'degraded time-image,' Kant's needed separation of subject and law, and Benjamin/Agamben's state of exception, he shows Eagle Eye inverting law and subject to justify preemptive war and turn biopolitical labor into the labor of subjection.
- ch. 12 "Seeing Soldiers, Seeing Persons Wittgenstein, Film Theory, and Charlie Chaplin’s Shoulder Arms" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Hilsabeck argues that Wittgenstein's notion of aspect perception ("seeing as") is not a phenomenology of illusion, as film theorists like Allen and Turvey take it, but an ethical matter of articulating experience within forms of life and language games. He reads Chaplin's Shoulder Arms through this lens: Doughboy's tree-disguise gag and his repurposing of war objects (Limburger cheese as grenade, gramophone horn as snorkel) demonstrate imaginative, ethical vision, while the German soldier who cannot see the tree-as-man exhibits "aspect blindness." The film makes viewers' willingness to "see anew" a test of attunement and mutual acknowledgment, casting the environment of WWI trench warfare and mechanized shock as what stifles this imaginative seeing.
- ch. 13 "Part 2. War as Condition of Self-Formation and Self-Dissolution" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, René Descartes, Gilbert Ryle, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud — The Unexamined Life; Mind–Body Dualism; The Ghost in the Machine — Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.
- ch. 15 "The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Embodiment (the lived body); Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.
- ch. 16 "“All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche — Philosophical Skepticism; Self-Reliance — Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."
- ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Buddha — Forgiveness; The State of Nature; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.
- ch. 18 "Part 3. The Ethical Tribulations of War" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films" **·** Judith Butler — Objectification — Pötzsch uses cognitive film theory (Murray Smith's alignment and allegiance, paradigm scenarios and schemata) to argue that Beaufort, Waltz with Bashir, and Lebanon, though hailed as antiwar films, covertly reinforce a militarist "scopic regime" through the "ubiquitously absent enemy." Formal devices—the tank scope's tunnel vision in Lebanon, shot/reverse-shot and voice-over confined to Israeli soldiers, the animated flashbacks of Waltz with Bashir—align and ally viewers exclusively with Israeli troops framed as helpless victims, while the Palestinian other stays faceless, voiceless, and objectified (the staggering Lebanese woman, the trauma displaced onto dead dogs and horses). Drawing on Judith Butler's frames of war and "ungrievable" lives, he reads this as Kimmerling's latent cognitive militarism that denies the enemy's competing subjectivity and forecloses nonviolent alternatives.
- ch. 20 "General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War" **·** Immanuel Kant, Martha Nussbaum — Just War Theory; Humanity as an End in Itself; Respect for Persons — Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.
- ch. 21 "The Work of Art in the Age of Embedded Journalism Fiction versus Depiction in Zero Dark Thirty" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Plato — Allegory of the Cave; Just War Theory — Evans argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty fails morally and epistemically because its immersive 'boots-on-the-ground' realism traps the viewer inside Maya's single point of view, so we can never see the CIA torture program's lunacy the way an outside witness would. Drawing on Wittgenstein's Tractatus claim that the subject is a limit of the world (the eye that cannot see itself), she shows how the film effaces its own privileged viewpoint to pass off a partial view as impartial reality. Against this she sets a Platonic point that genuine reality is glimpsed only through fiction that ironically juxtaposes contrasting viewpoints, citing scenes like the SEALs' banter and Maya's final weeping where the film briefly becomes true art. The 'depiction is not endorsement' defense collapses because the narrative logic still credits torture with finding bin Laden.
- ch. 22 "Part 4. War, Nature, and the Absolute" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Vernacular Metaphysics On Terrence Malick’s The Thin Red Line" **·** Martin Heidegger, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Being-Toward-Death; The Meaning of Life — Pippin reads Malick's The Thin Red Line as deliberately invoking then refusing Hollywood war-movie conventions (group solidarity, trackable characters, heroic assault) so the viewer is left 'lost' and forced toward a metaphysical rather than political or sentimental reckoning with death. Through unattributed poetic voice-overs—Train's Manichean questions, Witt's search for the calm 'immortality' he saw in his dying mother, Welsh's cynicism, Bell's romantic idealism—and lingering non-plot shots of nature bathed in sunlight, the film pursues a 'vernacular metaphysics': ordinary soldiers straining ordinary speech to ask what it is to live under certain death. Pippin aligns this disclosive, prediscursive truth of the image with the Hegel-to-Heidegger-Merleau-Ponty tradition of art as truth-bearer, while Witt's Emersonian 'one big soul' and his self-sacrifice ('all things shining') stage the film's unresolved question of whether nature and death can be seen as good.
- ch. 24 "War and Its Fictional Recovery On-Screen Narrative Management of Death in The Big Red One and The Thin Red Lin" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Death Drive (Thanatos); The Unconscious — Bronfen takes Freud's 'Thoughts for the Times on War and Death' (life 'recovers its full content' when war forces us to believe in death) and his theory of the death drive and the uncanny double as a template for how war films manage mortality through fiction. In Fuller's The Big Red One, the nameless Sergeant's guilt-driven distinction between killing and murder, his Nazi double Schroeder, and the compulsively repeated stabbing scene at the crucifix let the hero convert contingent slaughter into a restitutive story where survival is 'the only glory,' echoing Freud's Eros–Thanatos struggle. In Malick's The Thin Red Line, Private Witt splits not into warlike and peacetime selves but into bodily and spiritual presence, embracing death as transcendence into 'shining light' that doubles the light of cinema itself. Both films strike a pact with the viewer, who dies with the heroes yet safely survives them.
- ch. 25 "“Profoundly Unreconciled to Nature” Ecstatic Truth and the Humanistic Sublime in Werner Herzog’s War Films" **·** Immanuel Kant, Martin Heidegger — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Meaning of Life — LaRocca argues against Thomas Weiskel that the 'humanistic sublime' is not an oxymoron, using Herzog's war films (Lessons of Darkness, Little Dieter Needs to Fly, Rescue Dawn) to show a sublime that returns us to the human at the limit of existence rather than transcending it. Building on Kant's link between the sublime and human dignity—and Kant's claim that sublimity lies in our ideas, not in nature—he reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' (fabrication that exceeds the 'accountant's truth') as the vehicle: staged monologues, borrowed music, and recontextualized documentary footage disclose an inner reality. Herzog's Heideggerian gloss on aletheia as un-concealment aligns cinema itself with truth, and Dengler's bear ('the only friend I had was death') exemplifies war as the space of radical mortality where the humanistic sublime dawns for the safe spectator, contrasted with Malick's more Darwinian, nature-indifferent vision.
