## The Philosophy of Werner Herzog

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "1-A01-LEX" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Foreword" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche — Phenomenology — The editors' introduction argues that Herzog, despite branding himself an anti-intellectual who dismisses critics with 'Go for it, losers!' and lives 'with as little reflection as possible,' has a genuine philosophy of filmmaking centered on 'ecstatic truth' against the 'accountant's truth.' It reads his persona of 'false Herzogs' and doppelgangers as itself a rhetorical construction, and invokes Wittgenstein's 'Don't think, but look!' to frame Herzog's demand that viewers approach films like Grizzly Man and Fitzcarraldo with open eyes rather than academic categories. It surveys each contributor's essay as a way of restoring the 'effability' of Herzog's work.
- ch. 7 "“I Am What My Films Are”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Phenomenology — David LaRocca listens to Herzog's essayistic, self-mythologizing pronouncements in autobiographical documentaries like 'I Am My Films' and 'Werner Herzog: Filmemacher,' arguing that Herzog practices a 'vigorous essayism' that yields 'ecstatic truth' from fabrication (as in the story of walking to Paris to save Lotte Eisner, or seeing God who turned out to be a power-station worker). Drawing on Deleuze's remark on the defenseless walker and a Nietzschean stress on what is 'healthiest,' LaRocca connects Herzog's virtue of filmmaking-on-foot and his Rogue Film School anti-pedagogy to a 'humanistic sublime' that returns us to human limits and mortality rather than transcending them.
- ch. 8 "Herzog’s Sublime and Ecstatic Truth" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Patricia Castello Branco argues that Herzog's sublime is Burkean and physiological rather than Kantian and transcendental: in Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man the protagonists' encounter with overwhelming nature defeats reason and works through the body (Kinski's distorted performance, Treadwell's death) rather than confirming reason's supremacy as in Kant's Critique of Judgment. She maps Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' onto Nietzsche's Dionysian from The Birth of Tragedy, where the principium individuationis dissolves and the hero merges with nature's creating-and-destroying flux, and glosses ecstatic truth via Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment reached through fabrication and stylization.
- ch. 9 "The Conquest of Uselessness as a Practice of Film and Thought" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze — The Übermensch — Daniele Dottorini reads Herzog's filmmaking as a 'conquest of the useless' through the figures of the Tightrope Walker (Philippe Petit), the Traveler, and the Pilgrim, whose bodily effort and risk over the abyss subtract film from any utilitarian logic. He aligns them with the tightrope walker of the prologue to Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, poised between animal and Overman, and uses Deleuze and Guattari's 'conceptual personae' from What Is Philosophy? to argue that Herzog becomes his own characters. The carrying of the ship over the mountain in Fitzcarraldo and Steiner's ecstatic ski-flight exemplify ecstatic truth (aletheia) as an unveiling that transfigures the world into music.
- ch. 10 "Filmmaking and Philosophizing against the Grain of Theory Herzog and Wittgenstein" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, René Descartes, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Language Games; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Mihai Ometita pairs Herzog's anti-intellectualism with Wittgenstein's later philosophy, arguing that the obstinacy of Herzog's protagonists (Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo) and the dogmatism of Wittgenstein's interlocutors are two faces of an unbounded attachment to a single theory. Herzog's dictum 'An ape is an ape' echoes Wittgenstein's motto that everything is what it is, warning against forced metaphor (the smoking monkey in Echoes from a Somber Empire). Citing the Big Typescript and On Certainty, Ometita reads philosophy's difficulty as one of the will, and treats Aguirre's 'delirium' and Fitzcarraldo's 'dream' as quasi-nonsense that resists hasty diagnoses of madness; he invokes Descartes's window and Merleau-Ponty on film being perceived, not thought.
- ch. 11 "Nature and Natural Meaning in Grizzly Man" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant — The World as Will; Anthropocentrism; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Marc Furstenau reads Grizzly Man as Herzog's philosophy of nature, arguing that Herzog's vision of nature as chaos, hostility, and murder mirrors Schopenhauer's terrifying Will and the fact/value split, and that Herzog blames Timothy Treadwell's sentimental faith in natural harmony for his and Amie Huguenard's deaths while secretly sharing Treadwell's amor fati. Using Iris Murdoch's Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals and Mary Midgley's Beast and Man, Furstenau contends that both Herzog and Schopenhauer succumb to an 'outrageous simplicity' that denies animal agency; against them he argues, via Midgley, that culture is natural and interspecies sympathy is real, reading Treadwell's extreme close-up of the bear (where Herzog sees 'only the overwhelming indifference of nature') as evidence of imaginative continuity between human and animal.
- ch. 12 "Reflections from the Abyss Herzog’s Philosophy of Death" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Epicurus — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Death Is Nothing to Us — M. Blake Wilson traces Herzog's philosophy of death and the 'abyss' across Grizzly Man and Into the Abyss, examining how Herzog frames human, animal, and self-killings and refuses the retributive impulse. Against Kant's demand that murderers must die and Matthew Kramer's purgative rationale for capital punishment, Wilson enlists Nietzsche's warnings about the drive to punish and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us,' while contrasting Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' with the 'accountant's truth' via journalistic and bear-attack literature (Jans, Herrero) that accuses Herzog of a 'Hollywoodized' portrait of Treadwell. He coins 'vivicide' for the killing of a human by a non-human animal and questions whether Bear 141 committed murder or was merely a scavenger.
- ch. 13 "Fake News and Ecstatic Truths" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Perspectivism; Truth as What Works — Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.
- ch. 14 "The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse" **·** Martin Heidegger, Immanuel Kant, William James — The Question Concerning Technology; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Ian Alexander Moore reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' through Heidegger's account of truth as aletheia (unconcealment) and 'The Origin of the Work of Art,' arguing that Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph and Wagner Prelude in Lessons of Darkness and Lo and Behold elevate viewers into a sublime, ecstatic state that discloses a truth beyond the 'accountant's' factual. He connects the slow-motion ski-jumps of The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner to Heidegger's ecstatic standing-outside-oneself, and treats Lessons of Darkness's burning Kuwaiti oil fields as an apocalyptic un-covering. He also warns that planetary information technology (echoing Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology) threatens the very oblivion of ecstatic truth.
- ch. 15 "The Film Artist as Discoverer of the Marvels of Everyday Life a Kracauerian Reading of Werner Herzog" **·** Walter Benjamin — The Aura of the Artwork — Christopher Turner reads Herzog through Siegfried Kracauer's Theory of Film, arguing that Herzog, like Kracauer's 'film artist as explorer,' redeems physical reality by transfiguring the boring, habitual everyday into marvels. Herzog's warning about the extinction-level 'lack of adequate imagery' is aligned with Kracauer's redemption of the familiar, and films like Land of Silence and Darkness (deaf-blind Fini Straubinger) and Even Dwarfs Started Small reveal 'the unfamiliar in the familiar.' Turner invokes Benjamin (via Miriam Hansen) on the modern decline of Erfahrung into isolated Erlebnis to frame Herzog's discovery of a deeper, mysterious physical reality obscured by scientific abstraction.
- ch. 16 "Werner Herzog and the Documentary as a Revelatory Practice" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Edmund Husserl — Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body) — Antony Fredriksson argues that Herzog's documentaries are not veridical fact-representations but a 'revelatory practice,' aligning Herzog's ecstatic-versus-accountant's-truth distinction with phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty, Husserl, Waldenfels). Using Merleau-Ponty's reading of Fabrice at Waterloo, he claims lived experience is contingent and pre-narrative, and that films like La Soufriere (a catastrophe that never happens), White Diamond (swifts behind the waterfall), and Echoes from a Somber Empire (the nicotine-addicted monkey) reveal the alien, attention-grabbing world beyond habitual seeing — a 'pathos' that reads the viewer rather than neutrally recording facts.
- ch. 17 "On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society" **·** Theodor Adorno, Karl Marx, Gilles Deleuze — The Culture Industry; Alienation — Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.
- ch. 18 "Herzog’s Philosophy of Masculinism" **·** Gender Performativity; Objectification — Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.
- ch. 19 "Herzog’s Post-Tragic Aesthetic" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, G.W.F. Hegel — Despair (sickness unto death); Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Anthony Eagan and Simon Thornton apply Kierkegaard's theory of tragedy (from the aesthete 'A' in Either/Or, plus the demonic in The Sickness unto Death) to argue that Timothy Treadwell (Grizzly Man) and Aguirre (Aguirre, the Wrath of God) are not tragic but comic figures. Both cross Herzog's 'invisible borderline' by asserting pure subjectivity over fate, romanticizing nature while ignoring the ambiguous collision of freedom and necessity that constitutes genuine tragedy. Treadwell freely engineers his own preventable death (so it cannot be tragic pain), and Aguirre, drifting in circles as self-proclaimed wrath of God, personifies the demonic refusal to repent — a 'post-tragic' comedy that aches.
- ch. 20 "Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Plato, Socrates — The General Will; The Unexamined Life — Tyler Tritten argues that Even Dwarfs Started Small and Stroszek are not principally political but share an essence: the impotency of the powerless dramatized through cyclical, repetitive motion (circling trucks, ski lifts, and above all chickens). He defends Herzog's 'apoliticism' — citing Herzog's preference for the medieval melior pars over numerical voting (echoing Rousseau's general will versus the popular vote, and Socrates against the many) — as locating the human condition beneath contingent social conditions. The handless, cannibalistic, circumambulating chicken becomes the emblem of a self-consuming nature and a humanity too proportionate to the beast, provoking a pure, aching laughter as the only revolt.
- ch. 21 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 22 "Contributors" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of the Beats

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; Cosmopolitanism — Elkholy's editorial introduction defines 'Beat' (the New York/West Coast writers) versus 'beat' (a lifestyle of weariness and disaffiliation), tracing the term through Kerouac, Ginsberg's 'Howl,' and Snyder. She frames the Beats' turning-inward and self-marginalization philosophically, noting that Brustein's charge that beats pursue aimless 'kicks' echoes Kierkegaard's critique of the Romantics as engaged in purposeless, rootless striving that evades responsibility. Against this she sets Holmes's reading of beat detachment as a search for meaning and belief, and casts the Beats' global travels as anticipating an emerging cosmopolitanism.
- ch. 7 "I. The Beats Creating a Subculture" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy and Non-Philosophy of Potato Salad" **·** Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Plato — Deconstruction; Allegory of the Cave — Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.
- ch. 9 "Laugh of the Revolutionary Diane di Prima, French Feminist Philosophy, and the Contemporary Cult of the Beat H" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud — Feminism; Objectification — Quinn reads Diane di Prima's serial poem 'Loba' and 'Memoirs of a Beatnik' through Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and its call to 'écriture féminine'—women writing the body. She argues di Prima's she-wolf/Medusa figure, sex-positive candor, and refusal of narrative closure enact Cixous's boundless feminine writing, while Cixous's anti-Freudian, anti-Lacanian mockery of 'penis envy' and the 'big dick' illuminates di Prima's transgressive motherhood and bisexuality. Against the male Beats' dismissal of women writers (and Beauvoir's foremother status), the essay centralizes di Prima as a serious feminist philosopher-poet rather than a nostalgic icon.
- ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" **·** John Stuart Mill, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — The Harm Principle; Utopia and Dystopia; Buddhism — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- ch. 11 "Being-at-Home Gary Snyder and the Poetics of Place" **·** Martin Heidegger, Dogen, Henry David Thoreau — Deep Ecology; Zen Buddhism; Transcendentalism — Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.
- ch. 12 "II. Beat Identities Selfhood and Experimentation" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "From Self-Alienation to Posthumanism The Transmigration of the Burroughsian Subject" **·** Jacques Derrida, Jacques Lacan, Karl Marx — Deconstruction; Alienation; The Mirror Stage — Bolton argues William S. Burroughs's fragmented subjects—split by a parasitic 'Other Half' or word virus—are not postmodernism's dissolved nonsubjects but practitioners of a productive self-alienation. He aligns Burroughs's multiply-named, body-swapping characters (Mr. Bradley Mr. Martin, Joe the Dead) with Lacan's split subject constituted in language and with Derrida's iterable 'mark' and 'third that walks beside you' as an absent-present that dissolves binaries. Through Naked Lunch, Nova Express, and The Western Lands the Burroughsian subject transmigrates from Marxian/Hegelian alienation to N. Katherine Hayles's posthuman, gaining agency by extending into its technologized environment.
- ch. 14 "“I am not an I” Performative (Self)Identity in the Poetry of Bob Kaufman" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, The Buddha — Existence Precedes Essence; Embodiment (the lived body); Ahimsa (nonviolence) — Pynn reads Bob Kaufman's poems ('Forget To Not,' 'Would You Wear My Eyes?,' 'Benediction,' 'Jail Poems') as enacting a performative, intersubjective selfhood: against Beauvoir's 'flavor of death' in American conformity and Sartre's dictum that existence precedes essence, Kaufman replaces the drive to invincibility with 'nakedness' and vulnerability. Merleau-Ponty's embodied intercorporeity and Buddhist ontology—impermanence, non-self, compassion, and ahimsa—let the poet's 'I am not an I' burn the isolated ego into a communal 'thousand me's,' with slavery's trauma inscribed on the body and Kaufman's 1963 Buddhist vow of silence as liberating practice.
- ch. 15 "Tongues Untied Beat Ethnicities, Beat Multiculture" **·** Kwame Anthony Appiah — Cosmopolitanism; Double Consciousness — Lee surveys the neglected ethnic and multicultural seams running through Beat authorship—Ginsberg's Jewish 'Howl' and 'Kaddish,' Kerouac's French-Canadian 'Ti Jean' and the cross-ethnic geography of 'On the Road,' Ferlinghetti's and di Prima's Italian America, and Chicano, Asian American, and Black Beat outriders (Acosta, Frank Chin, Baraka, Ted Joans, Kaufman). He frames these through multicultural theory—Said, Spivak, Bhabha, and especially Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitan account of ethnicity as interstitial—arguing Beat writing foreshadows the field of multicultural studies, a 'tongue untied' whose transnational, race-inflected voices reach back to 'Howl' and 'On the Road.'
- ch. 16 "Joanne Kyger “Descartes and the Splendor Of” Bridging Dualisms through Collaboration and Experimentation" **·** René Descartes, Judith Butler, Zhuangzi — Mind–Body Dualism; Gender Performativity; The Cogito — Falk analyzes Joanne Kyger's 1968 experimental video 'Descartes' and its script 'Descartes and the Splendor Of,' a condensed rewrite of the 'Discourse on Method' that subverts Descartes's mind-body dualism and privileging of reason. Kyger deflates the cogito with slang ('to doubt is a drag'), substitutes Buddhist, Taoist (Zhuangzi's butterfly dream), and Confucian terms, and—voicing and performing Descartes as a woman doing housework and as 'Mother God'—feminizes the most masculine of professions. Reading this through Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' and gender performativity, Falk shows the parody destabilizes the mind/body, male/female hierarchy Cartesian dualism underwrites.
- ch. 17 "III. Beat Avant-Garde Spontaneity and Immediacy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — Existentialism; The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence — Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.
- ch. 19 "Wholly Communion Poetry, Philosophy, and Spontaneous Bop Cinema" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Rhizome; Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Sterritt reads Peter Whitehead's 1965 film 'Wholly Communion,' shot at London's International Poetry Incarnation, as 'spontaneous bop cinema' embodying Beat poetics through Bakhtin's dialogic/carnivalesque and the schizoanalysis of Deleuze and Guattari. Ginsberg's drunken recitation of 'The Change' becomes a 'body without organs' entering the 'chaosmos' on the plane of immanence; Jandl's sound poetry is pure Deleuzian sensation. Adrian Mitchell's anti-Vietnam 'To Whom It May Concern' is read through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati and Deleuze's 'difference in repetition,' its incantatory counter-words a materialist line of flight against the order-words of war.
- ch. 20 "High Off the Page Representing the Drug Experience in the Work of Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Gilles Deleuze — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Erik Mortenson argues that Kerouac's and Ginsberg's drug writing works 'through the body' to transmit the altered temporality of intoxication to the reader, using Merleau-Ponty's account of original speech and the lived body as gesture, and Deleuze and Guattari's 'Body Without Organs' and speeds. Marijuana expands the present into Kerouac's long exfoliating sentences and empathetic 'digging' (Visions of Cody, On the Road), while Benzedrine contracts it into the accelerated confessional rush of The Subterraneans; Ginsberg's LSD poems ('Lysergic Acid,' 'Wales Visitation') hit the limit of representing timelessness. The chapter concludes the writing lets the nonuser get 'high off the page' without the dependency Deleuze and Guattari warn of.
- ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" **·** The Buddha, Dogen — Zen Buddhism; Non-Self (anatman); Emptiness (sunyata) — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- ch. 22 "Spontaneity, Immediacy, and Difference Philosophy, Being in Time, and Creativity in the Aesthetics of Jack Ker" **·** Shankara, René Descartes — Atman and Brahman; Duration (durée) — David Need contrasts three theories of 'being in time' behind the aesthetics of spontaneity: Kerouac's debt to Spengler's organic cycles of civilization (a stereoscopic, dualist view where an arbitrary measure like a candle or page limns deep being), Olson's use of Whitehead's 'concrescence' in 'Projective Verse' (a monist, all-at-once projection of new monads), and Cage's use of Coomaraswamy's Vedanta, where silence is sabdabrahman and chance imitates Nature. He argues the real fault line is the old monist-vs-dualist divide (Advaita brahman vs. Cartesian dualism), and that each artist's notion of creative freedom follows from which metaphysical schema he borrowed, so our quarrels with the Beats reflect our own metaphysical stakes.
- ch. 23 "IV. Beat Politics Ethics and Affinities" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Two Ways of Enduring the Flames The Existential Dialectics of Love in Kierkegaard and Bukowski" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Jacques Lacan — Philosophy of Love; The Leap of Faith; Despair (sickness unto death) — Andreas Seland argues that Kierkegaard and Bukowski offer opposed responses to a Romantic 'paradox of love': the beloved is a dialectical object, part inner imago (Shelley's veiled maid in 'Alastor,' Stendhal's crystallization, Lacan/Zizek) and part uncontrollable external person, and this gap breeds despair. Kierkegaard's Knight of Faith in Fear and Trembling resolves it by infinite resignation and the absurd leap, internalizing the gap and severing the tie to the real to love the princess only interiorly. Bukowski's Chinaski in Women does the opposite, deliberately choosing unstable 'Lydia-object' women who embody the gap, seeking the insecurity itself as a line of flight beyond bourgeois love and even beyond himself.
- ch. 25 "Anarchism and the Beats" **·** Karl Marx, Henry David Thoreau, Carl Jung — Anarchism; Civil Disobedience; Class Struggle — Ed D'Angelo argues the Beats had a philosophy after all: a romantic bohemian anarchism that made poetry a means to a religious transformation of consciousness, with political change following consciousness rather than the reverse. He shows Ginsberg inverting Plato's rationalist hierarchy (grounding reason in imagination and the body) and reads Beat 'criminality' as a shamanic journey to the unconscious underworld, distinct from Mailer's macho 'White Negro' hipster. He traces their lineage through Greenwich Village bohemia, Proudhon/Bakunin/Kropotkin anarchism, and pacifist anarchists like Rexroth and Dellinger, arguing the Beats rejected Marxist materialism and class warfare, and that the movement was 'born' out of Rexroth's anarchist poetry circle at the 1955 Six Gallery reading of 'Howl.'
- ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" **·** Arne Naess, Baruch Spinoza, Dogen, Aldo Leopold — Deep Ecology; Emptiness (sunyata); Anthropocentrism — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- ch. 27 "William Burroughs as Philosopher From Beat Morality to Third Worldism to Continental Theory" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Jacques Derrida, Herbert Marcuse, Frantz Fanon — Bad Faith; One-Dimensional Man; Deconstruction; Existence Precedes Essence — Jones Irwin makes the case for 'Burroughs as philosopher,' tracing an 'impassioned moralism' and antihumanism (human as adjective, not noun) that separates him from other Beats and postmodernists. He links Burroughs's critique of alienation to Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and to Sartrean existentialism and bad faith ('there are no victims, just accomplices'), and reads the Beats' 'third force' Third Worldism via Freire, Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, and Paz. Close readings of Naked Lunch's 'Bradley the Buyer' and the sex-and-death delirium of 'AJ's Annual Party' connect Burroughs to Artaud's body without organs, Bataille's Sadean tradition, and Derrida's deconstruction of embodiment and 'distance touching.'
- ch. 28 "List of Contributors" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers

- ch. 1 "Preface" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Part - 1 The Coen Brand of Comedy and Tragedy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Raising Arizona as an American Comedy" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Plato, Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — Self-Reliance; Allegory of the Cave; Authenticity — Gilmore reads Raising Arizona as a classical comedy (bad-beginning-to-good-ending) about the American 'optative mood' of self-creation, using Hi McDunnough's outlaw-to-family arc and his name-as-height-metaphor to figure Emerson's aspirational American self. He deploys Plato's two kinds of cave-laughter to distinguish the film's 'tender,' welcoming comedy (Hi and Ed, Gale and Evelle) from mocking ridicule, and frames Hi's need to abandon outlaw identity via Heidegger's Augenblick and Badiou's 'event' sparked in Ed's mug-shot flash. Nietzsche on dreams-as-origin-of-metaphysics grounds the film's dream/reality tension, and Hi's over-identification with the outlaw universal is glossed as Sartrean bad faith.
- ch. 9 "The Human Comedy Perpetuates Itself Nihilism and Comedy in Coen Neo-Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Hannah Arendt — The Death of God; The Last Man; Will to Power — Hibbs argues that neo-noir turns classic noir's grim fatalism comic by making nihilism a working assumption, and that Nietzsche supplies the diagnosis: the 'death of God,' the passive 'last man,' and the aristocratic 'pathos of distance' of will-to-power super-antiheroes (Hannibal Lecter, the villains of Cape Fear/Basic Instinct). He reads The Big Lebowski as the Coens' comic leveling of nihilism, with Walter insisting the Germans are 'nihilists' and 'cowards' and the Dude 'abiding,' showing that full nihilism cannot be lived. In Fargo and Raising Arizona, Marge's 'banality of virtue' (a comic counterpoint to Arendt's banality of evil) and the resilience of familial/procreative instinct reassert a comic order over the noir trap.
- ch. 10 "Philosophies of Comedy in O Brother, Where Art Thou" **·** Henri Bergson, Søren Kierkegaard — Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); The Stages on Life's Way — McFarland explains the comedy of O Brother through Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' (the chain-gang pratfall where McGill forgets he is shackled, the toon-like plasticity of the escapees) and Kierkegaard's account of the comic as unresolved contradiction, like men bustling on a sinking ship. He argues the Klan-rally set piece refuses Jamesonian 'pastiche' by grounding its Wizard-of-Oz and Odyssey allusions in real historical guilt, forcing the postmodern aesthete-viewer, as in Kierkegaard's Either/Or, from the aesthetic to the ethical stage. The subverted ending—Penny rejecting the non-bona-fide ring—enacts Kierkegaard's view that marriage is comic because it 'binds' time and acknowledges contradiction rather than resolving it.
- ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Heraclitus, Albert Camus, Henry David Thoreau — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Everything Flows / Logos; The Absurd; Fate and Foreknowledge — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- ch. 12 "Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — The End of Grand Narratives; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.
- ch. 13 "Part - 2 Ethics Shame, Justice, and Virtue" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- ch. 15 "Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty" **·** John Rawls, Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Niccolò Machiavelli — Justice as Fairness; The Veil of Ignorance; The Social Contract — Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.
- ch. 16 "Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing" **·** David Hume, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Social Contract; Justice in the Republic — Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.
- ch. 17 "“Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Epicurus, John Locke, Aristotle — The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality; The Categorical Imperative; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.
- ch. 18 "No Country for Old Men as Moral Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard, Bernard Williams — The Categorical Imperative; Teleological Suspension of the Ethical — McFarland reads the film as moral philosophy: Sheriff Bell faces a post-Kantian predicament, able to reconstruct how crimes happen but unable to 'measure' why, and dooms himself by tying duty to an outcome (his promise to make Llewelyn safe) rather than to Kant's unconditional imperative, so failure yields Bernard Williams-style shame. Llewelyn is cast against Kierkegaard's Abraham/Brutus distinction as a tragic hero who cannot suspend the ethical, while Chigurh functions as an ironic anti-philosopher who alternately grounds killing in self-interest ('what good is a rule if it got you here?') and in a perverse Kantian promise-keeping, until Carla Jean restores moral responsibility by refusing his coin toss.
- ch. 19 "Part - 3 Postmodernity, Interpretation, and the Construction of History" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink" **·** Martin Heidegger, René Descartes, Aristotle — Dasein (being-there); Mind–Body Dualism; Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.
- ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" **·** Michel Foucault — The End of Grand Narratives; Power/Knowledge; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- ch. 22 "“A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, René Descartes, Jean-Paul Sartre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Everything Flows / Logos — Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.
- ch. 23 "Part - 4 Existentialism, Alienation, and Despair" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "“What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus — Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.
- ch. 25 "Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus — Despair (sickness unto death); Existentialism; The Absurd — Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.
- ch. 26 "Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence — Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.

## The Philosophy of the Western

- ch. 1 "Front 1" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Introduction Philosophy and the Western" **·** Aristotle, Plato — McMahon and Csaki's introduction argues that the western and philosophy are joined through the mimetic theory of art (the western as a mirror of frontier history) and through shared interest in identity, community, and morality. It frames the volume's four parts and previews each essay, noting that canonical western tropes trace back to Plato and Aristotle and that films like High Noon, Shane, and The Searchers dramatize abstract philosophical theories. It treats the western as an unexplored 'frontier' for philosophic analysis rather than defending one thesis of its own.
- ch. 6 "Part 1 The Cowboy Way The Essence of the Western Hero" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "“Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns" **·** René Descartes, Aristotle — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Existentialism; Stoicism; Man as Political Animal — Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.
- ch. 8 "Civilization and Its Discontents The Self-Sufficient Western Hero" **·** Aristotle, Baruch Spinoza, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Self-Reliance; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Den Uyl builds a composite philosophic picture of self-sufficiency from Aristotle's autarkeia (reason-guided virtuous activity, requiring external goods and civilization) and Spinoza's freedom as acting from one's own nature guided by adequate ideas, then tests it on John Ford's heroes. In The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, Tom Doniphon is 'procedurally' self-sufficient in the precivilized West while Ransom Stoddard embodies civilized reason, and neither can inhabit the other's world. He argues the western's deepest value is Emersonian self-reliance—fidelity to one's own unique nature (the 'cactus rose')—which civilization threatens even as it enables Aristotelian flourishing.
- ch. 9 "Mommas, Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Pragmatists" **·** William James, John Dewey, Charles Sanders Peirce — Pragmatism; Truth as What Works — Csaki argues that John Wayne became the ultimate cinematic cowboy because his characters embody classical American pragmatism. Using William James's squirrel-and-tree parable and Dewey's account of 'inquiry' transforming an indeterminate situation, he reads Rooster Cogburn's split-second raft decision and Wil Anderson's hiring of schoolboys in The Cowboys as pragmatic problem-solving from experience. He treats the 'code of the West' not as fixed absolutes but as rules applied pragmatically (Rooster shooting men in the back, the cowboys letting Long Hair be dragged to death), where truth is what can be assimilated, verified, and made to 'work.'
- ch. 10 "Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes — Labor Theory of Property; The State of Nature; Natural Rights; The Social Contract — Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.
- ch. 11 "Landscapes of Gendered Violence Male Love and Anxiety on the Railroad" **·** The Male Gaze; Objectification; Ecofeminism — Collins analyzes the railroad in Tycoon and both versions of 3:10 to Yuma, drawing on feminist critics (Irigaray, Bordo, Grosz, Haraway, Merchant) who expose a masculinist 'panoramic' epistemology coding mind as male and passive nature/landscape as female. She argues trains destabilize rather than confirm this mastery: in Tycoon, Johnny Munroe conflates conquering the feminized Andean landscape with dominating his wife Maura, yet the bridge and train fail; in the 2007 Yuma, the railroad's promise of masculine legitimacy is sustained only by 'cruel optimism' and male homosocial love between Dan Evans and Ben Wade, over anxieties about racial Others (Apache, Chinese laborers).
- ch. 12 "Part 2 The Code of the West The Cowboy and Society" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The State of Nature; Labor Theory of Property; The Social Contract; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- ch. 14 "Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Existentialism; Zen Buddhism — Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.
- ch. 15 "From Dollars to Iron The Currency of Clint Eastwood's Westerns" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Søren Kierkegaard — Master and Slave Morality; Perspectivism; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Stages on Life's Way — McNaron traces Clint Eastwood's evolving western hero from the amoral 'Man with No Name' to The Outlaw Josey Wales, using Will Wright's plot typology plus Nietzsche, Aristotle, and Kierkegaard. He reads the Eastwood antihero's 'manly nihilism' and prizing of strength and style through Nietzsche's master/slave morality and perspectivism, his virtues (self-control, phronesis) through Aristotle, and his elevation of the aesthetic over the ethical/religious against Kierkegaard's stages. The film's central claim—that only words with 'iron' behind them (Josey and Ten Bears's pact) can found genuine community, unlike government's 'double tongues'—grounds a transcendental argument about the conditions for authentic community and justified vengeance.
- ch. 16 "The Duty of Reason Kantian Ethics in High Noon" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — The Categorical Imperative; Autonomy of the Will; Humanity as an End in Itself; Deontology — Evans argues that Marshal Will Kane in High Noon is Kant's ideal moral agent, acting from duty and a good will rather than from consequences. He shows the townsfolk, Kane's friends, Harvey Pell, Helen Ramirez, and Amy all reasoning consequentially or heteronomously (the mayor privileging the town's finances, Mildred lying about Sam per Kant's essay on the supposed right to lie), while Frank Miller's revenge is a maxim that cannot be universalized. Kane's maxim of standing against lawlessness regardless of cost satisfies all three formulations of the categorical imperative—universal law, humanity as an end, and autonomy—making him a member of the kingdom of ends and contrasting Kant with Mill's utilitarianism.
- ch. 17 "Part 3 Outlaws Challenging Conventions of the Western" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 18 "The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident" **·** Martha Nussbaum, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — The Categorical Imperative; Virtue Ethics (arete); Deontology — Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.
- ch. 19 "“Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche — Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; The Death of God — Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.
- ch. 20 "No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern)" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Thomas Nagel — Virtue Ethics; Deontology; Moral Luck — William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'
- ch. 21 "The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller" **·** Martha Nussbaum, Aristotle — Binary Oppositions; Deontology — Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.
- ch. 22 "Part 4 On the Fringe The Encounter with the Other" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The State of Nature — Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.
- ch. 24 "Regeneration through Stories and Song The View from the Other Side of the West in Smoke Signals" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, John Dewey, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau — Pragmatism; Transcendentalism — Richard Gilmore reads Smoke Signals—the first feature written, directed, and coproduced by Native Americans—against Slotkin's myth of regeneration through violence, arguing it offers regeneration through stories and song instead. Drawing on Wilshire's claim that pragmatism is 'aboriginal,' he links Emerson and Thoreau's transcendentalism and Peirce's 'law of mind' to Deloria's American Indian metaphysics and Hyde's gift economy: Arlene's fry-bread story and Thomas's storytelling repair broken relationships, and Victor's final act of forgiving his father (and withholding that Arnold caused the fatal fire) is read as the film's central gift, completing relationships that violence had severed.
- ch. 25 "Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Simone de Beauvoir — The Dialectic; Woman as the Other; The Male Gaze — Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.
- ch. 26 "Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche, G.W.F. Hegel, Michel Foucault — Master–Slave Dialectic; Will to Power; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Jennifer L. McMahon gives an existential account of Americans' ambivalence toward horses in westerns: because horses mirror human anxiety, herd-boundness, and the flight instinct that Sartre and Heidegger locate at the core of being, we transfer our self-loathing onto them and, driven by Nietzsche's will to power and Hegel's lord-and-bondsman struggle for recognition, we break them to prove our own mastery. Reading breaking scenes in All the Pretty Horses and The Horse Whisperer via Foucault's Discipline and Punish (the round pen as panopticon producing 'docile bodies'), she contrasts films like Hidalgo and The Electric Horseman that model Hegelian reciprocity, urging us to 'let go, turn in, and hook on' rather than dominate.
