## The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Foreword" *(no index entry yet)* — Tom Morris recounts how the 2004 volume Harry Potter and Philosophy: If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts showed that academics were finding real wisdom in Rowling's series, and how he went from skeptic to reading all seven books six times and writing his own book on their insights into courage, love, and death. He presents this new collection, written after the series ended, as a 'Philosophical De-coder Ring' that reveals the deepest story behind the novels.
- ch. 8 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Introduction" **·** Plato — Philosophy of Love; Immortality and the Soul; Personal Identity — The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.
- ch. 10 "PART ONE - THE HORCRUX OF THE MATTER DESTINY, IDENTITY, AND THE SOUL" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Philosophical Conceptions of the Soul" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Unknown" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Immortality and the Soul — This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.
- ch. 16 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Ghosts and “Going On”" **·** Immortality and the Soul — The section argues that everyday talk of soul mates, soulful art, and baring one's soul is metaphorical talk about our deepest emotions, love, and conscience, not commitment to an immaterial substance, and that even materialists can keep the vocabulary rather than translate Hoagy Carmichael into talk of C-fibers firing. It then forecasts the chapter's conclusion about Rowling: her Potter-world soul mixes this sentimental view with metaphysics borrowed from the Cartesian and sentience views.
- ch. 18 "The Dementor’s Kiss" **·** Immortality and the Soul — The section argues that materialism is false in the Potter universe by cataloguing the ways souls outlive bodies: Hermione's claim that a sword through Ron would leave his soul untouched, the voices beyond the Ministry's veil, Nearly Headless Nick's ghostly imprint of a wizard who refused to 'go on,' Voldemort's wraith-like survival, and the 'neither ghost nor truly flesh' shades summoned from Voldemort's wand and by the Resurrection Stone. It sets up dementors and Horcruxes as the next tests of what souls are.
- ch. 19 "Horcruxes" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity; Immortality and the Soul — Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.
- ch. 20 "A Plausible View" **·** René Descartes — Immortality and the Soul; Mind–Body Dualism — Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.
- ch. 21 "NOTES" **·** Mind–Body Dualism; Immortality and the Soul — The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'
- ch. 22 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 23 "Mind-Body Distinctions" **·** Personal Identity — Opening Eric Saidel's chapter, the section takes Sirius's tail-chasing as Padfoot in Order of the Phoenix as its puzzle: is Sirius a man sometimes in a dog's body, a dog sometimes in a man's body, or a third 'someone' who persists through the change? It widens the question to Pettigrew, Rita Skeeter, McGonagall, werewolf Lupin, boggarts, and Polyjuice transformations, framing it as a question about identity and the mind-body relation.
- ch. 24 "Whose Reasons" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity — The section applies the Cartesian division of persons into mind plus body, generating four possible descriptions of Padfoot such as Sirius's mind in a dog's body, and shows each fails: McGonagall's 'non-being' quip cannot house Sirius's vanished body, and neither pairing explains why Padfoot both chases his tail and stands on his hind legs to see Harry off at King's Cross. So the mind-body distinction cannot say what the transformed Sirius is.
- ch. 25 "A Step in the Right Direction" **·** Personal Identity — Recasting the puzzle as a question of whose reasons cause Padfoot's actions, the section shows that strategy fails too: Harry as Runcorn and Ron as Cattermole act on Harry's and Ron's own reasons, never on those of the men whose bodies they wear, and dogs chase tails because it feels good, not for reasons at all. So reasons cannot explain either Padfoot's tail-chasing or werewolf Lupin's attacks, which come from his blood while his reasons would restrain him.
- ch. 26 "A Unified Self" **·** Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity — The section tries a division of labor in which Sirius's mind explains his human gestures while his dog's body explains the tail-chasing, tested by the thought experiment of Sirius having become a bear instead, who would have done bear things rather than chase a tail he never had. But the price is absurdity: pleasure must reside in the body, giving Padfoot's body reasons of its own that could clash with Sirius's mind, as in 'I didn't want to chase my tail, but my body wanted to,' so the mind/body split buckles.
- ch. 27 "NOTES" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body); Personal Identity — The section rejects the 'captain of a ship' picture of mind directing body, quoting Descartes himself on being so 'compounded and intermingled' with the body as to form 'a single whole,' and reads the Polyjuice episodes as proof: Harry in Runcorn's body naturally 'thunders' with a powerful voice and punches with an enormous fist, while Luna recognizes Harry through 'Barny's' face, impossible if mind and body were separable. The conclusion is that transformed people are unified man-dog wholes, and that even Muggle changes such as weight loss, learning to ride a bike, or Crouch-as-Moody show that changing our bodies changes who we are.
- ch. 28 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "Varieties of Prophecy" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge — The section sets up Jeremy Pierce's chapter by contrasting Trelawney the 'old fraud,' whose tea leaves, tarot, and crystal balls yield elastic generalities and false death forecasts, with the two predictions Dumbledore calls her only 'real predictions,' which McGonagall and the centaur Firenze also treat as different in kind. It asks what distinguishes genuine prophecy from fortune-telling in a world where magic might connect tea leaves or dreams to actual future events.
- ch. 30 "Fallible Prophecies" **·** Aristotle — Fate and Foreknowledge; Free Will vs Determinism — Crediting Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed, the section distinguishes fallible from infallible prophecies and builds a seven-fold menu of how a Seer could access the future, from fallible sense-based guessing like Muggle weather reports and Trelawney's usual act, through probabilities over possible futures, to infallible access to a deterministic outcome or to the actual fixed future. The question becomes which of these Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.
- ch. 31 "Self-Fulfilling Prophecies" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge — The section argues that Dumbledore treats even the real prophecy as fallible, telling Harry he is 'quite free to turn your back on the prophecy,' which suggests likelihood rather than guarantee. Yet the involuntary trance source, Trelawney's spade readings that fit the hidden Harry she cannot see, and the lightning-struck tower card point to occasional access to possible or fixed futures beyond mere category-1 guessing.
- ch. 32 "Destiny" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge — Testing whether Trelawney's first prophecy was self-fulfilling, the section deploys Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus story, where a prediction that causes its own fulfillment would be the prophet's deed rather than a revelation of what was going to happen. It concludes the prophecy did not make Voldemort attack: he chose Harry as the half-blood he saw himself in, acting on incomplete information from Snape's interrupted eavesdropping, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish real predictions from Trelawney's usual fare.
- ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Fate and Foreknowledge — The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.
- ch. 34 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" **·** Fate and Foreknowledge — The section argues the second real prophecy, about the servant rejoining the Dark Lord that night, cannot be merely 'likely but fallible': Wormtail's escape depended on a chain of improbable contingencies such as Lupin forgetting his Wolfsbane potion and the last-minute switch of Secret-Keeper. The first prophecy likewise required Voldemort to mark Harry through events, from Snape's plea to Lily's sacrifice, that flow from the prophecy itself, so genuine prophecy needs a stronger tie to the actual future than probability.
- ch. 35 "NOTES" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Fate and Foreknowledge — The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.
- ch. 36 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 37 "PART TWO - THE MOST POWERFUL MAGIC OF ALL" *(front)*
- ch. 38 "Snape and the Many-Splendored Thing" **·** Philosophy of Love — The section opens the Deavels' chapter with the puzzle of Dumbledore's 'ironclad reason' for trusting Snape even after Snape kills him, recalling McGonagall's 'he trusted... always,' and names the answer: Snape's unrequited love for Lily, which leads circuitously to his redemption. It previews the philosophical questions about the nature and varieties of love and its power to blind judgment that the chapter will bring to Snape's story.
- ch. 39 "The Abandoned Boys" **·** Plato — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Philosophy of Love — Surveying eros, philia, and agape, from the Weasleys' romantic love to Voldemort's never having wanted a friend to 'God is love,' the section draws on Plato's Symposium, where crude physical desire is progressively refined toward the beautiful and divine, to argue that love is primarily a choice of the will rather than a feeling. Hence Snape's continuing dislike of Harry is no evidence against his transformation by love; acting for others' good despite his emotions is precisely the testimony to it.
- ch. 40 "Snape the Occlumens" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Philosophy of Love — The section positions Snape as the third 'abandoned boy' beside Harry and Voldemort, a half-blood from an unhappy home for whom Hogwarts, as Harry observes, is where all three 'found home.' Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche while Harry opened his heart to friends and grew into integrity, and the section asks what makes this 'complicated amalgam of darkness and light,' Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.
- ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Philosophy of Love; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — The section reads Snape's double life through the definition of love shared by writers from Aristotle to Aquinas, willing the good of the other for the other's own sake: he protects people he dislikes because his love for Lily wills their good. As an Occlumens he empties himself of feeling to lie to Voldemort's face, concealing rather than renouncing his love for Lily, and only while dying from Nagini's bite does he freely offer Harry the memories revealing that Harry is a Horcrux.
- ch. 42 "A Work in Progress" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Philosophy of Love — Tracing Snape's love from the greedy boyhood watching of Lily and the Mudblood rupture through his plea to save Lily alone, which draws Dumbledore's 'You disgust me,' the section judges it short of Aristotle's beloved as a 'second self,' since he wanted Lily's good only as it related to him. Diotima's teaching in the Symposium that 'love is wanting to possess the good forever' and Benedict XVI's love as 'an ongoing exodus out of the closed inward-looking self' frame how Snape's unrequited love gradually 'gives birth in beauty' to virtue in him.
- ch. 43 "NOTES" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Philosophy of Love; Forgiveness — The section argues that vice and virtue are habits built up over time: Snape still rages at Harry-as-James and sneers at Tonks's wolf Patronus as 'weak,' yet his own doe Patronus, matching Lily's, is the magical emblem of his transformation by love. Contrasting friends, who strengthen the soul's integrity by sharing joys and sorrows, with Voldemort, whose Horcruxes give him eight 'selves' while making him less human, it reads remorse as what knits a damaged soul back together, sealed by Harry's forgiveness and the name 'Albus Severus.'
- ch. 44 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 45 "Violently Pink Products" *(front)*
- ch. 46 "Little Hangleton" **·** Philosophy of Love — The section collects the love-potion material of Half-Blood Prince: Fred and George's 'violently pink products' at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Amortentia's mother-of-pearl sheen and the smell of freshly mown grass that Hermione dare not finish naming, Slughorn's warning that it causes 'a powerful infatuation or obsession' rather than love, and Ron's Romilda Vane episode from spiked Chocolate Cauldrons. This sets up the chapter's question of what kind of person would actually use one, answered by Voldemort's mother.
- ch. 47 "Real Love or Mere Infatuation" **·** Philosophy of Love — Retelling Dumbledore's reconstruction for Harry, the section sets Merope Gaunt's love potion beside the Imperius Curse, one of the three unforgivable curses that robs victims of their will, as the two ways she might have won Tom Riddle Sr., noting that Harry immediately pairs them as will-robbing magic. Dumbledore's guess that Merope 'could not bear to continue enslaving him' and stopped dosing him, only to be abandoned and left to die, raises the chapter's question of what this loveless origin has to do with the prophecy.
- ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" **·** Harry Frankfurt — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Philosophy of Love — The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.
- ch. 49 "NOTES" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophy of Love — Against the obvious reading of Voldemort's loveless begetting, the section argues he is 'not his mother's son': he imitates Marvolo and Salazar Slytherin, while Merope, on Aristotle's principle that we are what we consistently do, redeemed herself by stopping the potion, renouncing magic entirely, and choosing love over hate at the cost of her life. Character is destiny only if forged by genuinely free choices rather than blood or fate, so Merope shows not even the most tragic beginnings are destined for darkness, while Voldemort, who never loved and never wanted a friend, chose otherwise, leaving Harry as the true mother's son, shielded by 'a more ancient and powerful magic than any potion.'
- ch. 50 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 51 "The Feminist Debate So Far" *(front)*
- ch. 52 "Radical vs. Liberal Feminism" **·** Feminism — The section maps the feminist critical divide over the series: Schoefer, Heilman, and Gallardo-C. and Smith charge the books with replicating demeaning gender stereotypes, noting no girl is heroic like Harry and no woman wise like Dumbledore, while Kern, Gladstein, and Zettel answer with context, pairing Lavender and Parvati's silliness with Dean and Seamus, Trelawney with fake Lockhart, and Madam Pince with Filch, and pointing to Umbridge and Bellatrix as female villains who command as much fear as any Death Eater. The pervasive giggling girls debate serves as the section's lightning rod.
- ch. 53 "More Wonderful and More Terrible than Death" **·** Mary Wollstonecraft, John Stuart Mill — Feminism — The section distinguishes liberal feminism, historically grounded in Mary Wollstonecraft, Harriet Taylor Mill, and John Stuart Mill's Enlightenment view that women are rational individuals entitled to equal rights, criticized here for measuring success on masculine terms so that McGonagall and Hermione's achievements count while Molly Weasley's motherhood gets short shrift. It then explains second-wave radical feminism and its 'sex/gender system' analysis of rigid masculine/feminine trait pairings, and reads Gallardo-C. and Smith's 'Cinderfella' interpretation of the series, in which evil displays 'phallic power' even in Umbridge's hypermasculine control while Harry's kindness and selflessness embody feminine values, an association the section traces from St. Gertrude through Gandhi's 'life without love is death' to C.S. Lewis's analysis of the kinds of love.
- ch. 54 "The Triumph of Love" **·** Feminism; Philosophy of Love; Forgiveness — Reading the series' set pieces as the triumph of traditionally feminine values over masculine aggression, the section moves from Lily's sacrificial love burning Quirrell, through Harry sparing Pettigrew for Lupin's and Sirius's sake, to love expelling Voldemort during the Ministry possession, where 'it was your heart that saved you' and Dumbledore names a force 'more wonderful and more terrible than death.' Harry's kindness to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby pays off in the Horcrux hunt, his plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse' redefines true manhood as incorporating the feminine, and the Forest sacrifice wins the war with a defensive Expelliarmus rather than a duel, showing love more important than aggression.
- ch. 55 "NOTES" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 56 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 57 "PART THREE - POTTERWATCH FREEDOM AND POLITICS" *(front)*
- ch. 58 "The Dangers of Patriotism" **·** Communitarianism; Cosmopolitanism — Andrew Mills opens the essay 'Patriotism, House Loyalty, and the Obligations of Belonging' by treating Hogwarts House membership as a model of patriotism: Hermione should back the Gryffindor Quidditch team and help Ron and Harry earn House points, and would be a traitor if she helped Crabbe and Goyle or sabotaged Harry's Nimbus 2000 so Hufflepuff won. He asks whether this loyalty is a virtue, as our admiration for patriotic leaders and soldiers suggests, or a vice that would make patriots resemble Voldemort and the Death Eaters.
- ch. 59 "Death Eaters and Discrimination" **·** Cosmopolitanism — The chapter takes up the case that patriotism is a vice, quoting Tolstoy's definition of patriotism as 'the desire for the exclusive good of one's own nation' and Emma Goldman's charge that patriotism rests on conceit, arrogance, and egotism about the accident of birthplace. Mills argues this gives patriots a Voldemort-like sense of superiority, forcing other nations to serve one's interests 'at the tip of a wand or at the barrel of a gun,' since preferring compatriots for something unchosen mirrors preferring people by blood status.
- ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" **·** Jeremy Bentham, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism — Against Death Eater blood-purity, the chapter sets the ethical tradition of equal moral worth: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' (the Minister of Magic's pain matters no more than a house-elf's or a Blast-Ended Skrewt's) and Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means. It applies this to Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and to Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against house-elf 'slave labor,' then asks how patriotic preference for compatriots differs in kind from racism and sexism.
- ch. 61 "Patriotism and Global Conflict" **·** Cosmopolitanism — The chapter argues that patriotism divides us when unity is needed: the Sorting Hat's fifth-year song fears Hogwarts will 'crumble from within' before external foes, and Ron's Triwizard jealousy of Hermione's friendship with Durmstrang champion Viktor Krum ('It's about winning!') shows national rivalry poisoning international goodwill. Dumbledore's lesson that 'we are only as strong as we are united' is extended to global crises like global warming and oil wars, with Dumbledore's Army as proof that House divisions dissolve when a common threat affects everyone equally.
- ch. 62 "Patriotism Restored" **·** Cosmopolitanism — The chapter adds a resource-consumption objection: if loving your country means securing the middle-class 'good life' for your countrymen, that requires cheap labor abroad and more than a fair share of scarce resources, just as Hogwarts students' comfort rests on enslaved house-elves. Mills concludes that defending patriotism requires recasting it so that it never conflicts with the equal moral standing of all people.
- ch. 63 "The Importance of Community" **·** Martha Nussbaum — Cosmopolitanism; Communitarianism — The chapter rehabilitates patriotism through Martha Nussbaum's cosmopolitanism: just as small Houses, House Cup competition, and family-like loyalty are the most effective means of giving every Hogwarts student the education she equally deserves, special care for compatriots can be justified 'in universalist terms,' as with parents who give their own children more love without thinking them morally more important. Patriotism is a virtue when it serves the interests of all countries' citizens and a vice when it fosters injustice and inequality, with Ron's Triwizard struggles showing how hard the line is to draw.
- ch. 64 "Human Flourishing and the Preservation of Dying Cultures" **·** Aristotle — Communitarianism; Man as Political Animal; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — The chapter defines communitarianism, the view that flourishing requires membership in a tradition-bound community, and reads the Death Eaters' blood-purity mantra as its violent extreme, noting Voldemort kills the Muggle Studies teacher for advocating cultural mixing and 'the dwindling of the purebloods.' Aristotle's claim that humans are 'political animals' grounds the idea that identity is community-constructed, illustrated by Harry's 'Boy Who Lived' identity and his misery 'under the stairs' cut off from the wizarding world; the chapter ends by weighing cultural preservation against individual liberty, as in debates over the oppression of women in traditional cultures.
- ch. 65 "NOTES" **·** Cosmopolitanism; Communitarianism; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — The chapter stages Jeremy Waldron's challenge, whether people need rootedness in an ancestral culture the way they need food, clothing, and shelter, through the question of whether centaurs like Firenze should stay in the Forbidden Forest or assimilate into the wizarding world. It answers with a cosmopolitan reading of Harry's victory: his fluency in both Muggle and wizard worlds and his fellowship with Ron, Muggle-born Hermione, half-giant Hagrid, werewolf Lupin, part-veela Fleur, and centaur Firenze show that flourishing in the modern world requires moving among cultures rather than preserving purity.
- ch. 66 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 67 "Is Dumbledore a Libertarian" **·** The Minimal State — Admiraal and Reitsma open 'Dumbledore's Politics' by defining political libertarianism, a minimal state whose only legitimate task is protecting citizens from force, fraud, and theft, and report the claims of Travis Prinzi and law professor Benjamin Barton that Dumbledore is a small-government libertarian and the series 'an impregnable invective against government.' They object that the books contain no free-market or antiwelfare themes, Dumbledore never advocates any general political philosophy despite holding posts as Headmaster, Supreme Mugwump, and Chief Warlock, and he never utters stock libertarian slogans about self-ownership or the government that governs least.
- ch. 68 "Barton’s Libertarian Interpretation of the Potter Series" **·** John Locke — The Minimal State — The chapter rebuts Prinzi's three arguments one by one: Dumbledore's distrust of power (cauldron-thickness regulations, Buckbeak's condemnation, Harry's underage-magic trial) does not make him libertarian, since Lord Acton's 'power corrupts' is accepted across political theories including America's checks and balances; his gradual, consent-respecting approach to freeing house-elves and his defense of despised minorities (the last giants, Hagrid, Lupin, Firenze) value liberty but not the distinctively robust libertarian right, which, as Locke's point about the civil magistrate and the 'care of souls' shows, also forbids paternalism and punishing victimless vices. Finally, Dumbledore's hands-off headmastership, letting Snape humiliate Neville and staying distant from Harry's battles, is not libertarian policy at all: even a libertarian official must protect people under his authority from abuse, schools are not states, and the state has no business inculcating the self-reliance Dumbledore wants his students to develop.
- ch. 69 "NOTES" **·** The Minimal State — The chapter answers Barton's indictment of the Ministry, a prison designed to 'suck all life and hope' from inmates, trials without defense counsel, truth serum, constant surveillance, no elections, and a controlled press, by insisting that exasperation with bad governance is not an argument for the nightwatchman state: the Ministry also employs honest officials like Arthur Weasley, and corrupt Supreme Court justices should be replaced, not the court downsized. It adds that Rowling, who wrote the books on welfare and donated to Labour, is an unlikely libertarian, so the series at most demands better government rather than minimal government.
- ch. 70 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 71 "Plato and Dumbledore Separated at Birth" **·** Plato — The Philosopher King — Opening 'Dumbledore, Plato, and the Lust for Power,' the chapter pairs Dumbledore's 'those who are best suited to power are those who have never sought it' with Plato's 'a city in which those who are going to rule are least eager to rule is necessarily best.' Against Lord Acton's resigned 'power corrupts,' it presents Plato's remedy, reserving power for the reluctant rather than the power-hungry, as the lesson of the entire series' climax.
- ch. 72 "Fudge and Umbridge The Lessons of Obviously Unfit Power-Brokers" **·** Plato — The Philosopher King; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — The chapter draws tight parallels between Plato's political life and Dumbledore's: both watched gifted, power-hungry pupils betray their cities (Alcibiades and Tom Riddle), both recoiled from tyrannical regimes (the Thirty under Critias; the duel with Grindelwald that killed his sister), and both turned from politics to education, founding the Academy and leading Hogwarts. It explains the Republic's philosopher-rulers, their four cardinal virtues, and the decades of training meant to 'distinguish the Potters from the Malfoys,' then introduces Glaucon's Ring of Gyges as Plato's test of who can resist invisible power, the legend Rowling mirrors in the Deathly Hallows and Harry's invisibility cloak, with Voldemort's unicorn-blood survival showing how the tyrant's life burns short.
- ch. 73 "Voldemort and Dumbledore Two Tempted by Power" **·** Plato — The Philosopher King; Virtue Ethics — The chapter grades would-be Ministers of Magic on Plato's ruler criteria: Dolores Umbridge fails utterly, her 'I must not tell lies' blood-quill detentions and multiplying Educational Decrees exposing a lust for power that grows with her authority and a total lack of courage, wisdom, justice, and self-control. Cornelius Fudge's insecurity breeds dictatorial damage control, trashing Harry in the press and rigging his hearing over the dementor attack on Dudley, so that craving power, he loses it; both are Platonic object lessons in how not to rule.
- ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" **·** Plato, Immanuel Kant, Socrates — The Philosopher King; Humanity as an End in Itself; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — The chapter reads Tom Riddle as Plato's unfit ruler: from the orphanage ('I can make them hurt if I want to') he violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means, treating even his 'friends' as followers, killing Lily despite Snape's devotion, and splitting his soul for Horcruxes. Dumbledore, offered the Ministry repeatedly yet refusing because 'power was my weakness and my temptation,' has the Socratic self-knowledge that he cannot be trusted with power, and that self-awareness, not flawless virtue, is what keeps him from Grindelwald's and Voldemort's path and makes him the series' nearest philosopher-ruler.
- ch. 75 "NOTES" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); The Philosopher King — The chapter argues Harry passes the Ring of Gyges test that Voldemort fails: despite years of invisible freedom under the Cloak he never exploits it, refuses Scrimgeour's offer of his dream job to serve the whole wizarding community, hunts Horcruxes instead of making them, and at eleven alone retrieves the Sorcerer's Stone from the Mirror of Erised precisely because he does not want to use it. This indifference to the lure of power is exactly the Platonic qualification Dumbledore and Plato both demand of those fit to rule.
- ch. 76 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 77 "PART FOUR - THE ROOM OF REQUIREMENT A POTTER POTPOURRI" *(front)*
- ch. 78 "Truth in Fiction" *(no index entry yet)* — Tamar Szabo Gendler opens with Rowling's Carnegie Hall announcement that Dumbledore is gay and the third kind of fan response, challenging her authority to add facts to a finished series ('the author no longer possesses the authority to create new thoughts, feelings, and realities'). She reframes the dispute as the philosophical problem of truth in fiction, asking what determines the facts of a story world, the canonically expressed text, the readers, the author's thoughts, or the genre's conventions, and notes that nobody disputed Rowling's other interview-only revelations about Neville marrying Hannah Abbott, Lupin's impoverished life, or Petunia's almost farewell.
- ch. 79 "So, Is Dumbledore Gay" **·** David Lewis, Aristotle — Possible Worlds — The chapter argues the historian's model fails for fiction: by David Lewis's point that 'every way that a world could possibly be is a way that some world is,' there are endlessly many Harry Schmotter and Harry Plotter worlds, so the storyteller must decide rather than discover which one is the world of Harry Potter. Gendler distinguishes primary truths (the 4,100 pages, minus inconsistencies like the silver versus scarlet prefect badge and the S-bend versus U-bend) from secondary truths (Hermione has ten fingers; Cedric Diggory does not play for the Red Sox), shows the 'maximal inclusiveness principle' proves too much, and closes with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics advice that exactness must fit the subject matter, so secondary truths need only rules of thumb.
- ch. 80 "Closing Speculations Genre" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer, Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); Possible Worlds — Weighing the four criteria against 'Dumbledore is gay,' the chapter finds it no primary truth but arguably suggested by the text, Dumbledore's confession that Grindelwald's ideas 'inflamed' him and the absence of any heterosexual interest. It sets the anti-intentionalist view held by Wimsatt, Beardsley, Gadamer, Barthes, Foucault, and Derrida, that language is a social creation so texts must speak for themselves and there are as many Potter worlds as readers, against E. D. Hirsch's intentionalism and Rowling's own claim 'He is my character,' concluding that most fans rightly accept her announcement as an oral appendix alongside all her interview backstories.
- ch. 81 "NOTES" **·** Heteronormativity — The chapter tests the genre constraint: one might argue Dumbledore's sexuality cannot be true because children's-genre worlds like Goodnight Moon exclude adult sexuality, but Potter's book-length Hagrid and Madame Maxime flirtation and Snape's unrequited love for Lily defeat that, and the young-adult convention that adults' desires stay invisible to youthful protagonists instead explains the canon's silence. Gendler reads the books' metaphorical treatment of minority identity, Tonks marrying werewolf Lupin, Hermione's house-elf campaign, the Mudblood and pureblood talk, as catching readers in an act of unwitting toleration, while Dumbledore's love for his intellectual equal Grindelwald does real plot work in blinding him.
- ch. 82 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 83 "Choices" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life; Personal Identity — Opening 'Choices vs. Abilities: Dumbledore on Self-Understanding' with Socrates' 'know thyself,' Bassham frames the books as Harry's progress from appearance to reality: the boy under the stairs who thinks himself ordinary gradually learns who he is. The pivot is the end of Chamber of Secrets, where Harry, alarmed that he shares Parseltongue and Slytherin potential with Voldemort, receives Dumbledore's dictum 'It is our choices, Harry, that show us what we truly are, far more than our abilities,' which Bassham sets out to test.
- ch. 84 "How Revealing Are Our Choices" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Deontology — The chapter builds on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of choice (prohairesis) as 'deliberative desire' for things within our power and a better test of character than actions, then distinguishes three senses of choice. Internal-choice is Draco deciding but failing to kill Dumbledore; act-choice is Dumbledore's poor youthful choices; and motive-choice is captured by Kant's two shopkeepers who both refuse to cheat customers, one from fear of jail and one from honesty, so that only knowing the motive reveals the choice's moral worth.
- ch. 85 "Abilities" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Personal Identity — The chapter argues motive-choices reveal character best: Hermione's rule-breaking for Dumbledore's Army does not make her a habitual rebel since character is habit, as Aristotle says, and Snape's apparently loyal Death Eater acts concealed his fidelity to Dumbledore and Lily, so bare acts mislead; Harry's decision to enter the Chamber to save Ginny, acted on despite the dangers, is genuinely revealing. But the wizarding world complicates self-knowledge: Harry's vision as Voldemort attacked Arthur Weasley, the implanted memory framing Morfin Gaunt for the Riddle murders, and the firewhiskey scenario of Imperius Curse, Polyjuice Potion, and memory charms can make it undecidable whether it was really you who chose, since the boundaries between self and other are thinner there.
- ch. 86 "How Revealing Are Our Abilities" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Potentiality and Actuality — The chapter analyzes ability as a 'fuzzy concept': abilities are powers or capacities that come in degrees and vary with circumstance, like speaking seventy versus three hundred words of Mermish or conjuring a chipmunk Patronus only when relaxed. Choices, by contrast, are definite acts, Pettigrew's betrayal of Harry's parents and Harry's breakup with Ginny to protect her admit of no question, and this act-versus-capacity contrast explains why choices are the clearer self-revealers.
- ch. 87 "Beyond Choices Toward a Deeper Self-Understanding" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics — The chapter concedes Dumbledore's claim with qualifications: trivial, universal, unconscious, innate, or unrecognized abilities (Harry's Parseltongue before Sorcerer's Stone) reveal nothing, and the qualities Slytherin prized in Harry, resourcefulness, determination, and a certain disregard for rules, are morally neutral, since Voldemort's resourcefulness serves domination and immortality while Harry's saves his friends and fights tyranny. Yet abilities won only through hard work and self-sacrifice, and ethical capacities like empathy, prudence, and resilience do disclose character, so honest self-reflection about abilities matters too.
- ch. 88 "Unknown" **·** The Unexamined Life; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — The chapter uses Gilderoy Lockhart as the failure case of self-knowledge by introspection: convinced he is a great Defense teacher and duelist, he cannot manage a cage of Cornish pixies, is floored by Snape's Expelliarmus, and removes all the bones from Harry's arm, because his rose-colored 'cognitive blinders' mean he looks but does not see. Bassham then previews four remedies for self-knowledge, each illustrated in the books: cultivate habitual self-examination, stay alert to irrational tendencies, get help from friends, and challenge yourself.
- ch. 89 "Unknown" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — The chapter urges the Socratic examined life as a standing habit rather than a crisis response, since, as Thomas Pangle observes, most of us reflect seriously only when in trouble. Dumbledore is the model: knowing his besetting weakness was love of power, he refused the Ministry repeatedly, and after losing his 'moral compass completely' over Grindelwald he chose a celibate scholarly life, using the Pensieve's third-person view of his own memories, which makes it 'easier to spot patterns and links,' as an instrument of self-examination.
- ch. 90 "Unknown" **·** Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Speciesism — Against Aristotle's definition of humans as the 'rational animal,' the chapter catalogues wizarding irrationality, Percy's rule fetish, Malfoy's racism and classism, Ron's jealousy, Hagrid's blind affection for dangerous creatures, Fudge's closed-mindedness, and Luna's credulity, culminating in the wizards' blindness to house-elf slavery, excused because elves like Winky have been conditioned to find freedom shameful. Hermione's point that internalized oppression justifies nothing is one Harry finally absorbs, digging Dobby's grave with his own hands and writing 'Here lies Dobby, a Free Elf.'
- ch. 91 "Unknown" **·** Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Because we each view life from our own 'personal mini-cam,' we can be too close to ourselves to see truly, so friends serve as honest mirrors in which we see ourselves as we really are. Hermione shows Harry his insensitivity to Cho, the trio helps Neville overcome his painful shyness, and Hagrid teaches Ron that friendship should not be wrecked by petty jealousy, while the friendless Dursleys, Lockhart, and Slughorn never progress in self-understanding.
- ch. 92 "The Ultimate Measure of a Person" **·** Lucretius — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics — Quoting Lucretius, that in danger and peril 'the mask is torn off, the reality remains,' the chapter argues that ordinary behavior is stereotypical and only situations of challenge and adversity reveal what kind of person someone truly is. Harry and his friends pass repeated tests of courage, loyalty, intelligence, and resourcefulness and emerge humble but battle-tested heroes like Frodo's fellowship, with Ron's temporary abandonment in Deathly Hallows the instructive exception.
- ch. 93 "NOTES" *(notes)*
- ch. 94 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 95 "Positioning Our Prejudgments" *(no index entry yet)* — Garver opens 'The Magic of Personal Transformation' by contrasting the Dudley who treats Harry 'like a dog that had rolled in something smelly' with the Deathly Hallows Dudley who leaves a cup of tea outside Harry's room, defies his parents, and shakes Harry's hand so that Harry sees a 'different personality.' He treats this as an epistemological puzzle about how the two boys came to know themselves and each other better, setting up the essay's account of knowing as a process of personal transformation in which encountering ourselves and others makes us better knowers.
- ch. 96 "The Ignorance of Ickle Dudleykins" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter presents Gadamer's claim that we can only interpret the world by coming to it with 'prejudgments,' the borrowed toolbox of questions, biases, and expectations without which anything we try to understand stays 'like a container sealed shut.' Whether prejudgments help or hinder depends on holding them loosely enough to let the situation reshape them, setting down the hammer and finding the screwdriver when the world resists.
- ch. 97 "Betrayed by Biases" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Applying Gadamer to Dudley, the chapter shows how Petunia and Vernon's doting ('no finer boy anywhere,' 'big-boned' rather than dieting, 'wouldn't hurt a fly') armor Dudley's prejudgments against every challenge. His close encounter with the dementors, forcing him to relive his worst moments, strips those rationalizations away so he finally sees himself as 'spoiled, pampered, bullying,' a radical readjustment that lets him recognize Harry's courage and feel gratitude and even affection.
- ch. 98 "Dangerous Dreams" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter generalizes the pattern across the series: Harry's anti-Snape prejudice, misplaced trust in the fake Mad-Eye Moody and the Half-Blood Prince's potions book, Dumbledore's 'for the greater good' dreams with Grindelwald, Merope Gaunt's love-potion fantasy of Tom Riddle, the locket Horcrux magnifying the trio's suspicions until Ron storms off, and the Malfoys' underestimation of Voldemort all show prejudgments misreading reality until the pain of banging into it forces a rethink. Truth matters, Garver concludes, because false beliefs are an unreliable map for navigating the world.
- ch. 99 "The Cost of Overconfidence" **·** Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter details Harry's overconfidence about his dream-connection to Voldemort's mind: cocky that he uniquely understands Voldemort, he dismisses Dumbledore's warning that the link runs both ways, neglects his Occlumency lessons out of distrust for Snape and irritation with Hermione, and never sees why the training matters. Snape's taunt, 'Maybe they make you feel special, important,' suggests Harry's prejudgment that his visions are a privileged window is also a temptation feeding his sense of mission.
- ch. 100 "Memories Help Make Meaning" **·** Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter traces the fatal cost of Harry's unchecked prejudgments: trusting his O.W.L. dream-vision of Sirius being tortured, twisting Dumbledore's Occlumency warnings into confirmation that his dreams are real, and accepting Kreacher's cackling, self-interested testimony at Grimmauld Place without telling his friends the source, Harry launches the Department of Mysteries 'rescue' that gets Sirius killed. Garver softens the verdict, a fifteen-year-old with noble intentions, but the lesson stands: we see what we want to see through blinders we do not know we wear.
- ch. 101 "Moving Past Misdirection" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Hans-Georg Gadamer — Augustine on Time; Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter joins Augustine's Confessions analysis of time, where only in human experience does memory of the past meet anticipation of the future in the present, to Gadamer's view of prejudgments as tradition, memory 'passed down' that shapes how we approach the present. The Pensieve symbolizes this double, personal and social memory: Dumbledore's third-person viewing spots patterns, and the extracted memories of Riddle's orphanage sadism and the reconstructed testimonies of Hokey and Morfin Gaunt give Harry the knowledge of Voldemort's history, character, and vulnerabilities he needs to defeat him.
- ch. 102 "NOTES" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); Virtue Ethics — The essay's conclusion shows reality correcting every character's prejudgments: Dumbledore's wizard-supremacy dreams die with his sister, Merope's with the end of the love potion, Ron's with distance from the Horcrux, the Malfoys' when Voldemort threatens Draco, and Harry matures from naive boy to cocky teen to discerning young man. Garver draws the thesis that epistemology is inseparable from ethics, bravery and loyalty require true belief about danger and about Dumbledore's real faults, and Rowling's narrative misdirection makes readers undergo the same correction, so that following Harry's transformation we become better people, with even Dudley's change giving hope to the most resistant reader.
- ch. 103 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 104 "Tell Me One Last Thing" *(front)*
- ch. 105 "What Is Real" *(front)*
- ch. 106 "Going Mental" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave — Opens the Just in Your Head? essay by taking Dumbledore's reply to Harry (of course it is happening inside your head, but why should that mean it is not real?) as a live metaphysical and epistemological question about appearance versus reality, noting that even A. J. Ayer dismissed his own near-death experience as hallucination. It retells Plato's cave allegory and reads Harry and Dumbledore's descent into the creepy cave in Half-Blood Prince, plus Harry's worry that the King's Cross dialogue was just a shadow on the wall, as a modern image of prisoners mistaking appearances for reality.
- ch. 107 "Rowling as an Inkling" **·** Plato, George Berkeley, René Descartes, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Theory of Forms; Transcendental Idealism — Argues Dumbledore's remark dissolves a false dilemma: the Hermione-as-idea versus Emma Watson contrast shows that existing in the head need not mean unreal. It then surveys thinkers who agree that mind and reality overlap: Plato's forms (the many broomsticks as imperfect copies of the ideal broomstick), Descartes on knowing essences by reason, Kant's mind-constructed objects, Berkeley's esse est percipi, Mill's phenomenalism, and Yogacara Buddhism's consciousness-fabricated emptiness, concluding that what is in the head can be genuinely real.
- ch. 108 "Harry’s Near-Death Experience" **·** Alvin Plantinga, Elizabeth Anscombe — Develops the essay's boldest suggestion: reading Rowling through C. S. Lewis and the Inklings, whose associate Barfield convinced Lewis that if thought were a purely subjective event, logical and moral claims to truth would collapse, the germ of Lewis's argument from reason later refined by Plantinga and contested by Anscombe. On this view our logic participates in a cosmic Logos, which Christians identify with Christ, a point the chapter ties to Rowling's remark that it was no coincidence Harry's fateful dialogue happened at King's Cross, so what occurs in the head can genuinely put us in touch with reality.
- ch. 109 "NOTES" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson — Immortality and the Soul; Philosophical Skepticism — Surveys near-death-experience research from Moody's Life after Life to Susan Blackmore's debunking explanations (oxygen starvation, cultural variation) and argues the skeptical conclusion does not follow: a child's vision of her living dog Sparky on the other side could still be a genuine divinely created revelation happening wholly inside her head. It reads Harry's King's Cross way-station the same way, since wizards can channel themselves through portraits, ghosts, and Legilimency, and closes with Emerson's Over-Soul claim that moments of faith deserve to be ascribed more reality than ordinary experience.
- ch. 110 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" **·** Personal Identity; The Extended Mind — Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.
- ch. 112 "The Hallows of the Mind" **·** René Descartes, Thomas Hobbes — Mind–Body Dualism — Uses Rowling's light-made-liquid description of the Pensieve's silvery contents to stage the materialism versus dualism debate: Hobbes-style materialists can treat ghosts like Nearly Headless Nick and the strands of thought clinging to wands or leaking from dying wizards as matter, while Cartesian dualists find support in Harry's fear at King's Cross that he might exist only as disembodied thought. Snape's remark that the mind is a complex and many-layered thing frames how little is settled about the mind-brain relation.
- ch. 113 "Confundus!" **·** Andy Clark, David Chalmers — The Extended Mind — Challenges the assumption that the mind stops at the skull by deploying Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis: just as a prosthetic leg, Moody's magic eye, or Harry's holly-and-phoenix-feather wand can count as part of the body, Otto's notebook shows external storage functioning as memory itself rather than a mere aid. Tom Riddle's diary, where a memory acts and thinks for itself because a soul fragment lived in it, and Snape's memories being his whether in his head, a phial, or the Pensieve make physical location incidental to mental ownership.
- ch. 114 "Mischief Managed" **·** Andy Clark, David Chalmers — The Extended Mind — Defends the Otto case against the obvious objection that notebook entries are not conscious beliefs: most beliefs, like Ron's that Ireland beat Bulgaria at the Quidditch World Cup, are nonoccurrent anyway, and Rita Skeeter pausing to recall where Bathilda Bagshot lives works exactly like Otto consulting his notebook. Constant integration is what separates genuine mind-extension from mere aids, which is why Harry's borrowed Half-Blood Prince textbook, Neville's password list, and even Hermione's well-thumbed Hogwarts, A History stay outside the mind.
- ch. 115 "Lumos!" **·** John Locke, Andy Clark, David Chalmers — Personal Identity (memory theory); The Extended Mind; Personal Identity — Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.
- ch. 116 "NOTES" **·** Personal Identity; The Extended Mind — Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.
- ch. 117 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 118 "The Good" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Dewey — Opens Gregory Bassham's audit of Hogwarts: from a kid's point of view the school is paradise, all magic and no math, but he asks what the great philosophers of education, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and Dewey, would make of teaching and learning there. The chapter will weigh Susan Engel's claim that Hogwarts is a model school against problems documented by contemporary educational research.
- ch. 119 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 120 "Unknown" **·** John Dewey — Experience and Education — Concedes Hogwarts succeeds at its one job, teaching magic, and explains how: effective lessons like Lupin teaching Harry to conjure a Patronus and Harry training Dumbledore's Army proceed apprenticeship-style through demonstration, practice, individualized coaching, and mastery. This hands-on learning by doing, not Professor Binns's droning lectures or Umbridge's theory-only textbook assignments, is why students actually acquire magical skill.
- ch. 121 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 122 "Unknown" **·** John Dewey — Experience and Education — Applies Dewey's demand that education be part of life rather than preparation for some remote future, together with Whitehead's critique of inert, undigested knowledge: Hogwarts students see the practical payoff of Apparition, Transfiguration, and Defense Against the Dark Arts, which makes them eager learners, while Hagrid's Blast-Ended Skrewts and Trelawney's bogus crystal-ball gazing are the inert exceptions that prove the rule.
- ch. 123 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 124 "Unknown" *(no index entry yet)* — Catalogues the school's hazards, giant spiders and hostile centaurs in the Forbidden Forest, grindylows and a giant squid, the Whomping Willow, potions gone awry, injury-prone Quidditch and the Triwizard Tournament, and children carrying lethal wands, to argue that if Hogwarts really existed its danger would be indefensible. Magical medicine fixes much, but as Dumbledore says, no magic can reawaken the dead.
- ch. 125 "Unknown" *(no index entry yet)* — Grades the faculty from the competent and caring (Dumbledore, McGonagall, Flitwick, Sprout, Lupin) through the flawed (Hagrid, the disguised Crouch, the bullying Snape) to the downright crummy (Binns, Trelawney, Lockhart, Umbridge), then locates the deeper cause: the wizarding world has no teacher education or certification, so anyone from Hagrid to a homicidal impostor can take a classroom, making poor instruction structural rather than accidental.
- ch. 126 "The Ugly" **·** Plato, Aristotle, John Dewey, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Immanuel Kant — Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Argues the ugliest defect is curricular: Hogwarts teaches only vocational magic, giving students the tools of power without the wisdom to use them, and so fails Adler's three aims of secondary schooling and the aims every major philosopher of education defended, Plato's wisdom and just society, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Locke's virtue and wisdom, Rousseau's natural education, Kantian character, and Deweyan growth. Even allowing that Dumbledore's office is a school of virtue outside class, most students never get his mentorship, leaving wizards ill-equipped for problems like anti-Muggle bigotry.
- ch. 127 "Like Bertie Bott’s Every-Flavor Beans, a Mix" **·** Totalitarianism — Names pureblood supremacism, Voldemort's Nazi-like movement whose victory would mean totalitarianism, thought control, secret police, mock trials, and racial cleansing, as the greatest problem wizards face, and faults Hogwarts education for ignoring it: no antiracist teaching despite rampant slurs, silence about the oppressed house-elves of Hogwarts, A History, and Slytherin left as a hothouse breeding Death Eaters and fifth columnists. Against Prinzi's gradualist defense of Dumbledore as a persuasive libertarian, the chapter presses the fair question of why he did not do more.
- ch. 128 "NOTES" *(notes)*
- ch. 129 "Unknown" *(notes)*
- ch. 130 "PART FIVE - BEYOND THE VEIL DEATH, HOPE, AND MEANING" *(front)*
- ch. 131 "Remorse and Death" **·** Forgiveness — Opens Charles Taliaferro's essay by reading Fawkes's burning and rebirth as a clue to a philosophical model of moral repair: the wrongdoer must confess, feel sincere remorse, repudiate the pleasure or gain of the wrongdoing, and form new intentions, a kind of death to the old self like Christian baptism, after which the repaired relationship is reborn and the friend is seen in a new light. It then sets up Voldemort as the perversion of this pattern, spreading death by clinging to life while Harry and Dumbledore move to deeper life by accepting death.
- ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" **·** Forgiveness; Immortality and the Soul — Sharpens the remorse-versus-regret contrast through Voldemort's cold regret after having Nagini kill Snape, and shows true remorse at work in Dumbledore's confession about the Resurrection Stone ring, his arranged death at Snape's hand, and his tearful self-disclosure to Harry at King's Cross. Harry too must die to be regenerated: letting Voldemort strike him destroys the Horcrux inside so that his soul becomes whole and completely his own, while lesser purgings, like his furious outburst at Ron and Hermione, and his love for Ginny complete the pattern of dying to the old self.
- ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" **·** Immortality and the Soul; Forgiveness — Completes the inversion: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes Voldemort's soul, and only excruciating remorse could put it back together, something he will never attempt, while his evil literally disembodies him until he lives parasitically on the blood and limbs of others. Against this, Hermione's gloss on the Potters' gravestone, the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, means the soul survives whatever happens to the body, grounding the contrast between Voldemort's pathetic, unmourned end and the honored deaths of Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, and Colin Creevey.
- ch. 134 "The Fantasy Objection" **·** Personal Identity; Forgiveness — Takes up the integrity objection advanced by the Freudian psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: renunciation cannot change the fact that it was you who did the wrong, so posing as an altogether new person invites self-deception, as with the reformed alcoholic who still calls himself an alcoholic. Taliaferro grants the regeneration model can be abused but argues renewal requires something very close to dying to the past, using Snape, unable to confess his love for Lily, still nursing resentment, honored only when Harry names his son Severus, as the tragedy of reform without full renunciation.
- ch. 135 "Fawkes’s Secret" **·** Forgiveness — Answers the fantasy objection, that ethics drawn from a world of spells and talking portraits is escapist make-believe, by noting that Rowling's moral insight does not depend on the magic: loyalty, friendship, romantic love, fairness, opposition to enslavement, free the house-elves, and the roles of remorse, forgiveness, and reform are values of our own Muggle world. In the name of realism, the objector merely fails to engage the imagination.
- ch. 136 "NOTES" **·** Forgiveness — Closes the essay by asking why Fawkes never cured Dumbledore's ring-curse or blocked Snape's killing curse, and answers that the phoenix may have left Hogwarts only because his work was done: rupture, betrayal, and vice are healed by a death and rebirth in which one rises from the flames of remorseful confession a new person, with radically new desires, ready to rejoin relationships and community.
- ch. 137 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 138 "Death and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 139 "The Approaching Battle" **·** Martin Heidegger, Plato, Epicurus — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Death Is Nothing to Us — Frames death as philosophy's ultimate question and contrasts the Epicurean advice to be unconcerned since death is simply the end of us with Heidegger's authenticity: boldly facing that death may come at any moment keeps us from living half-asleep, a view Plato anticipated by teaching that true philosophers make dying their profession. Harry, confronted with death from infancy, lives authentically, while Voldemort's flight from death marks him as the inauthentic case the essay traces through the Deathly Hallows death march.
- ch. 140 "King’s Cross Station" **·** Martin Heidegger — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity — Reads Harry's walk into the Forbidden Forest, knowing he must die so the fragment of Voldemort's soul dies with him, his senses sharpening and gratitude welling for everything he never fully valued, as Heideggerian coming to terms with mortality rather than morbid brooding. Colin Creevey, the underage wizard who sneaks back to fight and falls, is offered as a second example of authentic living that recognizes limitations and seizes opportunities regardless of belief in an afterlife.
- ch. 141 "Reap a Destiny" **·** Martin Heidegger — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Immortality and the Soul — Interprets the King's Cross scene through Heidegger's counsel to choose an exemplar from the past and dialogue with them: Dumbledore, freshly repentant for his youthful hunger for glory, plays exactly that role in a way-station likened to purgatory, while the flayed child-like creature under the chair is Voldemort's soul beyond help. The chapter closes by linking his fear-driven quest for deathlessness to Tolkien's One Ring, in which Sauron poured his own life-force, both fantasy dark lords undone by the desire for deathlessness.
- ch. 142 "NOTES" **·** William James, Aristotle, Martin Heidegger, John Locke, Immanuel Kant, Blaise Pascal — Immortality and the Soul; Personal Identity (memory theory); Virtue Ethics (arete); Free Will vs Determinism — Uses William James's marginal motto, sow a thought and reap a destiny, together with Aristotle's account of how repeated acts shape the soul, to argue that Voldemort's maimed afterlife-state is the cumulative result of freely chosen evil he can no longer muster remorse to undo. Setting Heidegger's atheism against Rowling's depicted afterlife, and adding Locke's character-and-memory identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the soul's immortality must concern us, it concludes that if Rowling is right, every choice here is infinitely consequential.
- ch. 143 "Unknown" *(front)*
- ch. 144 "Fulfillment for Muggles and Wizards" *(front)*
- ch. 145 "Voldemort and the Sophists" **·** Socrates, Plato — Justice in the Republic — Opens the comparison of Harry's willingness to die in Deathly Hallows with Socrates' death for his convictions, placing both inside ethics, the inquiry into how we ought to live and what kind of people we ought to be. It presents the challenge of why be moral at all and introduces Plato's Republic answer, endorsed by Socrates, that being moral is necessary and sufficient for true happiness, noting that Socrates, like Harry against Voldemort, had enemies of his own.
- ch. 146 "The Common Good versus the Greater Good" **·** Plato, Socrates — Justice in the Republic; Tripartite Soul; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Casts the Harry-Voldemort conflict as Socrates versus the Sophists: Thrasymachus's Republic claim that the unjust always come out ahead describes Voldemort's exploitation of his followers' trust exactly. The flayed child under the chair at King's Cross enacts Plato's afterlife justice, and the Republic's tripartite soul and cardinal virtues explain why Harry's reason-ruled courage, wisdom, and justice make the moral life the rational choice, as rational as choosing bodily health over chronic illness.
- ch. 147 "Two Keys to the Good Life" **·** Utilitarianism — Contrasts the greater good, young Dumbledore and Grindelwald's For the Greater Good scheme to subjugate Muggles, under which the rights, dignity, and integrity of individuals are up for grabs whenever the majority benefits, with the common good, where sacrifice serves all, as in the civil rights movement's appeal to the good of the whole American community. Harry's choice to return from King's Cross and finish Voldemort defeats the greater-good revolution and realizes the common good of Muggles and wizards alike.
- ch. 148 "The End of the Story" **·** Socrates, Aristotle, Plato — The Unexamined Life; The Meaning of Life — Completes the parallel: Socrates died refusing to abandon the examined life, and his martyrdom, like Dumbledore's staged death that protected Snape's spying, served the common good, since there can be no common good without individual goodness. The chapter closes with two Muggle lessons, live devoted to something larger than yourself as Lily Potter, Dumbledore, Harry, King, Gandhi, Jesus, and Socrates did, and find mentors, as Harry found Dumbledore and as readers can find in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics or Confucius.
